shelves.title: BPH combination therapy: an alpha-blocker plus a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor beats either drug alone
shelves.question: In men with benign prostatic hyperplasia at risk of progression, does combination therapy (alpha-blocker plus 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor) prevent clinical progression, retention and surgery better than either drug alone?
shelves.mesh: Prostatic Hyperplasia · Drug Therapy, Combination · Doxazosin · Finasteride · Dutasteride · Tamsulosin · Disease Progression · Urinary Retention · Humans · Male · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: Two large, long, double-blind trials answer this the same way. In MTOPS (3,047 men, mean follow-up 4.5 years), overall clinical progression fell 39% relative on doxazosin and 34% relative on finasteride versus placebo, and 66% relative on the combination — significantly more than either drug alone; retention and invasive therapy fell on finasteride-containing arms, not on doxazosin alone. In CombAT (4,844 men with prostate volume ≥30 cm³), dutasteride plus tamsulosin beat tamsulosin on acute retention or BPH surgery over 4 years and beat both monotherapies on clinical progression and symptoms. The finasteride-alone anchor (PLESS, 3,040 men) shows where the retention/surgery benefit comes from: surgery 10% placebo vs 5% finasteride, retention 7% vs 3% over four years. The fence is selection: these were men with larger prostates and progression risk — the combination buys little for a small prostate or pure symptom relief, and it buys the side effects of both classes. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: MTOPS (McConnell 2003, NEJM): combination cut overall BPH progression by 66% relative — more than doxazosin (39% relative) or finasteride (34% relative) alone
cards.summary: 3,047 men randomised double-blind to placebo, doxazosin, finasteride or both, mean follow-up 4.5 years. Overall clinical progression (symptom-score rise ≥4 points, acute urinary retention, incontinence, renal insufficiency, or recurrent UTI) was significantly reduced by doxazosin (39% relative risk reduction, P<0.001) and finasteride (34% relative, P=0.002) versus placebo, and by 66% relative on combination therapy — significantly greater than either drug alone (P<0.001 for both comparisons). Retention and need for invasive therapy fell on combination and finasteride, not doxazosin. Symptom scores improved on all three active arms, combination superior to both.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (MTOPS), N Engl J Med 2003. The record's databank carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: 3,047 men with benign prostatic hyperplasia randomised to placebo, doxazosin, finasteride or combination therapy; mean follow-up 4.5 years. All participants were men; the record's abstract does not print a mean age.
cards.result: Risk of overall clinical progression versus placebo: doxazosin 39% relative reduction (P<0.001), finasteride 34% relative (P=0.002), combination 66% relative (P<0.001), combination significantly better than either monotherapy. Risks of acute urinary retention and need for invasive therapy were significantly reduced by combination therapy (P<0.001) and finasteride (P<0.001) but not by doxazosin.
cards.watchOut: A progression composite driven largely by symptom-score rises; the hard ends (retention, surgery) moved only on the finasteride-containing arms. Doxazosin is the alpha-blocker tested — CombAT (Reference 2) is the tamsulosin/dutasteride confirmation, not a repeat of this trial.
cards.source: McConnell JD et al. The long-term effect of doxazosin, finasteride, and combination therapy on the clinical progression of benign prostatic hyperplasia. N Engl J Med. 2003;349(25):2387-98. PMID 14681504

cards.headline: CombAT (Roehrborn 2010, Eur Urol): dutasteride + tamsulosin beat tamsulosin on retention/surgery over 4 years, and both monotherapies on progression
cards.summary: 4,844 men ≥50 years with symptomatic BPH, IPSS ≥12, prostate volume ≥30 cm³, PSA 1.5–10 ng/mL, randomised double-blind to dutasteride 0.5 mg, tamsulosin 0.4 mg or both for 4 years. Combination was significantly superior to tamsulosin (but not to dutasteride) on the primary endpoint of acute urinary retention or BPH-related surgery, and superior to both monotherapies on clinical progression, symptoms and flow rate. Cardiac-failure composite terms were imbalanced between arms, flagged by the authors.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, parallel-group trial (CombAT), Eur Urol 2010. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT00090103.
cards.people: 4,844 men aged ≥50 years with moderate-to-severe lower urinary tract symptoms due to BPH and prostatic enlargement (volume ≥30 cm³), recruited in the Americas and Europe. All participants were men; the record's abstract does not print a mean age.
cards.result: At 4 years, combination therapy significantly reduced the relative risk of acute urinary retention or BPH-related surgery versus tamsulosin monotherapy, but not versus dutasteride monotherapy; it significantly reduced the relative risk of BPH clinical progression versus both monotherapies and gave significantly greater symptom benefit than either monotherapy at 4 years. The record's abstract does not print the event counts or the percentage relative reductions for the primary endpoint, and none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: No placebo arm — CombAT cannot say how much of the benefit is drug versus natural history; MTOPS (Reference 1) carries the placebo comparison. Entry required an enlarged prostate (≥30 cm³): the result does not extend to men with small prostates, where a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor has little to shrink.
cards.source: Roehrborn CG et al. The effects of combination therapy with dutasteride and tamsulosin on clinical outcomes in men with symptomatic benign prostatic hyperplasia: 4-year results from the CombAT study. Eur Urol. 2010;57(1):123-31. PMID 19825505 · NCT00090103

cards.headline: PLESS (McConnell 1998, NEJM): finasteride alone halved surgery and retention over 4 years — the source of the combination's hard-outcome benefit
cards.summary: 3,040 men with moderate-to-severe symptoms and enlarged prostates randomised double-blind to finasteride 5 mg or placebo for 4 years. Surgery for BPH: 152 of 1,503 (10%) on placebo vs 69 of 1,513 (5%) on finasteride — a 55% relative risk reduction [95% CI 41–65], about 5 percentage points absolute. Acute urinary retention: 99 (7%) vs 42 (3%) — a 57% relative reduction [95% CI 40–69]. Symptom scores and flow rates improved and prostate volume fell on finasteride.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Finasteride Long-Term Efficacy and Safety Study, PLESS), N Engl J Med 1998. Pre-registration-era trial: the record carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: 3,040 men with moderate-to-severe urinary symptoms and enlarged prostate glands; outcome data complete for 2,760. All participants were men; the record's abstract does not print a mean age.
cards.result: Over 4 years: BPH surgery 10% (152/1,503) on placebo vs 5% (69/1,513) on finasteride (55% relative risk reduction, 95% CI 41 to 65); acute urinary retention 7% (99 men) vs 3% (42 men) (57% relative reduction, 95% CI 40 to 69). Mean symptom-score decrease 3.3 points on finasteride vs 1.3 on placebo (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Finasteride alone, in enlarged prostates, over years — the benefit is slow and anatomical, not a quick symptom fix; that is exactly why MTOPS and CombAT pair it with an alpha-blocker. Sexual side effects of 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors are fenced on Shelf #218 and in the PCPT record on Shelf #490.
cards.source: McConnell JD et al. The effect of finasteride on the risk of acute urinary retention and the need for surgical treatment among men with benign prostatic hyperplasia. N Engl J Med. 1998;338(9):557-63. PMID 9475762

cards.headline: Synthesis: two combination trials, one direction — progression, retention and surgery all favour the pair in enlarged prostates
cards.summary: Synthesis of Cards 1–3. MTOPS (doxazosin + finasteride, placebo-controlled) and CombAT (dutasteride + tamsulosin, no placebo) agree: combination therapy reduces clinical progression more than either drug alone, and the retention/surgery benefit tracks the 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor (PLESS). What the record does not establish: benefit in men with small prostates, any mortality effect (none was tested as an endpoint), or that one alpha-blocker or one 5-ARI is superior to the other — no head-to-head of combinations exists in these cards.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study; reads Cards 1–3 together.
cards.people: 7,891 men randomised in MTOPS and CombAT, plus 3,040 in PLESS; all men, mostly with enlarged prostates and moderate-to-severe symptoms.
cards.result: Combination relative reduction in overall clinical progression 66% versus placebo (MTOPS); retention/surgery benefit confirmed against tamsulosin at 4 years (CombAT); finasteride alone cut surgery from 10% to 5% and retention from 7% to 3% over 4 years (PLESS).
cards.watchOut: Quote the population with the result: men with enlarged prostates at risk of progression. Extrapolating the combination's benefit to every man with urinary symptoms overstates what these trials enrolled.
cards.source: Synthesis of PMID 14681504, PMID 19825505 and PMID 9475762 on this shelf; no additional source.

shelves.title: Desmopressin for nocturia: fewer night voids by a fraction, bought against hyponatremia
shelves.question: Does low-dose desmopressin reduce nocturnal voiding in adults with nocturia, and at what hyponatremia cost?
shelves.mesh: Nocturia · Deamino Arginine Vasopressin · Antidiuretic Agents · Hyponatremia · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Humans · Male · Female · Polyuria
shelves.balance: Low-dose desmopressin orally disintegrating tablet works a little, measurably, in both sexes — and its risk is the kind that has to be managed, not merely disclosed. In men (Weiss 2013, 385 patients), 50 µg and 75 µg cut nocturnal voids by 0.37 and 0.41 more than placebo and doubled the odds of a ≥33% response (OR 1.98 and 2.04), delaying the first void by about 40 minutes. In women (Sand 2013, 261 patients), 25 µg cut voids by 0.22 versus placebo (P=0.028), raised ≥33%-responder odds (OR 1.85), and delayed the first void by 49 minutes. Sodium is the fence: in the men's trial, sodium <130 mmol/L occurred in 2 men on 50 µg but 9 on 75 µg; the pooled hyponatremia analysis (Juul 2017) shows risk rises with dose, age, low baseline sodium and reduced kidney function, and that sex-specific minimum dosing (25 µg women, 50 µg men) plus baseline and early sodium monitoring would have screened out every clinically significant case in the trial data. Fractions of a void a night, in exchange for a monitoring obligation. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: Weiss 2013 (J Urol): desmopressin 50/75 µg in men — 0.37–0.41 fewer voids than placebo, first void delayed ~40 minutes; sodium <130 in 2 men on 50 µg vs 9 on 75 µg
cards.summary: 3-month randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of desmopressin orally disintegrating tablet 50 µg or 75 µg in 385 men with nocturia (≥2 nocturnal voids). Both doses significantly reduced nocturnal voids versus placebo (−0.37, P<0.0001; −0.41, P=0.0003) and increased the odds of a ≥33% reduction in voids (OR 1.98, P=0.0009; OR 2.04, P=0.0004). Time to first void rose by about 40 minutes versus placebo. Response appeared by week 1 and was sustained; quality-of-life and sleep measures improved significantly.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial, J Urol 2013. The record's databank carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: Full analysis set 385 men with nocturia, age range 20–87 years. The record's abstract does not print a mean age.
cards.result: Change in nocturnal voids versus placebo: −0.37 (50 µg, P<0.0001) and −0.41 (75 µg, P=0.0003). ≥33% responder odds ratios 1.98 (P=0.0009) and 2.04 (P=0.0004). Time to first void increased ~40 minutes versus placebo (P=0.006 and P=0.003). Serum sodium <130 mmol/L: 2 subjects (ages 74 and 79) on 50 µg vs 9 subjects on 75 µg.
cards.watchOut: The benefit is a third of a void a night; the harm gradient is dose-visible within this single trial (2 vs 9 hyponatremic men between 50 and 75 µg). The authors' 'minimum effective dose' framing is the safety message: 50 µg in men, with sodium monitoring per Card 3.
cards.source: Weiss JP et al. Efficacy and safety of low dose desmopressin orally disintegrating tablet in men with nocturia: results of a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo controlled, parallel group study. J Urol. 2013;190(3):965-72. PMID 23454402

cards.headline: Sand 2013 (J Urol): desmopressin 25 µg in women — 0.22 fewer voids than placebo (P=0.028), responder OR 1.85, first void delayed 49 minutes
cards.summary: 3-month randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of desmopressin orally disintegrating tablet 25 µg in 261 women with nocturia (≥2 nocturnal voids). Desmopressin significantly reduced mean nocturnal voids (−0.22, P=0.028) and increased ≥33%-responder odds (OR 1.85, P=0.006) versus placebo; time to first nocturnal void increased by 49 minutes (P=0.003). Response by week 1, sustained; quality of life and sleep quality improved significantly. Sodium stayed above 125 mmol/L throughout; 3 transient decreases below 130 mmol/L were recorded.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial, J Urol 2013. The record's databank carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: Full analysis set 261 women with nocturia, age range 19–87 years. The record's abstract does not print a mean age.
cards.result: Change in nocturnal voids versus placebo: −0.22 (P=0.028). ≥33% responder odds ratio 1.85 (P=0.006). Time to first nocturnal void +49 minutes versus placebo (P=0.003). Three transient serum-sodium decreases to <130 mmol/L; none below 125 mmol/L.
cards.watchOut: The women's dose (25 µg) is half the men's minimum — sex-specific dosing is a safety feature of this drug, not a detail. Effect size is again a fraction of a void; the responder analysis (OR 1.85, a relative measure) should be read beside the −0.22 absolute difference, as printed.

cards.headline: Juul 2017 (BJU Int): hyponatremia risk is dose-, age-, sodium- and kidney-function-driven — minimum sex-specific dosing plus monitoring screened out every significant case in the trial data
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of three desmopressin nocturia trials (orally disintegrating tablet, 10–100 µg) examining predictors of serum sodium <130 mmol/L. Dose, age, baseline serum sodium and estimated GFR were significant risk factors in both sexes. With minimum effective gender-specific dosing (25 µg women, 50 µg men), baseline sodium ≥135 mmol/L, and repeat monitoring at week 1 and month 1 for patients ≥65 years or on hyponatremia-associated medication, retrospective application showed only mild, non-clinically-significant hyponatremia remained; the proposed scheme would have omitted all patients who developed clinically significant hyponatremia from further treatment.
cards.type: Pooled meta-analysis of three randomised trials, BJU Int 2017. The record's databank carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: Participants of three clinical trials of desmopressin ODT for nocturia, men and women, doses 10–100 µg. The record's abstract does not print the pooled N, mean age or sex breakdown, and none are printed here.
cards.result: Significant predictors of hyponatremia: dose, age, baseline serum sodium and eGFR in both sexes (plus arthritis and bone-disease drugs in men; raised monocytes and absence of lipid-modifying drugs in women). Retrospective application of the minimum-dose-plus-monitoring scheme: no clinically significant hyponatremia would have occurred among patients kept on treatment.
cards.watchOut: A retrospective application of a monitoring scheme to the trials that generated it is a plausibility demonstration, not prospective validation — the card reports the authors' finding in those terms. The actionable content (check sodium first, recheck early in older patients) stands on the risk-factor analysis.
cards.source: Juul KV et al. Low-dose desmopressin combined with serum sodium monitoring can prevent clinically significant hyponatraemia in patients treated for nocturia. BJU Int. 2017;119(5):776-784. PMID 27862898

cards.headline: Synthesis: a real, small, dose-priced benefit — prescribe the minimum sex-specific dose with sodium checks, or not at all
cards.summary: Synthesis of Cards 1–3. Efficacy: −0.22 to −0.41 voids per night versus placebo across the two pivotal trials, responder odds ratios 1.85–2.04 (relative), first void delayed 40–49 minutes. Harm: hyponatremia, dose-graded within the men's trial and predictable from age, baseline sodium and kidney function in the pooled analysis. The trials enrolled nocturia broadly; the later nocturnal-polyuria subgroup literature (e.g., PMID 30470646) suggests larger benefit where nocturnal polyuria is the mechanism, but that is a post hoc pooled analysis and is referenced here, not carded.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study; reads Cards 1–3 together.
cards.people: 385 men and 261 women in the pivotal trials; three trials pooled for the safety analysis (pooled N not printed in its record).
cards.result: Voids versus placebo: −0.37/−0.41 (men, 50/75 µg), −0.22 (women, 25 µg). Sodium <130 mmol/L: 2 vs 9 men at 50 vs 75 µg; 3 transient cases in the women's trial, none <125 mmol/L.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the responder odds ratios without the absolute void differences beside them; and do not start this drug in an older patient without a baseline sodium — the trials' own safety data are the fence.
cards.source: Synthesis of PMID 23454402, PMID 23454404 and PMID 27862898 on this shelf; no additional source.

shelves.title: MRI before prostate biopsy: the PRECISION pathway
shelves.question: Does an MRI-first pathway (biopsy only if MRI is suspicious, targeted cores) detect more significant cancer with fewer biopsies than systematic TRUS biopsy (PRECISION; PROMIS as the accuracy anchor)?
shelves.mesh: Biopsy/adverse effects,methods · Intention to Treat Analysis · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Prostate/diagnostic imaging,pathology · Prostatic Neoplasms/diagnostic imaging,pathology · Quality Control · Risk Assessment
shelves.balance: LIKELY: The randomised PRECISION trial (500 biopsy-naïve men) found an MRI-first pathway — biopsy only if MRI is suspicious, targeted cores only — detected more clinically significant cancer than standard TRUS biopsy (38% vs 26%; adjusted difference 12 percentage points, 95% CI 4-20) and less clinically insignificant cancer (adjusted difference -13 points, -19 to -7), while 28% of the MRI group avoided biopsy altogether. The paired accuracy study PROMIS (576 men, all receiving MRI, TRUS biopsy and template mapping biopsy) explains why: MRI sensitivity for clinically significant cancer was 93% vs 48% for TRUS biopsy, at lower specificity (41% vs 96%). Detection endpoints only — no mortality claim. Whether to test at all (PSA screening) is home on Shelf #212.

cards.headline: Kasivisvanathan 2018 (PRECISION): MRI-first detected more significant cancer (38% vs 26%) and less insignificant cancer, and 28% of men avoided biopsy
cards.summary: Kasivisvanathan 2018 (PRECISION): MRI-first detected more significant cancer ( 38% vs 26% ) and less insignificant cancer, and 28% of men avoided biopsy.
cards.people: 500 men with a clinical suspicion of prostate cancer who had not undergone biopsy previously, assigned to MRI with or without targeted biopsy (252) or standard transrectal ultrasonography-guided biopsy (248); the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: In the MRI-targeted biopsy group, 71 of 252 men (28%) had MRI results that were not suggestive of prostate cancer, so they did not undergo biopsy. Clinically significant cancer was detected in 95 men (38%) in the MRI-targeted biopsy group, as compared with 64 of 248 (26%) in the standard-biopsy group (adjusted difference, 12 percentage points; 95% CI 4 to 20; P=0.005). MRI, with or without targeted biopsy, was noninferior to standard biopsy, and the 95% confidence interval indicated superiority of this strategy. Fewer men in the MRI-targeted biopsy group received a diagnosis of clinically insignificant cancer (adjusted difference, -13 percentage points; 95% CI -19 to -7; P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Expert-centre MRI quality and reporting are part of the intervention; the trial measures detection, not treatment outcomes or mortality, and men whose MRI was not suggestive were not biopsied, so significant cancers missed in that group are inferred, not counted.
cards.source: Kasivisvanathan V et al. MRI-Targeted or Standard Biopsy for Prostate-Cancer Diagnosis. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(19):1767-1777. PMID: 29552975. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02380027, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Ahmed 2017 (PROMIS): against template mapping biopsy, MRI was far more sensitive than TRUS biopsy (93% vs 48%) but less specific (41% vs 96%)
cards.summary: Ahmed 2017 (PROMIS): against template mapping biopsy, MRI was far more sensitive than TRUS biopsy (93% vs 48%) but less specific (41% vs 96%).
cards.type: Multicentre, paired-cohort, confirmatory diagnostic accuracy study
cards.people: 576 men (740 enrolled) with prostate-specific antigen concentrations up to 15 ng/mL and no previous biopsy, who underwent 1.5 Tesla multiparametric MRI followed by both TRUS biopsy and template prostate mapping biopsy, each test conducted and reported blind to the others; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: On template mapping biopsy, 408 (71%) of 576 men had cancer, with 230 (40%) clinically significant (Gleason score 4+3 or higher, or maximum cancer core length 6 mm or longer). For clinically significant cancer, multiparametric MRI was more sensitive (93%, 95% CI 88-96) than TRUS biopsy (48%, 42-55; p<0.0001) and less specific (41%, 36-46, vs 96%, 94-98; p<0.0001). Using MRI to triage men might allow 27% of patients to avoid a primary biopsy and diagnosis of 5% fewer clinically insignificant cancers; if subsequent TRUS biopsies were directed by MRI findings, up to 18% more cases of clinically significant cancer might be detected. 44 (5.9%) of 740 patients reported serious adverse events, including 8 cases of sepsis.
cards.watchOut: A paired accuracy study against an intensive reference standard (template mapping biopsy), not a randomised management trial — its management consequences are modelled in its conclusions, and its serious adverse events largely reflect undergoing three procedures.
cards.source: Ahmed HU et al. Diagnostic accuracy of multi-parametric MRI and TRUS biopsy in prostate cancer (PROMIS): a paired validating confirmatory study. Lancet. 2017;389(10071):815-822. PMID: 28110982. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01292291, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Minimally invasive BPH therapy: prostatic urethral lift and water-vapour therapy against sham
shelves.question: Do office-based minimally invasive therapies relieve benign prostatic hyperplasia symptoms versus sham while preserving sexual function — prostatic urethral lift in the L.I.F.T. study, and water-vapour (Rezūm) therapy in its sham-controlled trial with five-year follow-up?
shelves.mesh: Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms/etiology,surgery · Prostatic Hyperplasia/complications · Suburethral Slings · Cross-Over Studies · Erectile Dysfunction/epidemiology,etiology · Hyperthermia, Induced/adverse effects,methods,statistics & numerical data · Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms/diagnosis,etiology,therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two separate sham-controlled randomised trials, of two different office-based therapies, both beat sham on prostate symptoms and flow and both preserved sexual function — the urethral lift in L.I.F.T. (206 men, symptom-score reduction 11.1 vs 5.9 points at 3 months, sustained to 12 months) and water-vapour therapy in the Rezūm trial (197 men, symptom score reduced 48% at 5 years, surgical re-treatment 4.4%). Two blinded sham-controlled trials pointing the same way carry LIKELY. The claim is symptom and flow relief with sexual-function preservation, not prostate-volume reduction or a comparison with resection — #911 covers embolization against TURP and Shelf #482 covers combination drug therapy, and neither is re-carded here.

cards.headline: L.I.F.T. 2013: prostatic urethral lift beat sham on symptoms at 3 months (AUASI reduction 11.1 vs 5.9 points) and held the gain to 12 months, with no de novo sexual dysfunction
cards.summary: L.I.F.T. (2013): prostatic urethral lift beat sham on symptoms at 3 months (AUASI reduction 11.1 vs 5.9 points ) and held the gain to 12 months.
cards.people: 206 men aged at least 50 years with AUASI (American Urological Association Symptom Index) 13 or greater, maximum flow rate 12 ml per second or less and prostate volume 30 to 80 cc, randomised 2:1 to prostatic urethral lift (140) or sham rigid cystoscopy (66); the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The lift and sham AUASI reductions at 3 months were 11.1 ± 7.67 and 5.9 ± 7.66 points respectively (p=0.003), meeting the primary endpoint. In the lift arm AUASI fell from 22.1 at baseline to 11.0 at 3 months and 11.1 at 12 months (p<0.001), and peak flow increased 4.4 ml per second at 3 months, sustained at 4.0 ml per second at 12 months (p<0.001). Adverse events were typically mild and transient, and there was no occurrence of de novo ejaculatory or erectile dysfunction.
cards.watchOut: Sham control lasted 3 months; beyond that the comparison is the lift arm against its own baseline. The sham response itself was large (5.9 points), so the attributable device effect is the roughly 5-point gap, not the full 11-point fall.

shelves.title: Prostatic artery embolization vs TURP for benign prostatic hyperplasia
shelves.question: Does prostatic artery embolization match transurethral resection of the prostate on symptom relief in benign prostatic hyperplasia — and what is the trade in functional outcomes, adverse events and reintervention (the Abt randomised non-inferiority trial, with the UK-ROPE comparison alongside)?
shelves.mesh: Embolization, Therapeutic/methods · Prostate/blood supply,surgery · Prostatic Hyperplasia/surgery,therapy · Embolization, Therapeutic/adverse effects,methods,psychology · Hemospermia/etiology · Length of Stay/statistics & numerical data · Postoperative Pain/etiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In the one randomised trial (Abt 2018, 103 patients), embolization's symptom improvement at 12 weeks was close to resection's (IPSS reduction 9.23 vs 10.77 points) but non-inferiority was formally NOT shown (difference 1.54 points, 95% CI −1.45 to 4.52; p=0.17 for non-inferiority), and TURP was clearly better on flow, residual urine, prostate-volume reduction and desobstruction, while embolization caused fewer adverse events (36 vs 70). The UK-ROPE comparison pinned at build is observational and propensity-matched, not randomised as drafted, and it agrees: median symptom improvement 10 points after embolization vs 15 after TURP, with no evidence of non-inferiority, and a 20% reoperation rate. One randomised trial plus a concordant observational comparison caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Abt 2018: embolization's symptom relief was close to TURP's at 12 weeks, but non-inferiority was not shown — and TURP won every functional measure while embolization had fewer adverse events (36 vs 70)
cards.summary: Embolization vs TURP (2018): symptom relief was close at 12 weeks (IPSS reduction 9.23 vs 10.77 points ), but non-inferiority was not shown — and TURP won every functional measure.
cards.people: 103 patients aged 40 years or older with refractory lower urinary tract symptoms secondary to benign prostatic hyperplasia, randomised at a Swiss tertiary centre; 48 (embolization) and 51 (TURP) reached the primary endpoint at 12 weeks; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Mean IPSS reduction at 12 weeks was −9.23 points after embolization and −10.77 after TURP; the difference of 1.54 points in favour of TURP (95% CI −1.45 to 4.52) was within the 3-point margin numerically, but non-inferiority could not be shown (P=0.17), and IPSS did not differ significantly on superiority testing (P=0.31). At 12 weeks embolization was less effective than TURP on maximum flow (change 5.19 vs 15.34 mL/s; difference −10.15, −14.67 to −5.63; P<0.001), postvoid residual (−86.36 vs −199.98 mL; P=0.003), prostate volume (−12.17 vs −30.27 mL; P<0.001) and desobstructive effectiveness (56% vs 93% shifted to a less obstructive category; P=0.003). Fewer adverse events occurred after embolization than TURP (36 vs 70 events; P=0.003).
cards.watchOut: Single centre, open label, 12-week primary endpoint and about 100 patients: this trial can show the two are close on symptoms, not that they are equivalent over the years when reintervention accrues. The trialists themselves said longer comparative follow-up is needed before embolization is routine.
cards.source: Abt D et al. Comparison of prostatic artery embolisation (PAE) versus transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) for benign prostatic hyperplasia: randomised, open label, non-inferiority trial. BMJ. 2018 Jun 19;361:k2338. PMID: 29921613. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02054013, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: UK-ROPE (Ray 2018): in a prospective registry with propensity matching — not a randomised trial — embolization improved symptoms by a median 10 IPSS points vs 15 for TURP, with a 20% reoperation rate
cards.summary: UK-ROPE (2018): in a prospective registry with propensity matching — not a randomised trial — embolization improved symptoms by a median 10 IPSS points vs 15 for TURP.
cards.type: Prospective observational registry study with propensity-matched comparison (NOT randomised)
cards.people: 305 patients recruited across 17 UK centres: 216 underwent prostatic artery embolization and 89 underwent TURP; 65 closely matched pairs were formed for the propensity comparison; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Embolization produced a median 10-point IPSS improvement from baseline at 12 months; TURP produced a median 15-point improvement. In the propensity-matched pairs there was no evidence of embolization being non-inferior to TURP on IPSS or quality of life. Embolization had a reoperation rate of 5% before 12 months and 15% after 12 months (20% total) and a low complication rate: of 216 patients, one had sepsis, one required transfusion, four had local arterial dissection, four had a groin haematoma, and two had non-target embolization presenting as self-limiting penile ulcers. 71% of embolization cases were outpatient or day cases, whereas 80% of TURP cases required at least one night in hospital.
cards.watchOut: Observational and propensity-matched: men referred for embolization differ from men referred for resection in ways matching cannot fully remove, so this card supports the randomised trial's direction but cannot carry a comparative claim on its own. The topic draft described UK-ROPE as a randomised comparison; its own record shows it is an observational registry study, and it is carded as such.

cards.headline: Synthesis: close on symptoms, behind on function, gentler up front — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Close on symptoms, behind on function, gentler up front — POSSIBLE. UK-ROPE is observational and is labelled as such on its card.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Abt 2018 (103 randomised patients, 12 weeks) and UK-ROPE (305 registry patients, 216 embolization / 89 TURP, 65 matched pairs, 12 months).
cards.result: The randomised and observational evidence agree on the shape of the trade: embolization relieves symptoms nearly as much as TURP in the short term (IPSS reductions 9.23 vs 10.77 points in Abt; median 10 vs 15 points in UK-ROPE), is objectively weaker on flow, emptying and prostate shrinkage, causes fewer early adverse events, is usually a day case — and carries a reoperation tail (20% by beyond 12 months in UK-ROPE) that a 12-week trial cannot see. Non-inferiority was not formally shown in either source, which is why the shelf does not print it. Office-based minimally invasive therapies against sham are Shelf #910; neither is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Radiation and contrast exposure, named in the drafted question, are not quantified in either carded abstract; no figure for them is printed on this shelf.

shelves.title: Refractory overactive bladder: bladder botulinum toxin vs sacral neuromodulation (ROSETTA)
shelves.question: In women with refractory urgency incontinence, does onabotulinumtoxinA bladder injection beat sacral neuromodulation on leakage episodes — and what does each cost in urinary infection, retention and revision (ROSETTA), read against the botulinum toxin pivotal placebo trial?
shelves.mesh: Acetylcholine Release Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Botulinum Toxins, Type A/therapeutic use · Injections, Intramuscular · Lumbosacral Plexus · Patient Selection · Transcutaneous Electric Nerve Stimulation/adverse effects,methods · Urinary Incontinence, Urge/therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Botulinum toxin's efficacy is anchored twice — against placebo in the phase 3 Nitti trial (557 patients; incontinence episodes −2.65 vs −0.87 per day, 22.9% vs 6.5% completely continent) and head-to-head in ROSETTA (381 women), where it reduced urgency incontinence episodes slightly more than sacral neuromodulation (−3.9 vs −3.3 per day; difference 0.63, 95% CI 0.13 to 1.14) — a small edge the ROSETTA authors themselves call of uncertain clinical importance, bought with more urinary infections (35% vs 11%) and transient self-catheterisation (8% at 1 month), against 3% device revision/removal for neuromodulation. Two randomised trials, one placebo-controlled and blinded, carry LIKELY for efficacy; the choice between the two procedures remains a harms-and-preference trade, not a rout.

cards.headline: ROSETTA 2016: botulinum toxin beat sacral neuromodulation by 0.63 urgency-incontinence episodes per day — statistically significant, clinically uncertain — with urinary infections in 35% vs 11%
cards.summary: ROSETTA (2016): botulinum toxin beat sacral neuromodulation by 0.63 urgency-incontinence episodes per day — statistically significant, clinically small.
cards.people: 381 women with refractory urgency urinary incontinence randomised at 9 US centres to cystoscopic intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA 200 U (192) or sacral neuromodulation (189); the intention-to-treat population was 364 women, mean (SD) age 63.0 (11.6) years.
cards.result: Over 6 months, onabotulinumtoxinA reduced daily urgency incontinence episodes more than neuromodulation (−3.9 vs −3.3 episodes per day; mean difference 0.63; 95% CI 0.13 to 1.14; P=.01), with greater improvement in symptom bother (−46.7 vs −38.6 on the Overactive Bladder Questionnaire Short Form; P=.002), treatment satisfaction and endorsement. Urinary tract infections were more frequent with onabotulinumtoxinA (35% vs 11%; risk difference −23%; 95% CI −33% to −13%; P<.001). Self-catheterisation was needed by 8% at 1 month and 2% at 6 months in the onabotulinumtoxinA group; neuromodulation device revisions and removals occurred in 3%. The authors conclude the small daily improvement is of uncertain clinical importance.
cards.watchOut: Open-label (the procedures cannot be blinded), 200 U dose — higher than the 100 U licensed dose tested in the pivotal trial below — and a 6-month horizon that cannot capture repeat-injection cycles or long-term device revisions.

PMID: 27701661. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the MEDLINE record carries no databank registry entry.

cards.summary: OnabotulinumtoxinA vs placebo (2013): incontinence episodes −2.65 vs −0.87 per day ; 22.9% vs 6.5% became completely continent.
cards.people: 557 patients with overactive bladder and urinary incontinence inadequately managed with anticholinergics, with 3 or more urgency incontinence episodes in 3 days and 8 or more micturitions per day, randomised 1:1 to intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA 100 U or placebo; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: OnabotulinumtoxinA significantly decreased daily urinary incontinence episodes versus placebo (−2.65 vs −0.87, p<0.001), and 22.9% vs 6.5% of patients became completely continent. shelves.title: Ureteric stones: shockwave lithotripsy vs ureteroscopy (TISU)
shelves.question: For adults with a ureteric stone needing intervention, is shockwave lithotripsy non-inferior to ureteroscopic treatment on stone clearance without further intervention — the TISU trial, against the earlier distal-stone randomised comparison?
shelves.mesh: Kidney Calculi · Lithotripsy/adverse effects · Ureter · Ureteral Calculi/diagnosis,therapy · Ureteroscopy/adverse effects · Urinary Calculi · Lithotripsy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: TISU (613 participants) found shockwave lithotripsy (SWL) non-inferior to ureteroscopy (URS) only against a generous prespecified 20% margin: 22.1% of the SWL group vs 10.3% of the URS group needed further treatment to clear the stone (absolute difference 11.7%, 95% CI 5.6% to 17.8%, in favour of URS) — so SWL met the letter of non-inferiority while URS was better on the trial's own primary outcome and, in the trialists' words, on overall clinical outcomes. The older Pearle trial (64 patients, distal stones only, older HM3 lithotriptor) found equal stone resolution (91% in each group) with shorter procedures and more same-day discharge for SWL. Two randomised trials, but the large one's margin was wide and its direction favours URS — POSSIBLE for SWL as an acceptable first-line option, not LIKELY equivalence.

cards.headline: TISU 2021: SWL was non-inferior to ureteroscopy only within a 20% margin — 22.1% vs 10.3% needed further treatment to clear the stone
cards.summary: TISU (2021): SWL was non-inferior to ureteroscopy only within a 20% margin — 22.1% vs 10.3% needed further treatment to clear the stone.
cards.people: 613 participants over 16 years with a single ureteric stone clinically deemed to require intervention, randomised at UK centres to up to two sessions of shockwave lithotripsy (306) or ureteroscopy (307); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Further treatment to clear the stone was needed by 67 patients (22.1%) in the SWL arm vs 31 (10.3%) in the URS arm — an absolute risk difference of 11.7% (95% CI 5.6% to 17.8%) in favour of URS, inside the 20% threshold set for demonstrating non-inferiority of SWL. The trialists conclude SWL is non-inferior on that definition and is an outpatient, non-invasive treatment with cost advantages, while overall clinical outcomes favoured URS, reflecting contemporary practice.
cards.watchOut: A 20% non-inferiority margin is wide: 'non-inferior' here is compatible with one extra patient in nine needing a second procedure after SWL. Unblindable by nature, and stone location/size mix across the whole ureter makes the average result a poor guide to any single stone.
cards.source: Dasgupta R et al. Shockwave Lithotripsy Versus Ureteroscopic Treatment as Therapeutic Interventions for Stones of the Ureter (TISU): A Multicentre Randomised Controlled Non-inferiority Trial. Eur Urol. 2021 Jul;80(1):46-54. PMID: 33810921. Registry ID: ISRCTN92289221, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Pearle 2001: for distal ureteral stones, SWL and ureteroscopy both cleared 91% — SWL was faster, more often outpatient, and trended less morbid
cards.summary: Distal ureteral stones (2001): SWL and ureteroscopy both cleared 91% — SWL was faster, more often outpatient, and trended less morbid.
cards.people: 64 patients with solitary, radiopaque distal ureteral calculi 15 mm or less in largest diameter, randomised to shock wave lithotripsy with an HM3 lithotriptor (32) or ureteroscopy (32); the groups were comparable in age, sex, body mass index, stone size, hydronephrosis and time to treatment, per the abstract, which gives no mean age figure.
cards.result: Procedural and operating-room times were significantly shorter for SWL than ureteroscopy (34 and 72 vs 65 and 97 minutes), and 94% of SWL patients vs 75% of ureteroscopy patients were discharged home the day of the procedure. At mean follow-up of 21 and 24 days, imaging in 91% of patients in each group showed resolution of the target stone in all imaged studies. Minor complications occurred in 9% (SWL) and 25% (ureteroscopy) — a non-significant difference; no ureteral perforation or stricture occurred. Patient satisfaction was 94% vs 87%, and cost favoured ureteroscopy by $1,255 assuming outpatient treatment for both.
cards.watchOut: Distal stones only, 64 patients, and a first-generation HM3 lithotriptor in 2001: its equal-clearance result does not transfer to proximal stones, modern lithotriptors or modern slim ureteroscopes — which is exactly the gap TISU was run to fill.
cards.source: Pearle MS et al. Prospective randomized trial comparing shock wave lithotripsy and ureteroscopy for management of distal ureteral calculi. J Urol. 2001 Oct;166(4):1255-60. PMID: 11547053. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: both clear stones; ureteroscopy clears more first time, lithotripsy asks less of the patient up front
cards.summary: Both clear stones; ureteroscopy clears more first time, lithotripsy asks less of the patient up front — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: TISU (613 participants, all ureteric stones) and Pearle 2001 (64 patients, distal stones ≤15 mm).
cards.result: The two trials, twenty years apart, agree that both modalities work and disagree only on emphasis: Pearle's small distal-stone trial found identical clearance with an easier patient journey for SWL, while TISU's large pragmatic trial found URS clearly better at one-and-done clearance (89.7% vs 77.9% needing no further treatment) with SWL's non-inferiority resting on a 20% margin. Medical expulsive therapy (drugs to pass a stone) is Shelf #484 and stone-recurrence prevention is Shelf #483 and drafted #594; neither is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial answers which modality for an obstructed, infected kidney or a solitary kidney — emergency drainage questions sit outside both randomisations.
cards.source: Synthesis of Dasgupta R et al. Eur Urol. 2021;80(1):46-54. PMID: 33810921; Pearle MS et al. J Urol. 2001;166(4):1255-60. PMID: 11547053. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Peyronie's disease: collagenase injections (IMPRESS I and II)
shelves.question: Does intralesional collagenase clostridium histolyticum reduce penile curvature and bother versus placebo in Peyronie's disease — the twin IMPRESS phase 3 trials?
shelves.mesh: Clinical Trials, Phase III as Topic · Hathewaya histolytica/enzymology · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Schedule · Injections, Intralesional · Maximum Tolerated Dose · Microbial Collagenase/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: LIKELY — for a modest benefit: The twin IMPRESS phase 3 trials (832 men in total, identical double-blind placebo-controlled designs, reported in one paper) found collagenase improved penile curvature by a mean 34% (−17.0 degrees) vs 18.2% (−9.3 degrees) on placebo (p<0.0001), with a small advantage on the Peyronie disease symptom bother score (−2.8 vs −1.8; p=0.0037). Two concordant phase 3 trials carry LIKELY, but the size of the win belongs on the shelf face: about 8 degrees of curvature beyond placebo and one point of bother, against a treatment burden of up to 8 injections and three serious corporeal ruptures, surgically repaired. Collagenase for Dupuytren's contracture (drafted #685) is the same enzyme in a different organ and trial programme and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: IMPRESS I and II 2013: collagenase improved curvature by 34% vs 18.2% on placebo (−17.0 vs −9.3 degrees) and bother by −2.8 vs −1.8 points; three corporeal ruptures occurred
cards.summary: IMPRESS I and II (2013): collagenase improved curvature by 34% vs 18.2% on placebo (−17.0 vs −9.3 degrees) and bother by −2.8 vs −1.8 points.
cards.type: Two identical phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials, reported in one paper with a post hoc pooled analysis
cards.people: IMPRESS I examined 417 subjects and IMPRESS II 415 subjects — men with Peyronie disease, stratified by baseline penile curvature (30 to 60 vs 61 to 90 degrees) and randomised 2:1 to collagenase or placebo, receiving up to 8 injections of 0.58 mg over a maximum of 4 treatment cycles with penile plaque modelling; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: In the post hoc pooled analysis, collagenase-treated men showed a mean 34% improvement in penile curvature (mean change −17.0 ± 14.8 degrees) compared with a mean 18.2% improvement on placebo (−9.3 ± 13.6 degrees; p<0.0001). The mean change in Peyronie disease questionnaire symptom bother score was −2.8 ± 3.8 vs −1.8 ± 3.5 (p=0.0037). Three serious adverse events (corporeal rupture) were surgically repaired.
cards.watchOut: The pooled figures are a post hoc meta-analysis of the two trials, and the placebo arms improved substantially on their own (18.2% curvature, −1.8 bother) — the attributable drug effect is the gap, roughly 8 degrees and 1 bother point. Men with curvature outside 30–90 degrees were not studied.
cards.source: Gelbard M et al. Clinical efficacy, safety and tolerability of collagenase clostridium histolyticum for the treatment of peyronie disease in 2 large double-blind, randomized, placebo controlled phase 3 studies. J Urol. 2013 Jul;190(1):199-207. PMID: 23376148. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the MEDLINE record carries no databank registry entry.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two concordant phase 3 trials, a real but modest gain — LIKELY, sized honestly
cards.summary: Two concordant phase 3 trials, a real but modest gain — LIKELY, sized honestly.
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: IMPRESS I (417 men) and IMPRESS II (415 men), twin phase 3 trials in one report.
cards.result: This shelf is the twin-trial pattern in its cleanest form: two identically designed blinded trials, one pooled result — curvature improvement 34% vs 18.2% relative to baseline in each arm's own terms, an absolute gap of about 7.7 degrees, and a 1-point bother advantage, with corporeal rupture as the serious harm to consent for. That is LIKELY benefit of modest size, not transformation of the disease. The currency sweep's single hit — a pilot of hyaluronic acid with an enzymatic mix — is a different injectate and is not carded. Collagenase for Dupuytren's contracture (drafted #685) shares only the enzyme and is fenced, not re-carded.
cards.watchOut: No trial here compares collagenase with surgery (plication or grafting) or with traction; men choosing between injection and an operation are outside this evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gelbard M et al. J Urol. 2013;190(1):199-207. PMID: 23376148. Registry ID as on the card above.

shelves.title: Erectile dysfunction: the PDE5 inhibitor pivotal trials
shelves.question: Do oral PDE5 inhibitors restore erectile function versus placebo — sildenafil in its pivotal NEJM trial programme, and tadalafil in the trial that established its 24–36-hour window?
shelves.mesh: 3',5'-Cyclic-GMP Phosphodiesterases/antagonists & inhibitors · Administration, Oral · Coitus · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Erectile Dysfunction/drug therapy · Phosphodiesterase Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Piperazines/adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two different drugs of the class each beat placebo decisively in double-blind trials: sildenafil in its two-study pivotal programme (861 men across the dose-response and dose-escalation studies; 69% vs 22% of intercourse attempts successful in the escalation study's last 4 weeks) and tadalafil 20 mg in a dedicated duration trial (348 men; successful attempts 59.2% vs 28.3% at 36 hours and 52.9% vs 29.1% at 24 hours after dosing). Two randomised blinded programmes, concordant and large in relative terms with absolute attempt-success rates printed beside them, carry LIKELY. Headache, flushing and dyspepsia are the class price on both cards. Testosterone questions are Shelves #344 and #568 and are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Goldstein 1998: sildenafil worked across two pivotal studies — 69% vs 22% of intercourse attempts successful, 5.9 vs 1.5 successful attempts per month
cards.summary: Sildenafil pivotal studies (1998): 69% vs 22% of intercourse attempts successful on sildenafil versus placebo.
cards.type: Two sequential double-blind, placebo-controlled studies (24-week dose-response; 12-week flexible dose-escalation) with an open-label extension
cards.people: 532 men with erectile dysfunction of organic, psychogenic and mixed causes in the dose-response study (sildenafil 25, 50 or 100 mg or placebo) and 329 different men in the dose-escalation study, of whom 225 entered a 32-week open-label extension; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Increasing sildenafil doses were associated with improved erectile function (p<0.001 for the achieving and maintaining questions of the International Index of Erectile Function); at 100 mg the mean score for achieving erections was 100 percent higher than at baseline (4.0 vs 2.0 of a possible 5). In the last 4 weeks of the dose-escalation study, 69% of intercourse attempts were successful on sildenafil vs 22% on placebo (P<0.001), with mean successful attempts per month of 5.9 vs 1.5 (P<0.001). Headache, flushing and dyspepsia were the most common adverse effects in the dose-escalation study, occurring in 6% to 18% of men; 92% of men completed the 32-week extension.
cards.watchOut: 1998, pre-registration era, industry-run pivotal programme in men without the nitrate co-therapy and severe cardiovascular exclusions that govern real-world prescribing — the abstract reports efficacy and common nuisance effects, not the cardiovascular safety assessment that later defined the class's cautions.
cards.source: Goldstein I et al. Oral sildenafil in the treatment of erectile dysfunction. Sildenafil Study Group. N Engl J Med. 1998 May 14;338(20):1397-404. PMID: 9580646. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial.

cards.headline: Porst 2003: tadalafil 20 mg still worked a day and a half later — successful attempts 59.2% vs 28.3% at 36 hours and 52.9% vs 29.1% at 24 hours
cards.summary: Tadalafil (2003): 20 mg still worked a day and a half later — successful attempts 59.2% vs 28.3% at 36 hours and 52.9% vs 29.1% at 24 hours.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial
cards.people: 348 men with erectile dysfunction (mean age 57 years), stratified by baseline severity, randomised to tadalafil 20 mg (175) or placebo (173), with intercourse attempts assigned to about 24 or about 36 hours after dosing over two 4-week intervals; 327 men (94%) completed the trial.
cards.result: Thirty-six hours after tadalafil dosing, 59.2% of intercourse attempts were successful versus 28.3% on placebo (P<0.001); at about 24 hours the proportions were 52.9% vs 29.1% (P<0.001). Headache, flushing, dyspepsia and myalgia occurred significantly more often with tadalafil than placebo (all P<0.05).
cards.watchOut: A single-dose-window design: it proves responsiveness persists to 36 hours, not that daily function, satisfaction over months or outcomes in men who failed sildenafil are equivalent; attempt-level percentages also count multiple attempts per man.
cards.source: Porst H et al. Efficacy of tadalafil for the treatment of erectile dysfunction at 24 and 36 hours after dosing: a randomized controlled trial. Urology. 2003 Jul;62(1):121-5. PMID: 12837435. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the MEDLINE record carries no databank registry entry.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the class effect is real and large; the two anchors answer different questions — does it work, and how long does it last
cards.summary: The class effect is real and large; the two anchors answer different questions — does it work, and how long does it last — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the sildenafil pivotal programme (532 + 329 men) and the tadalafil duration trial (348 men, mean age 57).
cards.result: Sildenafil's programme establishes the class against placebo (69% vs 22% successful attempts); tadalafil's trial establishes the practical difference men ask about — a responsiveness window extending to 36 hours (59.2% vs 28.3% successful attempts at that point). Both sets of percentages are attempt-level absolute rates, printed as such. Neither anchor studies men for whom PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated or ineffective, and neither is a head-to-head drug comparison. Testosterone for sexual function lives on Shelves #344 and #568 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not read the tadalafil 36-hour figure as superiority over sildenafil: different trials, different designs, no direct comparison carded on this shelf.

shelves.title: Male stress incontinence after prostate surgery: sling vs artificial urinary sphincter (MASTER)
shelves.question: In men with urodynamic stress incontinence after prostate surgery, is a synthetic male sling non-inferior to an artificial urinary sphincter on patient-reported incontinence — the MASTER non-inferiority trial, its health-technology-assessment report, and its 24-month outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Prostate · Suburethral Slings/adverse effects · Urinary Incontinence · Urinary Incontinence, Stress/diagnosis,surgery · Urodynamics · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Pain
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: MASTER is ONE large randomised trial (380 men) with three reports — the 12-month primary report, the HTA monograph, and the 24-month outcomes found in the currency sweep and carded here — and a single trial caps at POSSIBLE however many reports it has. On its strict composite definition the sling was non-inferior to the artificial sphincter at both 12 months (incontinence rates 87.0% vs 84.2% still wet; non-inferiority p=0.003 against a 15% margin) and 24 months (difference −0.006, 95% CI −0.092 to 0.080), symptoms and quality of life improved substantially in both groups and satisfaction was high — yet nearly every secondary outcome favoured the sphincter, symptom scores were better with it (ICIQ-UI SF 7.5 vs 8.7 at 12 months), and by 24 months more sling patients had needed further surgery (11% vs 2%). Most men in both groups were still not completely dry: that is the honest headline. Female stress-incontinence shelves (#249, #486) are a different population and are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: MASTER 2021: the sling was non-inferior to the artificial sphincter on the strict continence definition at 12 months — but 87.0% vs 84.2% of men were still incontinent, and secondary outcomes favoured the sphincter
cards.summary: MASTER (2021): the sling was non-inferior to the artificial sphincter on the strict continence definition at 12 months (incontinence 87.0% vs 84.2% on that strict definition).
cards.people: 380 men with bothersome urodynamic stress incontinence after prostate surgery, randomised at 27 UK centres 1:1 to the male transobturator sling (190) or artificial urinary sphincter (190); the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: At 12 months, incontinence rates on the strict composite patient-reported definition were 134/154 (87.0%) for the sling vs 133/158 (84.2%) for the sphincter (difference 3.6% [95% CI −11.6 to 4.6], p for non-inferiority = 0.003, against a 15% margin). Symptom scores (ICIQ-UI SF) fell from 16.1 and 16.4 at baseline to 8.7 (sling) and 7.5 (sphincter) (mean difference 1.4 [0.2 to 2.6], p=0.02). Serious adverse events were few (6 vs 13 men). Quality of life improved and satisfaction was high in both groups, but all other secondary outcomes showing significant differences favoured the sphincter, as did post hoc analyses.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority against a wide 15% margin on a strict composite in which most men in both arms count as failures: 'non-inferior' must never be printed without the 87%/84% still-wet rates and the sphincter's secondary-outcome advantage beside it.
cards.source: Abrams P et al. Outcomes of a Noninferiority Randomised Controlled Trial of Surgery for Men with Urodynamic Stress Incontinence After Prostate Surgery (MASTER). Eur Urol. 2021 Jun;79(6):812-823. PMID: 33551297. Registry ID: none in this record's databank fields — the trial's ISRCTN49212975 registration is stated in the HTA and 24-month records carded below.

cards.headline: MASTER HTA 2022: the full assessment agrees — sling non-inferior (risk difference −0.034, −0.117 to 0.048), symptoms improved in both groups, and the sling cost less
cards.summary: MASTER HTA (2022): the full assessment agrees — sling non-inferior (risk difference −0.034 ), symptoms improved in both groups.
cards.type: Health technology assessment monograph of the same randomised trial, with a parallel non-randomised cohort and economic evaluation
cards.people: The same 380 randomised men (190 per group) plus a non-randomised preference cohort of 99 of 100 recruited men, in 28 UK NHS urological centres; men with prior sling/sphincter surgery, unresolved bladder-neck contracture or stricture were excluded; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The male sling was non-inferior to the artificial sphincter on continence at 12 months (intention-to-treat estimated absolute risk difference −0.034, 95% CI −0.117 to 0.048; non-inferiority p=0.003). ICIQ-UI SF scores fell from 16.1 to 8.7 (sling) and 16.4 to 7.5 (sphincter) (12-month mean difference 1.30, 0.11 to 2.49; p=0.032). Serious adverse events were few (8 vs 15 events). Quality-of-life scores improved, satisfaction was high in both groups, secondary outcomes with significant differences favoured the sphincter, outcomes in the non-randomised cohort were similar, and the sling cost less than the sphincter (the abstract gives no figure in the record fetched).
cards.watchOut: This is a second report of the SAME trial as the card above, not a second trial: it adds the economic and preference-cohort picture and must be counted once as evidence. Its cost conclusion is UK NHS-specific.
cards.source: Constable L et al. Synthetic sling or artificial urinary sphincter for men with urodynamic stress incontinence after prostate surgery: the MASTER non-inferiority RCT. shelves.title: Bladder pain syndrome / interstitial cystitis: amitriptyline and pentosan
shelves.question: Do the two long-standing oral drugs for bladder pain syndrome beat placebo — amitriptyline in treatment-naïve patients, and pentosan polysulfate in the Nickel randomised trial — and how thin is the benefit?
shelves.mesh: Amitriptyline/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Analgesics, Non-Narcotic/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Cystitis, Interstitial/drug therapy · Pain/drug therapy · Pain Measurement · Placebos · Statistics, Nonparametric
shelves.balance: Split — POSSIBLE for amitriptyline at adequate dose; LIKELY that pentosan does not work: Foster 2010 (271 treatment-naïve patients) missed its primary endpoint overall (response 55% vs 45% on placebo, p=0.12) and found benefit only in the subgroup that actually reached 50 mg or more (66% vs 47%, p=0.01) — a comparison the authors note was not specified in advance, which caps that half at POSSIBLE. Nickel 2015 (368 patients, 24 weeks, two pentosan doses against placebo, stopped early for futility at interim) found responder rates of 39.8% and 42.6% on pentosan vs 40.7% on placebo — a clean null in the largest test of the drug, carrying LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) under the library's large-null reasoning, tempered by its early termination. Both trials also show how large the placebo/context response is in this syndrome: 45% and 40.7% of placebo patients responded.

cards.headline: Foster 2010: amitriptyline missed its primary endpoint overall (response 55% vs 45%, p=0.12) — the win was only in patients who reached 50 mg or more (66% vs 47%)
cards.summary: Amitriptyline (2010): missed its primary endpoint overall (response 55% vs 45% , p=0.12) — the win was only in patients who reached 50 mg or more.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (both arms also received a standardised education and behavioural programme)
cards.people: 271 treatment-naïve subjects with interstitial cystitis/painful bladder syndrome randomised to amitriptyline (titrated from 10 mg toward 75 mg daily over 6 weeks) or placebo; 231 (85%) provided the 12-week global response assessment; participants were primarily women (83%) and white (74%), with a median age of 38 years.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat analysis, moderate or marked improvement was reported by 55% on amitriptyline vs 45% on placebo (p=0.12) — not significant. Among the 207 subjects who achieved a dose of at least 50 mg, the response rate was significantly higher on amitriptyline (66%) than placebo (47%) (p=0.01). The authors conclude amitriptyline plus education and behavioural modification did not significantly improve symptoms overall in treatment-naïve patients, but may benefit persons who can achieve 50 mg or more daily.
cards.watchOut: The positive result is a subgroup defined by a post-randomisation event (dose achieved), which the authors state was not specified in advance: patients who tolerate 50 mg differ from those who cannot, so this is hypothesis-grade evidence, and the 45% placebo response shows how much of the apparent effect is context and the behavioural programme both arms received.
cards.source: Foster HE Jr et al. Effect of amitriptyline on symptoms in treatment naïve patients with interstitial cystitis/painful bladder syndrome. J Urol. 2010 May;183(5):1853-8. PMID: 20303115. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00124306, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Nickel 2015: pentosan did nothing at either dose — responders 39.8% (once daily) and 42.6% (three times daily) vs 40.7% on placebo over 24 weeks
cards.summary: Pentosan (2015): did nothing at either dose — responders 39.8% and 42.6% vs 40.7% on placebo over 24 weeks.
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (terminated early after an unblinded interim analysis)
cards.people: 368 adults with interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome (ICSI total score 8 or greater) randomised to pentosan polysulfate sodium 100 mg once daily, 100 mg three times daily, or placebo for 24 weeks; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: There was no statistically significant difference between either pentosan group and placebo, or between the two pentosan doses, on the primary endpoint (30% or greater reduction in ICSI total score): responders were 48/118 (40.7%) on placebo, 51/128 (39.8%) on once-daily pentosan and 52/122 (42.6%) on three-times-daily pentosan. Pentosan was well tolerated, with 10.2% to 13.3% across groups discontinuing due to an adverse event. An unblinded interim analysis at 6 years, with 54% of the 645-patient target enrolled, led to early termination.
cards.watchOut: Early termination means the trial is smaller than planned — but the observed rates sit almost exactly on top of each other, so more enrolment was very unlikely to reveal a meaningful effect; the null is informative, not merely underpowered. Eligibility was symptom-based without cystoscopy, so a cystoscopy-defined subgroup could in principle differ.

cards.summary: A maybe at adequate dose for amitriptyline, a no for pentosan — against a 40–45% placebo response — Split: POSSIBLE · LIKELY (pentosan ineffective).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Foster 2010 (271 randomised, 231 assessed) and Nickel 2015 (368 randomised).
cards.result: The two long-standing oral drugs split: amitriptyline's case rests on a non-prespecified dose subgroup (66% vs 47%) after an overall null (55% vs 45%) — POSSIBLE, worth a trial in a patient who can reach 50 mg, never a promise; pentosan's case collapsed in its largest placebo test (about 40% responders in every arm) — LIKELY ineffective at the doses studied. shelves.title: Non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer: maintenance BCG
shelves.question: Does maintenance bacillus Calmette-Guérin after induction reduce recurrence and progression in recurrent Ta/T1 and carcinoma-in-situ bladder cancer versus induction alone — the Southwest Oncology Group randomised trial, read against the EORTC dose-and-duration trial?
shelves.mesh: Adjuvants, Immunologic/therapeutic use · BCG Vaccine/therapeutic use · Carcinoma in Situ/pathology,therapy · Carcinoma, Transitional Cell/pathology,therapy · Immunotherapy · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local/pathology,therapy · Neoplasms, Multiple Primary/pathology,therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: this shelf carries progression and survival outcomes in a cancer population, so it returns for personal review, per the flag on the topic draft, which the builder upholds): Maintenance BCG doubled median recurrence-free survival in the SWOG trial (76.8 vs 35.7 months, p<0.0001) and lengthened worsening-free survival (p=0.04), with 5-year overall survival of 83% vs 78% as reported, no significance claimed for survival in the abstract. The EORTC trial (1,355 patients) then answered how much maintenance: full dose for 3 years beat one-third dose for 1 year on disease-free interval (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.94), the extra years helped only high-risk patients and only at full dose, and there were NO differences in progression or survival in EORTC — so the recurrence benefit is LIKELY, while any progression or survival benefit remains unproven and is not claimed on this shelf. Newer BCG-combination trials from the currency sweep are fenced in the synthesis, not carded.

cards.headline: SWOG (Lamm) 2000: maintenance BCG doubled median recurrence-free survival (76.8 vs 35.7 months, p<0.0001) and lengthened worsening-free survival; 5-year survival 83% vs 78%
cards.summary: SWOG (2000): maintenance BCG doubled median recurrence-free survival ( 76.8 vs 35.7 months ) and lengthened worsening-free survival.
cards.type: Randomised trial of maintenance vs no maintenance after a common induction course (Southwest Oncology Group)
cards.people: 660 patients with carcinoma in situ or increased recurrence risk (2 or more episodes within the most recent year, or 3 or more tumours within 6 months) began a 6-week induction course of intravesical and percutaneous Connaught BCG; 550 consenting patients were then randomised to maintenance or none, and the 384 eligible patients disease-free at randomisation form the primary analytic group; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Estimated median recurrence-free survival was 35.7 months (95% CI 25.1 to 56.8) with no maintenance vs 76.8 months (64.3 to 93.2) with maintenance (log-rank p<0.0001). Median worsening-free survival (no progression to stage T2 or greater, cystectomy, systemic chemotherapy or radiation) was 111.5 months with no maintenance and not estimable with maintenance (log-rank p=0.04). Overall 5-year survival was 78% (no maintenance) vs 83% (maintenance) as reported, with no significance statement in the abstract. No toxicities above grade 3 were noted in the 243 maintenance-arm patients.
cards.watchOut: The survival figures are printed exactly as the abstract reports them — a 5-point difference with no test attached — and must not be quoted as a survival benefit; the trial's proven wins are recurrence and the worsening composite. The maintenance schedule was intensive (3 weekly instillations at 3, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 and 36 months) with percutaneous BCG, which modern practice does not replicate exactly, and withholding maintenance from patients with side effects may have understated severe toxicity, as the authors note.
cards.source: Lamm DL et al. Maintenance bacillus Calmette-Guerin immunotherapy for recurrent TA, T1 and carcinoma in situ transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder: a randomized Southwest Oncology Group Study. J Urol. 2000 Apr;163(4):1124-9. PMID: 10737480. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial.

cards.headline: EORTC (Oddens) 2013: full-dose 3-year maintenance beat one-third-dose 1-year on disease-free interval (HR 0.75) — with no differences in progression or survival
cards.summary: EORTC (2013): full-dose 3-year maintenance beat one-third-dose 1-year on disease-free interval (HR 0.75 ) — with no differences in progression or survival.
cards.type: Randomised, four-group non-inferiority trial of BCG dose (full vs one-third) and maintenance duration (1 vs 3 years)
cards.people: 1,355 patients with intermediate- and high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer randomised after transurethral resection to one of four BCG groups (one-third dose or full dose, for 1 or 3 years), with median follow-up of 7.1 years; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: There were no significant toxicity differences between one-third and full dose. The non-inferiority null hypotheses for both one-third dose and 1-year duration could not be rejected. One-third dose for 1 year was suboptimal compared with full dose for 3 years (hazard ratio 0.75; 95% CI 0.59 to 0.94; p=0.01). Intermediate-risk patients on full dose did not benefit from an additional 2 years; in high-risk patients, 3 years at full dose reduced recurrence compared with 1 year (hazard ratio 1.61; 95% CI 1.13 to 2.30; p=0.009, printed as reported for the 1-year vs 3-year contrast). There were no differences in progression or survival.
cards.watchOut: EORTC randomised dose and duration among patients all receiving maintenance — it cannot by itself prove maintenance beats none (that is SWOG's question), and its flat progression and survival results are the strongest evidence on this shelf that maintenance's benefit is recurrence, not progression or death.

cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: SWOG (384 patients in the primary analytic group) and EORTC 30962 (1,355 patients, median follow-up 7.1 years).

shelves.title: Single-dose gemcitabine after bladder tumour resection (SWOG S0337)
shelves.question: Does one intravesical dose of gemcitabine immediately after resection of suspected low-grade non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer reduce recurrence versus saline?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravesical · Antimetabolites, Antineoplastic/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Carcinoma, Papillary/drug therapy,pathology · Deoxycytidine/administration & dosage,adverse effects,analogs & derivatives · Incidence · Neoplasm Invasiveness · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local/epidemiology,prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One large, well-run double-blind trial (SWOG S0337, 406 patients) found a single post-resection gemcitabine instillation cut 4-year recurrence from a 47% Kaplan–Meier estimate on saline to 35% (hazard ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.90 — a relative measure, printed with its absolute rates beside it), with a larger relative effect in the confirmed low-grade subgroup (HR 0.53; 34% vs 54%) and no grade 4 or 5 adverse events. A single pivotal trial caps at POSSIBLE under the library's rules, however clean the result. Progression (5 vs 10 patients) and deaths (17 vs 25) were not significantly different and no progression or survival claim is made. Maintenance BCG for higher-risk disease is Shelf #918 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: SWOG S0337 (Messing) 2018: one gemcitabine dose after resection cut 4-year recurrence to 35% vs 47% on saline (HR 0.66, relative), with no grade 4–5 adverse events
cards.summary: SWOG S0337 (2018): one gemcitabine dose after resection cut 4-year recurrence to 35% vs 47% on saline (HR 0.66, relative), with no high-grade toxicity signal.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind clinical trial (23 US centres)
cards.people: 406 randomised eligible patients with suspected low-grade non-muscle-invasive urothelial cancer on cystoscopic appearance (median age 66 years; 84.7% men), assigned to intravesical gemcitabine 2 g in 100 mL saline (201) or saline alone (205) for 1 hour immediately after transurethral resection, and followed with cystoscopy and cytology for 4 years; 383 completed the trial.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat analysis, 67 of 201 gemcitabine patients (4-year estimate 35%) and 91 of 205 saline patients (4-year estimate 47%) recurred within 4.0 years (hazard ratio 0.66; 95% CI 0.48 to 0.90; P<.001 by 1-sided log-rank test) — a 34% relative reduction against a 12-percentage-point absolute difference in the 4-year estimates. Among the 215 patients confirmed to have low-grade non-muscle-invasive cancer, recurrence was 34 of 102 (34%) vs 59 of 113 (54%) (HR 0.53; 0.35 to 0.81; P=.001). Progression to muscle invasion occurred in 5 vs 10 patients (P=.22) and deaths from any cause in 17 vs 25 (P=.12), neither significant. There were no grade 4 or 5 adverse events and no significant differences in grade 3 or lower events.
cards.watchOut: Single trial, and its headline hazard ratio of 0.66 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band where a ratio on its own is not solid evidence — the shelf rests on the randomised design plus the absolute rates (35% vs 47%), not on the ratio alone. Enrolment was by cystoscopic suspicion of low-grade disease, so the intention-to-treat population includes some higher-grade tumours; the confirmed-low-grade subgroup is a subset analysis, albeit a large one.

cards.summary: A cheap, single, well-tolerated instillation with a real recurrence reduction — POSSIBLE on one trial.
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: SWOG S0337 (406 randomised patients, median follow-up 4.0 years).
cards.result: S0337 is the model single-trial shelf: large, blinded, saline-controlled, with a patient-important endpoint and absolute rates that make the benefit legible (about 12 fewer recurrences per 100 patients treated by 4 years on the trial's estimates). It earns POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, only because no second randomised trial against placebo or saline yet confirms it. The currency sweep found a small phase 2 trial comparing single-dose gemcitabine with single-dose mitomycin-C (recurrence comparable at 1 year in 92 analysed patients) — supportive of single-dose instillation as a class, but an underpowered active-comparator pilot, fenced here rather than carded. Multi-year maintenance immunotherapy for higher-risk disease is Shelf #918; the two shelves answer different risk strata and neither re-cards the other.
cards.watchOut: S0337 does not compare gemcitabine with mitomycin-C or BCG at adequate power, and says nothing about high-grade or muscle-invasive disease; do not extend the result beyond suspected low-grade non-muscle-invasive cancer.

shelves.title: Sublingual MV140 bacterial vaccine for recurrent urinary tract infection
shelves.question: In women with recurrent urinary tract infection, does daily sublingual MV140 (a whole-cell bacterial preparation) for three months reduce the proportion experiencing UTI episodes over the following nine months versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Urinary Tract Infections · Female · Middle Aged · Adult · Double-Blind Method · Administration, Sublingual · Aged · Adolescent · Young Adult · Secondary Prevention · Quality of Life
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a single randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (240 women). Over the 9-month efficacy period after treatment, the median number of UTI episodes was 0.0 in both MV140 groups versus 3.0 on placebo (P<0.001), and 56% (3-month course) and 58% (6-month course) of MV140 recipients stayed UTI-free versus 25% on placebo. The trial was industry-funded and its own authors describe it as of 'modest size and duration'; the 3- and 6-month courses performed alike, so no duration advantage is shown. Flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate — a single trial supports the shelf; withdraw or re-scope it if the developer rejects the exception. Distinct from Shelf #596 (methenamine hippurate as antibiotic-sparing prophylaxis) and Shelf #489 (cranberry products): a bacterial vaccine preparation is a different intervention aimed at the same condition.

cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial (1 year)
cards.people: 240 women aged 18–75 years from Spain and the United Kingdom with recurrent UTI (three or more episodes in a year, or two or more in six months), allocated 1:1:1 to MV140 for 3 months, MV140 for 6 months, or placebo for 6 months.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — number of UTIs in the 9 months after the 3-month intervention point — had a median of 0.0 episodes (IQR 0.0 to 1.0) in both MV140 groups versus 3.0 (0.5 to 6.0) on placebo (P<0.001). UTI-free proportions were 56% (3-month MV140, 95% CI 44% to 67%) and 58% (6-month) versus 25% (15% to 35%) on placebo. A total of 205 adverse events were registered in 101 participants (81 events in the placebo group, 76 and 48 in the MV140 groups, as printed).
cards.watchOut: Single trial funded by the manufacturer (Inmunotek) and a distributor; the abstract prints event counts of adverse events per group rather than patient counts, and no antibiotic-use or resistance outcomes. Three and six months of treatment did not differ, which argues against the longer course on this record.
