shelves.title: Enclomiphene citrate for secondary male hypogonadism: testosterone rises and sperm are preserved in one phase II trial
shelves.question: In men with secondary hypogonadism, does oral enclomiphene citrate raise testosterone and gonadotropins while preserving sperm production, compared with topical testosterone gel (which suppresses spermatogenesis)?
shelves.mesh: Enclomiphene/therapeutic use · Humans · Hypogonadism/drug therapy · Male · Oligospermia/prevention & control · Testosterone/blood
shelves.balance: One small phase II randomised trial supports the mechanism, and nothing more can honestly be claimed. In men with secondary hypogonadism, oral enclomiphene citrate (the specific tested product — an investigational selective estrogen receptor modulator that is not FDA-approved for this or any use, named here for clarification) raised morning testosterone, estradiol, and LH to levels similar to those on topical testosterone gel, while — unlike the gel — it also raised FSH and sperm counts were conserved (Wiehle 2014). The abstract reports directions of effect, not magnitudes or group sizes, and the outcomes are hormones and semen parameters over a short phase II horizon: no symptom, fertility (pregnancy), fracture, or safety outcomes are established. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — a single small phase II trial with laboratory endpoints, for a product without regulatory approval.

cards.headline: Wiehle 2014: enclomiphene raised testosterone and LH like testosterone gel, raised FSH as well, and sperm counts were conserved
cards.summary: Wiehle 2014: enclomiphene raised testosterone and LH like testosterone gel, raised FSH as well, and sperm counts were conserved
cards.people: Men with secondary hypogonadism in a randomised phase II clinical trial (community-dwelling men attending physician offices), comparing oral enclomiphene citrate with 1% topical testosterone gel. Main outcome measures: LH, FSH, testosterone, and semen analysis. The abstract does not state the number randomised or the treatment duration.
cards.result: Treatment with enclomiphene citrate increased morning serum testosterone, estradiol, and LH levels to levels similar to those obtained with topical testosterone gel. FSH and LH were increased with enclomiphene, and sperm counts were conserved. The authors conclude enclomiphene reverses the two hallmarks of secondary hypogonadism — low total testosterone and low or inappropriately normal LH — while preserving sperm production. No numerical hormone values, sperm counts, or p-values are given in the abstract.
cards.watchOut: Sponsor-linked authorship (the developer, Repros Therapeutics) and a phase II design: this is proof of mechanism, not of clinical benefit. The trial enrolled secondary hypogonadism only — enclomiphene requires a functioning hypothalamic-pituitary-testicular axis and cannot be extrapolated to primary testicular failure. Pregnancy and live-birth outcomes were not tested.
cards.source: Wiehle RD et al. Enclomiphene citrate stimulates testosterone production while preventing oligospermia: a randomized phase II clinical trial comparing topical testosterone. Fertil Steril. 2014. PMID: 25044085. Registry ID: NCT01270841, from the record. shelves.title: Premature ejaculation: dapoxetine triples latency time, from a low base
shelves.question: In men with premature ejaculation, do on-demand dapoxetine or the lidocaine–prilocaine metered spray (TEMPE) lengthen intravaginal ejaculatory latency time (IELT) compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Ejaculation · Benzylamines · Naphthalenes · Lidocaine · Prilocaine · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors · Treatment Outcome · Humans
shelves.balance: Two on-demand treatments lengthen the time to ejaculation in men with premature ejaculation — from a very low base, and only to a few minutes. In an integrated analysis of two phase 3 trials in 2,614 men, mean baseline intravaginal ejaculatory latency time (IELT) was about 0.90 minutes; at endpoint it was 1.75 minutes on placebo, 2.78 minutes on dapoxetine 30 mg, and 3.32 minutes on dapoxetine 60 mg (both p<0.0001 versus placebo). Nausea was dose-related: 8.7% at 30 mg and 20.1% at 60 mg. In a small phase 2 trial of 54 men, the TEMPE lidocaine–prilocaine metered spray increased IELT by 3.8 minutes versus 0.7 minutes on placebo — an adjusted ratio of 2.4 times, a relative measure. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a large, internally consistent dapoxetine programme plus a small supportive spray trial, with benefit best described honestly in absolute minutes.

cards.headline: Pryor 2006: dapoxetine raised IELT from about 0.90 minutes to 2.78 (30 mg) and 3.32 minutes (60 mg), versus 1.75 on placebo
cards.summary: Pryor 2006: dapoxetine raised IELT from about 0.90 minutes to 2.78 (30 mg) and 3.32 minutes (60 mg), versus 1.75 on placebo
cards.type: Integrated analysis of two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (Pryor 2006)
cards.people: 2,614 men with moderate-to-severe premature ejaculation in stable, heterosexual relationships, in a prospectively predefined integrated analysis of two identical 12-week randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials at 121 sites in the USA: placebo (n=870), dapoxetine 30 mg (n=874), or dapoxetine 60 mg (n=870), taken on demand 1–3 hours before anticipated sexual activity, with intravaginal ejaculatory latency time (IELT) measured by stopwatch.
cards.result: Mean IELT at baseline was 0.90 minutes (placebo), 0.92 (30 mg) and 0.91 (60 mg); at study endpoint it was 1.75 minutes for placebo, 2.78 minutes for dapoxetine 30 mg, and 3.32 minutes for dapoxetine 60 mg (p<0.0001 for both doses versus placebo), and both doses were effective on the first dose. Common adverse events (30 mg and 60 mg respectively) were nausea (8.7%, 20.1%), diarrhoea (3.9%, 6.8%), headache (5.9%, 6.8%), and dizziness (3.0%, 6.2%).
cards.watchOut: The relative gain is large but the absolute endpoint is still only about 3 minutes, with wide variability (endpoint SD 3.48 minutes at 30 mg and 3.68 at 60 mg). At the time of the trials, no drugs were approved for the treatment of premature ejaculation.
cards.source: Pryor JL et al.. Efficacy and tolerability of dapoxetine in treatment of premature ejaculation: an integrated analysis of two double-blind, randomised controlled trials. The Lancet. 2006. PMID: 16962882. Registry ID: NCT00211094 and NCT00211107. cards.headline: Dinsmore 2007: TEMPE spray increased IELT by 3.8 minutes versus 0.7 on placebo — an adjusted ratio of 2.4 times (relative) in 54 men
cards.summary: Dinsmore 2007: TEMPE spray increased IELT by 3.8 minutes versus 0.7 on placebo — an adjusted ratio of 2.4 times (relative) in 54 men
cards.people: 54 men aged 18–75 years with premature ejaculation (DSM-IV definition) in the UK and the Netherlands, randomised in a double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 study to TEMPE — a metered-dose aerosol spray containing a eutectic mixture of lidocaine and prilocaine, the tested product named in the publication — or placebo spray.
cards.result: The observed mean change in IELT from baseline to the end of treatment was 3.8 min in the TEMPE group and 0.7 min in the placebo group; adjusted for baseline and centre, IELT was 2.4 times higher in the TEMPE group than the placebo group (a relative measure; p<0.01). Index of ejaculatory control and sexual quality-of-life scores (patients and partners) also trended in TEMPE's favour. Mild-to-moderate local numbness occurred in 3 (12%) of the TEMPE-treated patients but did not lead to discontinuation, and 35 of 42 (83%) patients considered the spray easy to use.
cards.watchOut: A small, early-phase trial: only 54 patients were randomised, and the proportions reaching IELT thresholds of 2, 3 or 4 minutes on two occasions were higher with TEMPE but not statistically significantly different from placebo.
cards.source: Dinsmore WW et al.. Topical eutectic mixture for premature ejaculation (TEMPE): a novel aerosol-delivery form of lidocaine-prilocaine for treating premature ejaculation. shelves.title: Antioxidants for male infertility: the one rigorous placebo-controlled trial (MOXI) found nothing — live birth 15% vs 24% on placebo — against a positive but very-low-certainty pooled literature
shelves.question: In male infertility with abnormal semen parameters, do antioxidant supplements improve pregnancy and live-birth rates?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antioxidants/administration & dosage/pharmacology* · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Infertility, Male/drug therapy* · Insemination, Artificial, Homologous · Male · Ovulation Induction/methods · Pilot Projects · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Rate · United States
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the best trial and the pooled literature disagree, and the disagreement tracks trial quality. MOXI, the one large multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled trial (174 men with abnormal semen parameters or high DNA fragmentation), found antioxidants did not improve sperm concentration, motility, morphology or DNA fragmentation at 3 months, and cumulative live birth at 6 months was 15% on antioxidants versus 24% on placebo — numerically favouring placebo, not significantly (Steiner AZ et al., PMID: 32111479). The Cochrane review of 90 trials (10,303 men) pooled a benefit: live birth odds ratio 1.43 (95% CI 1.07 to 1.91) across 12 small trials with 246 live births, rated very-low-certainty — and when high-risk-of-bias studies were removed, the live-birth benefit disappeared (Peto OR 1.22, 0.85 to 1.75) (de Ligny W et al., PMID: 35506389). Clinical pregnancy was higher in the pooled analysis (OR 1.89, low certainty), and mild gastrointestinal discomfort was more common on antioxidants (OR 2.70). PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) in the rigorous trial / POSSIBLE (benefit) in the pooled low-certainty literature; Tier C: supplement evidence with a quality-dependent answer. The MOXI formulation's ingredients and doses are named in its record (vitamin C 500 mg, vitamin E 400 mg, selenium 0.20 mg, L-carnitine 1,000 mg, zinc 20 mg, folic acid 1,000 µg, lycopene 10 mg daily) but no brand or company is named — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Steiner 2020 (MOXI, 174 men, double-blind): antioxidants improved no semen parameter and no DNA fragmentation — live birth 15% vs 24% on placebo
cards.summary: Steiner 2020 (MOXI, 174 men, double-blind): antioxidants improved no semen parameter and no DNA fragmentation — live birth 15% vs 24% on placebo
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (MOXI, Steiner 2020)
cards.people: 174 men at nine US fertility centres with sperm concentration ≤ 15 million/mL, motility ≤ 40%, normal morphology ≤ 4% or DNA fragmentation > 25%, whose female partners were ovulatory, ≤ 40 years old, with documented tubal patency. Men were randomised to a daily antioxidant formulation (n = 85) — vitamin C 500 mg, vitamin E 400 mg, selenium 0.20 mg, L-carnitine 1,000 mg, zinc 20 mg, folic acid 1,000 µg, lycopene 10 mg — or placebo (n = 86) for 3–6 months; couples conceived naturally for 3 months, then with clomiphene/IUI for months 4–6. Primary outcome: live birth.
cards.result: At 3 months there were no significant between-group differences in changes in sperm morphology, motility or DNA fragmentation; the change in sperm concentration differed between groups in the direction favouring placebo (median −4.0 vs +2.4 million/mL). In the oligospermic, asthenospermic and high-DNA-fragmentation subgroups, 3-month values did not differ between arms. Cumulative live birth at 6 months was 15% on antioxidants versus 24% on placebo (not significant). The authors conclude antioxidants do not improve semen parameters, DNA integrity, pregnancy or live birth in male-factor infertility, while noting the sample-size limitation.
cards.watchOut: MOXI was stopped short of its full planned size and is underpowered for live birth on its own — its confidence intervals cannot exclude a modest benefit. But it is the only trial here with adequate blinding, a placebo and a live-birth primary outcome, and its point estimates favour placebo on the primary outcome. The record names the formulation's ingredients and doses but no brand or company — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: de Ligny 2022 (Cochrane, 90 trials, 10,303 men): pooled live birth OR 1.43 — very low certainty, and the benefit vanishes when high-bias-risk studies are removed
cards.summary: de Ligny 2022 (Cochrane, 90 trials, 10,303 men): pooled live birth OR 1.43 — very low certainty, and the benefit vanishes when high-bias-risk studies are removed
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 90 RCTs (de Ligny 2022, Cochrane)
cards.people: 90 randomised trials of oral antioxidant supplements versus placebo, no treatment or another antioxidant in 10,303 subfertile men attending fertility clinics, comparing 20 different antioxidants or combinations. Only 20 of the 67 meta-analysed studies reported clinical pregnancy and only 12 reported live birth — the review's central limitation.
cards.result: Live birth was higher on antioxidants (odds ratio 1.43, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.91; 12 RCTs, 1,283 men, 246 live births; very-low-certainty evidence) — an estimated 17–27% live-birth chance against an assumed 16% on placebo. Removing high-risk-of-bias studies abolished the effect (Peto OR 1.22, 0.85 to 1.75; 8 RCTs, 827 men). Clinical pregnancy was higher (OR 1.89, 1.45 to 2.47; low certainty). Miscarriage did not differ (OR 1.46, 0.75 to 2.83; very low certainty). Mild gastrointestinal discomfort was more common on antioxidants (OR 2.70, 1.46 to 4.99; low certainty). The reviewers conclude the evidence is inconclusive and call for large well-designed placebo-controlled trials reporting live birth.
cards.watchOut: The pooled benefit is carried by small trials at high risk of bias with poor reporting of randomisation and high attrition; the sensitivity analysis without them is null, which is also what the one rigorous trial (MOXI, carded on this shelf) found. Twenty different antioxidants are pooled as if one treatment — the review could not say which, if any, works.

cards.headline: Synthesis: believe the rigorous trial over the pooled small ones — SPLIT (no difference in MOXI / possible benefit in low-certainty pooling)
cards.summary: Synthesis: believe the rigorous trial over the pooled small ones — SPLIT (no difference in MOXI / possible benefit in low-certainty pooling)
cards.people: One multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled trial (MOXI, 174 men, live-birth primary outcome) set against a Cochrane synthesis of 90 mostly small trials (10,303 men) whose live-birth analysis rests on 12 trials and 246 events.
cards.result: MOXI: no improvement in any semen parameter or DNA fragmentation; live birth 15% vs 24% on placebo. Cochrane pooling: live birth OR 1.43 (very low certainty), falling to a null 1.22 when high-bias-risk trials are removed; clinical pregnancy OR 1.89 (low certainty); more mild gastrointestinal discomfort on antioxidants (OR 2.70). PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) in the rigorous trial / POSSIBLE (benefit) in the pooled low-certainty literature.
cards.watchOut: This is the library's recurring supplement pattern: many small positive trials, one careful trial, opposite answers. The honest clinical summary is that no antioxidant regimen has been shown to improve live birth in a trial designed well enough to detect it — and couples lose time, the scarcest resource in infertility care, while taking them.
cards.source: Synthesis of Steiner AZ et al. Fertility and Sterility. 2020 (PMID: 32111479); de Ligny W et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2022 (PMID: 35506389).

shelves.title: Aquablation versus TURP: identical 15.1-point IPSS gains at 1 year, fewer ejaculatory problems, and a 5-year symptom edge in 50–80 mL prostates — all from the one WATER programme
shelves.question: In men with benign prostatic hyperplasia and prostates of 30–80 mL, does Aquablation (robot-assisted waterjet ablation) relieve urinary symptoms as well as transurethral resection of the prostate, with fewer sexual side effects?
shelves.mesh: Ablation Techniques*/methods · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms/etiology/surgery · Male · Prospective Studies · Prostatectomy/methods · Prostatic Hyperplasia/complications/surgery · Time Factors · Transurethral Resection of Prostate · Treatment Outcome · Water
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised programme, followed to 5 years, answers this directly. In the WATER trial's 1-year report (Gilling PJ et al., PMID: 30552937; 181 men, prostates 30–80 mL), symptom-score improvement was identical after Aquablation and transurethral resection of the prostate (IPSS reduction 15.1 points in both), maximum flow improved by 10.3 versus 10.6 mL/s (p = 0.8632), prostate-specific antigen fell by about 1 point in both groups, and surgical retreatment within a year was 2.6% versus 1.5% (not significant), with no procedure-related adverse events after month 6. The 5-year report in the 50–80 mL subgroup (Oumedjbeur K et al., PMID: 37838991; 96 men) found a larger IPSS reduction with Aquablation (−14.1 versus −10.8, p = 0.02), a lower rate of Clavien-Dindo grade 1 persistent or grade 2+ events at 3 months (risk difference −23.1%), notably less de novo ejaculatory dysfunction (risk difference −21.9%), similar bleeding risk after 6 months, and a lower retreatment rate at 6 months (risk difference −14.4%). A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis (Chen DC et al., PMID: 37692142; 7 studies, 551 patients, mostly non-randomised) found IPSS improved by about 16.5 points at 3 months, sustained to 12 months, with sexual-function scores essentially unchanged (pooled effect −0.55, p = 0.321), while noting heterogeneity and publication-bias concerns. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): symptom relief matches TURP at 1 year and looks at least as durable at 5 years in medium prostates, with a genuine ejaculatory-function advantage — but the randomised base is a single trial programme, the 5-year figures come from a subgroup, and wider comparative durability data are still thin.

cards.headline: Gilling 2019 (WATER, 1 year): IPSS fell 15.1 points in both arms — Aquablation matched TURP on symptoms and flow, retreatment 2.6% versus 1.5%
cards.summary: Gilling 2019 (WATER, 1 year): IPSS fell 15.1 points in both arms — Aquablation matched TURP on symptoms and flow, retreatment 2.6% versus 1.5%
cards.people: 181 men with benign prostatic hyperplasia and moderate-to-severe lower urinary tract symptoms (prostates 30–80 mL), randomised double-blind at multiple centres to Aquablation (robot-assisted waterjet ablation) or electrocautery transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP). Primary safety endpoint: Clavien-Dindo grade 1 persistent or grade 2+ complications.
cards.result: At 12 months the reduction in International Prostate Symptom Score was 15.1 points after both TURP and Aquablation. Mean maximum urinary flow rate improved by 10.3 mL/s with Aquablation versus 10.6 mL/s with TURP (p = 0.8632). Prostate-specific antigen was reduced significantly in both groups by 1 point, similarly across groups (p = 0.9125). Surgical retreatment for BPH within 1 year was 1.5% (TURP) versus 2.6% (Aquablation), not significant. The rate of late complications was low, with no procedure-related adverse events after month 6.
cards.watchOut: A non-inferiority-style comparison at 1 year: 'the same' is the finding, and the confidence the field places in TURP's decades-long durability cannot transfer automatically. Blinding of a surgical trial is necessarily partial (patients and assessors), and the trial was run in prostates of 30–80 mL — results do not cover very large glands.
cards.source: Gilling PJ et al. Randomized Controlled Trial of Aquablation versus Transurethral Resection of the Prostate in Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia: One-year Outcomes. Urology. 2019. cards.headline: Oumedjbeur 2023 (WATER, 5 years, 50–80 mL subgroup): IPSS −14.1 versus −10.8 favouring Aquablation (p = 0.02), with ejaculatory dysfunction lower by a 21.9-point risk difference
cards.summary: Oumedjbeur 2023 (WATER, 5 years, 50–80 mL subgroup): IPSS −14.1 versus −10.8 favouring Aquablation (p = 0.02), with ejaculatory dysfunction lower by a 21.9-point risk difference
cards.people: 96 randomised men with prostate volumes of 50–80 mL from the WATER trial, identified prospectively for subgroup analysis and followed for up to 5 years after Aquablation or TURP. Primary efficacy endpoint: IPSS reduction at 6 months; primary safety endpoint: Clavien-Dindo complications at 3 months.
cards.result: Reduction in IPSS was significantly higher in the Aquablation group across 5 years of follow-up (−14.1 versus −10.8, p = 0.02). The Aquablation group had a significantly lower rate of Clavien-Dindo grade 1 persistent and grade 2 or higher events at 3 months (risk difference −23.1%). De novo postoperative ejaculatory dysfunction was notably lower with Aquablation (risk difference −21.9%), while the risk of bleeding remained similar after 6 months. The surgical and medical retreatment rate at 6 months was also lower with Aquablation (risk difference −14.4%).
cards.watchOut: This is a subgroup (50–80 mL) of the single WATER trial, not a second trial — 96 men, and 5-year follow-up of a surgical cohort always loses patients along the way. The late IPSS advantage was not the 1-year whole-trial picture (identical at 15.1 points), so read the 5-year gap as suggestive rather than settled.

cards.headline: Chen 2023 (systematic review/meta-analysis, 7 studies, 551 patients): IPSS improved ~16.5 points at 3 months and held to 12 months, sexual function essentially unchanged
cards.summary: Chen 2023 (systematic review/meta-analysis, 7 studies, 551 patients): IPSS improved ~16.5 points at 3 months and held to 12 months, sexual function essentially unchanged
cards.people: Systematic review of clinical trials of Aquablation for benign prostatic hyperplasia published to August 2021: 7 studies, 551 patients, mostly non-randomised series alongside the WATER trial; risk of bias assessed with ROBINS-I; pre- versus post-treatment changes pooled.
cards.result: At 3 months the International Prostate Symptom Score raw mean difference from baseline was −16.475 (95% CI −17.686 to −15.264; p < 0.001), with improvements sustained for 12 months. Maximum flow rate improved from pre- to 3 months postoperatively (the abstract prints the pooled change with an inconsistent point/CI pairing). The male sexual health questionnaire change pooled effect size was −0.55 (95% CI −1.621 to 0.531; p = 0.321) — no significant change. The authors note meta-analyses of some outcomes showed large statistical heterogeneity or evidence of publication bias, and that further research is required to confirm these preliminary results.
cards.watchOut: Pre–post pooling without a comparator cannot separate the operation's effect from regression to the mean and the natural history of treated BPH, and most included studies are uncontrolled series — this card supports the size and durability of symptom change and the preserved sexual function, not superiority over anything. Its flow-rate line is internally inconsistent in the abstract and is not relied on here.
cards.source: Chen DC et al. Aquablation in men with benign prostate hyperplasia: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Current urology. 2023. PMID: 37692142. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none listed in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: equal to TURP on symptoms and flow at 1 year, ahead on ejaculatory preservation, and still ahead on symptoms at 5 years in medium glands — from one trial programme
cards.summary: Synthesis: equal to TURP on symptoms and flow at 1 year, ahead on ejaculatory preservation, and still ahead on symptoms at 5 years in medium glands — from one trial programme
cards.people: The WATER randomised programme (181 men at 1 year; 96 men with 50–80 mL prostates at 5 years) plus a 7-study, 551-patient systematic review and meta-analysis.
cards.result: Symptoms: IPSS −15.1 both arms at 1 year; −14.1 versus −10.8 at 5 years in the 50–80 mL subgroup (p = 0.02). Flow: +10.3 versus +10.6 mL/s at 1 year. Retreatment: 2.6% versus 1.5% at 1 year (NS). Safety/sexual: fewer Clavien-Dindo grade 1-persistent/2+ events (risk difference −23.1%) and less de novo ejaculatory dysfunction (risk difference −21.9%) in the subgroup report; sexual-health scores unchanged in the meta-analysis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: One trial programme is the whole randomised foundation; independent replication and head-to-head data against laser enucleation (shelf #3043) do not exist in this record. Cost, anaesthesia requirements, and learning curve are outside these papers. Tier C is set because the evidence is a single RCT programme with a subgroup long-term report.

shelves.title: HoLEP versus TURP: identical symptom relief at a year, hospital stay 59 versus 86 hours and a much shorter catheter time — paid for with a longer operation and more early leakage
shelves.question: In men with benign prostatic hyperplasia, does holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) give symptom relief and flow rates at least as good as transurethral resection, with less bleeding and shorter catheter time?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Prostatic Hyperplasia/complications · Prostatism/etiology/surgery · Transurethral Resection of Prostate/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — efficacy is a draw; the perioperative course is where HoLEP wins in the randomised record. In the two-centre trial of Montorsi 2008 (PMID: 18405765; 100 men with obstructive benign prostatic hyperplasia), HoLEP and TURP showed no statistically significant differences in urodynamic findings or subjective symptom scores at 1, 6 or 12 months; HoLEP took longer in the operating room (74 ± 19.5 versus 57 ± 15 minutes, p < 0.05) but catheterisation time was far shorter (31 ± 13 versus 57.78 ± 17.5 — units as printed in the record — p < 0.001) and hospital stay shorter (59 ± 19.9 versus 85.8 ± 18.9 hours, p < 0.001); transient stress and urge incontinence were more common after HoLEP, overall complication rates were comparable, and erectile function was maintained in both groups. The wider synthesis (Ahyai SA et al., PMID: 20825758; meta-analysis of 23 randomised trials, 2,245 patients, across transurethral techniques) concluded that functional results and overall morbidity of the minimally invasive techniques, HoLEP among them, were statistically comparable to contemporary TURP, with technique-specific safety profiles. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for symptom relief HoLEP is TURP's equal on this record; its benefit is the shorter catheter time and hospital stay, bought with longer operating time, more transient incontinence, and a well-known operator learning curve that trial centres have already climbed — community results may lag trial results.

cards.headline: Montorsi 2008 (2-centre RCT, 100 men): no difference in symptoms or urodynamics at 12 months — but catheter time and hospital stay significantly shorter with HoLEP, operating time longer
cards.summary: Montorsi 2008 (2-centre RCT, 100 men): no difference in symptoms or urodynamics at 12 months — but catheter time and hospital stay significantly shorter with HoLEP, operating time longer
cards.people: 100 consecutive men with symptomatic obstructive benign prostatic hyperplasia (all with Schäfer grade > 2 obstruction at baseline), randomised at two centres to holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP, n = 52) or transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP, n = 48), assessed preoperatively and at 1, 6 and 12 months.
cards.result: At the 1-, 6- and 12-month follow-ups there were no statistically significant differences between the groups in urodynamic findings or subjective symptom scoring. Mean total operating-room time was significantly longer for HoLEP (74 ± 19.5 versus 57 ± 15 minutes, p < 0.05), while catheterisation time (31 ± 13 versus 57.78 ± 17.5, p < 0.001) and hospital stay (59 ± 19.9 versus 85.8 ± 18.9 hours, p < 0.001) were significantly shorter in the HoLEP group. Transient stress and urge incontinence were more common after HoLEP, although by 12 months results were comparable; the overall complication rate was comparable, and erectile function was maintained from baseline in each group.
cards.watchOut: The record prints catheterisation time without a consistent unit label (the TURP figure, 57.78, sits in hours alongside the hospital-stay figures); the direction and significance (p < 0.001) are clear, the exact unit should be checked in the full text before quoting hours. A 2002-recruited, two-centre trial from expert hands: HoLEP's learning curve is the classic reason real-world series look worse than trial results. The PubMed record carries no MeSH list for this paper.

cards.headline: Ahyai 2010 (meta-analysis, 23 RCTs, 2,245 patients): transurethral alternatives including HoLEP were statistically comparable to TURP on function and overall morbidity, with technique-specific safety profiles
cards.summary: Ahyai 2010 (meta-analysis, 23 RCTs, 2,245 patients): transurethral alternatives including HoLEP were statistically comparable to TURP on function and overall morbidity, with technique-specific safety profiles
cards.people: Meta-analysis of all randomised trials (1997–2009) comparing TURP with bipolar TURP, bipolar vaporisation, holmium laser enucleation (HoLEP), or potassium-titanyl-phosphate laser vaporisation for lower urinary tract symptoms from benign prostatic enlargement: 27 publications, 23 RCTs, 2,245 patients.
cards.result: The meta-analysis demonstrates statistically comparable efficacy and overall morbidity for the minimally invasive surgical techniques versus contemporary TURP. The type, category (minor versus major), and number of complications — the safety profile — vary specifically for each transurethral technique. The authors conclude the individual patient's clinical profile should be carefully assessed to identify the most appropriate transurethral technique.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports the pooled verdict qualitatively — comparable efficacy and morbidity — without printing HoLEP-specific effect sizes, so this card corroborates equivalence across the RCT literature rather than adding HoLEP numbers. The search closed in 2009; later trials are not in it.

cards.headline: Synthesis: equal symptom relief, shorter catheter and stay, longer operation — HoLEP's case is perioperative, and it depends on operator experience
cards.summary: Synthesis: equal symptom relief, shorter catheter and stay, longer operation — HoLEP's case is perioperative, and it depends on operator experience
cards.people: One two-centre RCT (100 men, 12 months) plus a 23-RCT meta-analysis (2,245 patients) of transurethral prostate procedures versus TURP.
cards.result: Symptoms/urodynamics: no significant differences at 1, 6 or 12 months in the RCT; comparable efficacy across the meta-analysis. Perioperative: operating time 74 versus 57 minutes (longer, HoLEP); catheterisation time and hospital stay (59 versus 85.8 hours) significantly shorter with HoLEP. Harms: more transient stress/urge incontinence early with HoLEP, comparable overall complications by 12 months; erectile function maintained in both arms. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Neither source here quantifies transfusion or bleeding rates directly, despite the question's bleeding limb — the shorter catheter/stay signal is the measured proxy, and a bleeding claim should not be quoted from this shelf. Enucleation's size-independence (its main real-world selling point for very large glands) is also outside these two records. Tier C is not set: an RCT plus a 23-trial meta-analysis agree on equivalence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Montorsi F et al. The Journal of urology. 2008 (PMID: 18405765); Ahyai SA et al. European urology. 2010 (PMID: 20825758).

shelves.title: Pregabalin for chronic prostatitis/pelvic pain: responders 47% versus 36% on placebo but p = 0.07 — the primary endpoint missed, and Cochrane calls it probably ineffective
shelves.question: In men with chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome (category III), does pregabalin reduce pain and pelvic-pain symptom scores compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Analgesics/therapeutic use · Canada · Chronic Disease · Double-Blind Method · Hospitals, University · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pelvic Pain/diagnosis/drug therapy/etiology · Pregabalin · Prostatitis/complications · Treatment Outcome · United States · gamma-Aminobutyric Acid/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the one dedicated trial missed its primary endpoint, and the Cochrane synthesis sides with the miss. In the NIH-network trial (Pontari MA et al., PMID: 20876412), 324 men with chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome received pregabalin (titrated 150 to 600 mg/day) or placebo for 6 weeks in a 2:1 ratio: the primary outcome — at least a 6-point decrease in the NIH Chronic Prostatitis Symptom Index total score — was reached by 47.2% (103/218) on pregabalin versus 35.8% (38/106) on placebo, which was not statistically significant (p = 0.07). Secondary measures leaned pregabalin's way (NIH-CPSI total and subscore reductions, p < 0.05; Global Response Assessment response 31.2% versus 18.9%, p = 0.02; McGill Pain Questionnaire improvement, p = 0.01), but the other outcomes did not differ, and the authors conclude pregabalin was not superior to placebo on the primary outcome. The Cochrane systematic review of pharmacological interventions for CP/CPPS (Franco JVA et al., PMID: 31899937; 99 studies, 9,119 men) states that moderate- to high-quality evidence indicates pregabalin may be ineffective for reducing prostatitis symptoms. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a near-miss primary endpoint with supportive secondaries is exactly the pattern that most often evaporates on replication, and the field's own synthesis grades pregabalin among the probably-ineffective options — it remains a maybe for an individual neuropathic-pain phenotype, not an evidence-backed CPPS treatment.

cards.headline: Pontari 2010 (NIH network, 324 men): 6-point NIH-CPSI response 47.2% on pregabalin versus 35.8% on placebo — p = 0.07, primary endpoint not met
cards.summary: Pontari 2010 (NIH network, 324 men): 6-point NIH-CPSI response 47.2% on pregabalin versus 35.8% on placebo — p = 0.07, primary endpoint not met
cards.people: 324 men with chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome (pelvic pain for at least 3 of the previous 6 months), randomised 2:1 across 10 North American tertiary centres to pregabalin (dose increased from 150 to 600 mg/day over the first 4 weeks) or placebo for 6 weeks. Primary outcome: a decrease of at least 6 points in the NIH Chronic Prostatitis Symptom Index (NIH-CPSI) total score.
cards.result: Of 218 men assigned pregabalin, 103 (47.2%) achieved at least a 6-point NIH-CPSI decrease at 6 weeks, versus 35.8% (38 of 106) on placebo (p = 0.07, exact Mantel-Haenszel test adjusting for clinical sites) — not statistically significant. Compared with placebo, pregabalin produced reductions in NIH-CPSI total score and subscores (p < 0.05), a higher Global Response Assessment response rate (31.2% versus 18.9%; p = 0.02), and improvement in total McGill Pain Questionnaire score (p = 0.01); results for the other outcomes did not differ between groups. The authors conclude pregabalin therapy for 6 weeks was not superior to placebo in the rate of a 6-point NIH-CPSI improvement.
cards.watchOut: Six weeks is short for a chronic pain syndrome, and a 2:1 randomisation with a p of 0.07 invites 'almost worked' readings — but the trial was powered for its primary endpoint and missed it; the significant secondaries are multiple, correlated symptom measures in a condition with a large placebo response (35.8% hit the responder threshold on placebo). Pregabalin's familiar harms (dizziness, somnolence, dependence potential) are not detailed in the abstract and belong in any individual decision.
cards.source: Pontari MA et al. Pregabalin for the treatment of men with chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome: a randomized controlled trial. Archives of internal medicine. 2010. cards.headline: Franco 2020 (Cochrane, 99 studies, 9,119 men): moderate- to high-quality evidence indicates pregabalin may be ineffective for CP/CPPS symptoms
cards.summary: Franco 2020 (Cochrane, 99 studies, 9,119 men): moderate- to high-quality evidence indicates pregabalin may be ineffective for CP/CPPS symptoms
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials of pharmacological therapies for chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome: 99 unique studies, 9,119 men, 16 types of pharmacological intervention, outcomes graded with GRADE; most comparisons had short-term follow-up and median participant age was 38 years.
cards.result: For pregabalin specifically, the review places it — with anticholinergics, Escherichia coli lysate (OM-89) and pentosan — among the interventions that moderate- to high-quality evidence indicates may be ineffective for the reduction of prostatitis symptoms. By contrast, alpha-blockers may reduce symptoms (low- to very low-quality evidence, NIH-CPSI reductions of >2 but <8 points) with more minor adverse events such as dizziness and hypotension, and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors, antibiotics, anti-inflammatories and phytotherapy probably cause a small decrease in symptoms (moderate- to low-quality evidence).
cards.watchOut: 'May be ineffective' at moderate-to-high quality is a stronger negative than most CPPS verdicts in this review — but it is a class-level summary across the pregabalin trials available to 2019, dominated by the Pontari trial carded here, so the two cards are not fully independent witnesses.
cards.source: Franco JVA et al. Pharmacological interventions for treating chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome: a Cochrane systematic review. BJU international. 2020. PMID: 31899937. cards.headline: Synthesis: primary endpoint missed (p = 0.07), secondaries positive, Cochrane unconvinced — pregabalin for CP/CPPS is a maybe at best
cards.summary: Synthesis: primary endpoint missed (p = 0.07), secondaries positive, Cochrane unconvinced — pregabalin for CP/CPPS is a maybe at best
cards.people: One NIH-network placebo-controlled trial (324 men, 6 weeks) and the Cochrane pharmacological review of CP/CPPS (99 studies, 9,119 men).
cards.result: Responder rate (≥6-point NIH-CPSI fall): 47.2% pregabalin versus 35.8% placebo, p = 0.07 — not significant. Secondary symptom measures: several significant in pregabalin's favour (global response 31.2% versus 18.9%, p = 0.02). Cochrane GRADE verdict on pregabalin: moderate- to high-quality evidence it may be ineffective. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: CP/CPPS is heterogeneous; a neuropathic-pain subgroup could still benefit, but no validated way to identify it exists in this record, and subgroup rescue after a missed primary endpoint is speculation. Tier C is set because the direct evidence is a single trial whose own synthesis-level grading leans negative.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pontari MA et al. Archives of internal medicine. 2010 (PMID: 20876412); Franco JVA et al. BJU international. 2020 (PMID: 31899937).

shelves.title: Tamsulosin to prevent post-operative retention: 10.3% versus 16.3% and 17.7% versus 19.8% in the two newest trials — both null, with only subgroup hints in the pooled hernia data
shelves.question: In adults having surgery under spinal anaesthesia or pelvic surgery, does perioperative tamsulosin prevent postoperative urinary retention compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Tamsulosin · Urinary Retention*/prevention & control/etiology · Hernia, Inguinal*/surgery · Anesthesia, Spinal* · Middle Aged · Sulfonamides*/therapeutic use · Adrenergic alpha-1 Receptor Antagonists*/therapeutic use · Herniorrhaphy*/adverse effects · Postoperative Complications*/prevention & control · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the two recent placebo-controlled trials carded here are both null, and the pooled literature agrees overall while leaving subgroup doors open. In Seyedinnavadeh 2025 (PMID: 40602006), 179 men over 50 having inguinal hernia repair under spinal anaesthesia received tamsulosin 0.4 mg before and after surgery or placebo: retention requiring catheterisation occurred in 10.3% versus 16.3% — a 6-point absolute gap that was not statistically significant (p = 0.242), with logistic regression confirming no significant prophylactic effect (p = 0.171). In Leffelman 2025 (PMID: 40220053), 161 women having mid-urethral sling placement received a single preoperative tamsulosin 0.4 mg tablet or placebo: retention rates were 17.7% versus 19.8% (p = 0.7420), with no differences in unplanned admissions, urinary tract infections, or hypotension, and only a non-significant trend in the subgroup without concomitant prolapse surgery (7.5% versus 16.7%, p = 0.142). The hernia-repair meta-analysis (Drahman A et al., PMID: 36952050; 8 RCTs of prophylactic alpha-blockade) found no overall prevention of retention, but significant reductions in the laparoscopic subgroup and in patients over 60 — subgroup findings of the kind that need prospective confirmation. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): routine perioperative tamsulosin to prevent retention is unproven; a benefit confined to older patients or specific operations remains possible but rests on subgroups set against null primary results.

cards.headline: Seyedinnavadeh 2025: retention 10.3% on tamsulosin versus 16.3% on placebo after hernia repair under spinal anaesthesia — not significant (p = 0.242)
cards.summary: Seyedinnavadeh 2025: retention 10.3% on tamsulosin versus 16.3% on placebo after hernia repair under spinal anaesthesia — not significant (p = 0.242)
cards.people: 179 men over 50 (mean age 63.37 ± 10.62 years) undergoing unilateral inguinal hernioplasty under spinal anaesthesia, randomised double-blind to tamsulosin 0.4 mg 8 hours before surgery and again 6–12 hours postoperatively (n = 87) or placebo on the same schedule (n = 92), monitored for postoperative urinary retention within 24 hours.
cards.result: Postoperative urinary retention requiring catheterisation occurred in 10.3% of the tamsulosin group and 16.3% of the placebo group; the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.242). Logistic regression showed no significant prophylactic effect of tamsulosin (p = 0.171), nor of hypertension (p = 0.166), diabetes mellitus (p = 0.196), or benign prostatic hyperplasia (p = 0.273). The authors conclude prophylactic tamsulosin did not significantly reduce retention after inguinal hernioplasty under spinal anaesthesia.
cards.watchOut: The point estimate favours tamsulosin by 6 absolute points but the trial is small — its confidence interval is compatible with anything from meaningful benefit to none, which is why the verdict is 'unproven' rather than 'disproven'. Two doses around one operation type in older men is a narrow test of the broader perioperative question.
cards.source: Seyedinnavadeh S et al. Prophylactic effect of Tamsulosin on postoperative urinary retention in Inguinal hernia repair under spinal anesthesia. American journal of surgery. 2025. randomised placebo-controlled trial (seyedinnavadeh 2025) 179 men over 50 (mean age 63.37 ± 10.62 years) undergoing unilateral inguinal hernioplasty under spinal anaesthesia, randomised double-blind to tamsulosin 0.4 mg 8 hours before surgery and again 6–12 hours postoperatively (n = 87) or placebo on the same schedule (n = 92), monitored for postoperative urinary retention within 24 hours. postoperative urinary retention requiring catheterisation occurred in 10.3% of the tamsulosin group and 16.3% of the placebo group; the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.242). logistic regression showed no significant prophylactic effect of tamsulosin (p = 0.171), nor of hypertension (p = 0.166), diabetes mellitus (p = 0.196), or benign prostatic hyperplasia (p = 0.273). the authors conclude prophylactic tamsulosin did not significantly reduce retention after inguinal hernioplasty under spinal anaesthesia. the point estimate favours tamsulosin by 6 absolute points but the trial is small — its confidence interval is compatible with anything from meaningful benefit to none, which is why the verdict is 'unproven' rather than 'disproven'. two doses around one operation type in older men is a narrow test of the broader perioperative question. seyedinnavadeh s et al. prophylactic effect of tamsulosin on postoperative urinary retention in inguinal hernia repair under spinal anesthesia. american journal of surgery. 2025. pmid: 40602006. registry id: none in the record. mesh: humans · male · tamsulosin · urinary retention*/prevention & control/etiology · hernia, inguinal*/surgery · anesthesia, spinal* · middle aged · sulfonamides*/therapeutic use · adrenergic alpha-1 receptor antagonists*/therapeutic use · herniorrhaphy*/adverse effects · postoperative complications*/prevention & control · aged · double-blind method · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Leffelman 2025: single preoperative tamsulosin dose before sling surgery — retention 17.7% versus 19.8% on placebo (p = 0.7420)
cards.summary: Leffelman 2025: single preoperative tamsulosin dose before sling surgery — retention 17.7% versus 19.8% on placebo (p = 0.7420)
cards.people: 161 patients with stress urinary incontinence undergoing elective mid-urethral sling placement at a single institution (81 placebo, 80 tamsulosin analysed), randomised double-blind to a single tamsulosin 0.4 mg tablet or placebo in the preoperative holding area on the day of surgery; sample size had been calculated for 160 patients.
cards.result: The incidence of postoperative urinary retention was similar between groups (17.7% tamsulosin versus 19.8% placebo, p = 0.7420). Secondary outcomes — unplanned admissions, urinary tract infections, and hypotension — did not differ significantly. A subgroup analysis of patients undergoing sling placement without concomitant prolapse surgery suggested a trend toward lower retention with tamsulosin (7.5% versus 16.7%, p = 0.142), which was not statistically significant. The authors conclude single-dose preoperative tamsulosin might not affect retention after sling placement, with or without concomitant reconstructive pelvic surgery.
cards.watchOut: A single 0.4 mg dose is the weakest version of the intervention — a null here does not test multi-day regimens. The population is women having pelvic surgery, a different retention mechanism (outlet surgery) from the male hernia/spinal population in the companion card; pooling the two settings mentally is a mistake.
cards.source: Leffelman A et al. Effect of Preoperative Tamsulosin on Postoperative Urinary Retention Prevention After Sling Placement: A Randomized Controlled Trial. International urogynecology journal. 2025. PMID: 40220053. Registry ID: NCT05753670. cards.headline: Drahman 2023 (meta-analysis, 8 RCTs, hernia repair): prophylactic alpha-blockade did not prevent retention overall — significant only in laparoscopic and over-60 subgroups
cards.summary: Drahman 2023 (meta-analysis, 8 RCTs, hernia repair): prophylactic alpha-blockade did not prevent retention overall — significant only in laparoscopic and over-60 subgroups
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of prophylactic alpha-blockade (tamsulosin, prazosin, alfuzosin and others) for prevention of postoperative urinary retention after open and/or laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair in adults; 8 RCTs provided numeric data for pooling; background retention rates after hernia repair are estimated at 5.9% to 38% worldwide.
cards.result: Overall, preoperative alpha-blocker administration before inguinal hernia repair did not prevent postoperative urinary retention (pooled estimate as printed: 95% CI 1.20 (0.96–1.49), I² = 34%). Subgroup analysis showed a statistically significant reduction in the laparoscopic group (0.66 (0.47–0.92), I² = 43%) and in older patients over 60 years (0.14 (0.08–0.23), I² = 0%); sex did not affect the result (0.62 (0.27–1.44), I² = 53%). The authors conclude prophylactic alpha-blockers did not prevent retention overall, that use especially in older patients should be considered, and that more RCTs are needed.
cards.watchOut: The abstract's overall pooled figure is printed in a garbled form ('95% CI 1.20 (0.96-1.49)') and is quoted here exactly as printed; its interval crosses 1, consistent with the authors' null conclusion. The positive subgroups (laparoscopic, over-60) are multiple-comparison findings against a null primary pool — hypothesis-generating, and the over-60 effect size (0.14) is implausibly large for a prophylactic drug, which itself argues for caution.
cards.source: Drahman A et al. Prophylactic alpha-blockade for prevention of post-operative urinary retention after inguinal hernia repair: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Hernia : the journal of hernias and abdominal wall surgery. 2023. PMID: 36952050. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: two null trials in two different operations, a null overall meta-analysis, and two subgroup signals — routine prophylaxis unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: two null trials in two different operations, a null overall meta-analysis, and two subgroup signals — routine prophylaxis unproven
cards.people: Two 2025 placebo-controlled trials (179 men, hernia repair under spinal anaesthesia; 161 women, sling surgery) plus an 8-RCT meta-analysis of alpha-blockade before inguinal hernia repair.
cards.result: Retention rates: 10.3% versus 16.3% (p = 0.242) and 17.7% versus 19.8% (p = 0.7420) — both non-significant. Meta-analysis: no overall prevention; significant subgroup reductions for laparoscopic repair and age over 60 only. Harms: no excess hypotension, admissions, or infections in the sling trial. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Retention prevention is operation-specific: spinal anaesthesia, hernia repair, and sling surgery have different mechanisms and baseline rates (roughly 10–20% in these trials), so a verdict earned in one setting should not be carried into another — including joint replacement or colorectal surgery, which are not in this record at all. Tier C is not set: several trials and a meta-analysis exist; they simply point to 'no overall effect' with subgroup uncertainty.
cards.source: Synthesis of Seyedinnavadeh S et al. American journal of surgery. 2025 (PMID: 40602006); Leffelman A et al. International urogynecology journal. 2025 (PMID: 40220053); Drahman A et al. Hernia : the journal of hernias and abdominal wall surgery. 2023 (PMID: 36952050).

shelves.title: Shockwave therapy for erectile dysfunction: 54% of pill-nonresponders regained penetration-hard erections versus 0% on sham — in small, 1-month, single-group trials
shelves.question: In men with erectile dysfunction, does low-intensity extracorporeal shockwave therapy improve erectile function compared with sham treatment?
shelves.mesh: Combined Modality Therapy · Double-Blind Method · Erectile Dysfunction/drug therapy/physiopathology/therapy · Humans · Male · Penis/physiopathology · Phosphodiesterase 5 Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Pilot Projects · Ultrasonic Therapy/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two small sham-controlled trials from one research group, pointing the same way, plus a supportive meta-analysis. In Vardi 2012 (PMID: 22425129), 67 men with organic erectile dysfunction who responded to phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors received 12 sessions of low-intensity shockwave therapy or sham after a washout month: the IIEF erectile-function domain rose by 6.7 ± 0.9 points versus 3.0 ± 1.4 (p = 0.0322), 19 treated men who initially could not achieve penetration-hard erections (hardness score ≤ 2) reached hardness ≥ 3 versus none on sham, and maximal post-ischaemic penile blood flow improved by 8.2 versus 0.1 mL/min/dL (p < 0.0001), with no discomfort or adverse effects reported. In Kitrey 2016 (PMID: 26694904), 58 men who had stopped phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors for lack of efficacy were randomised (37 shockwave, 18 sham analysed): 54.1% versus 0% achieved penetration-hard erections with the inhibitor after treatment (p < 0.0001), treatment was 'effective' by IIEF-EF change in 40.5% versus 0% (p = 0.001), and 56.3% of the sham group crossed over to shockwave then achieved penetration-hard erections. The meta-analysis of Dong L et al. (PMID: 31027441; 7 RCTs, 522 participants) found pooled IIEF-EF improvement favouring shockwave over sham (mean difference 1.99 points, 95% CI 1.35 to 2.63) and a large odds ratio for hardness-score improvement (OR 16.02, 95% CI 7.93 to 32.37). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): short-term erectile-function gains are consistent, but the trials are small, short (1 month post-treatment), largely from one group, use varying devices and protocols, and durability beyond the short term is unestablished in this record.

cards.headline: Vardi 2012: IIEF-EF rose 6.7 versus 3.0 points over sham (p = 0.0322), and 19 treated men regained penetration-hard erections versus none on sham
cards.summary: Vardi 2012: IIEF-EF rose 6.7 versus 3.0 points over sham (p = 0.0322), and 19 treated men regained penetration-hard erections versus none on sham
cards.people: 67 men with organic erectile dysfunction who were phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor responders, after a 1-month inhibitor washout, randomised 2:1 to 12 sessions of low-intensity extracorporeal shockwave therapy or sham therapy; erectile function and penile haemodynamics assessed before treatment and 1 month after the final session.
cards.result: The increase in International Index of Erectile Function–Erectile Function domain score was significantly greater in the treated group (mean ± SEM 6.7 ± 0.9 versus 3.0 ± 1.4, p = 0.0322). Nineteen treated men who were initially unable to achieve erections hard enough for penetration (Erection Hardness Score ≤ 2) achieved hardness ≥ 3 after treatment, compared with none in the sham group. Penile haemodynamics improved significantly in the treated group only (maximal post-ischaemic penile blood flow 8.2 versus 0.1 mL/min/dL, p < 0.0001). No man experienced discomfort or reported adverse effects. The authors describe this as the first randomised double-blind sham-controlled study of the therapy.
cards.watchOut: Labelled a pilot project in its own record: 67 men, 1 month of post-treatment follow-up, and a sham arm that itself gained 3.0 IIEF-EF points — a large placebo/context effect against which the added 3.7 points should be read. Participants were inhibitor responders, the easiest population to help.
cards.source: Vardi Y et al. Does low intensity extracorporeal shock wave therapy have a physiological effect on erectile function? Short-term results of a randomized, double-blind, sham controlled study. The Journal of urology. 2012. PMID: 22425129. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kitrey 2016: in PDE5-inhibitor nonresponders, 54.1% achieved penetration-hard erections after shockwave versus 0% after sham (p < 0.0001)
cards.summary: Kitrey 2016: in PDE5-inhibitor nonresponders, 54.1% achieved penetration-hard erections after shockwave versus 0% after sham (p < 0.0001)
cards.people: 58 men with vasculogenic erectile dysfunction who had stopped phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors because of no efficacy (all with Erection Hardness Score ≤ 2 on inhibitors), randomised double-blind to low-intensity shockwave treatment (37 men; 12 sessions of 1,500 pulses at 0.09 mJ/mm²) or sham probe (18 analysed); 16 sham patients later crossed over to shockwave. Erectile function was evaluated while receiving inhibitors, at baseline and 1 month after treatment end.
cards.result: In the shockwave group 54.1% achieved an erection hard enough for vaginal penetration (EHS 3), versus 0% in the sham group (p < 0.0001). By change in IIEF-EF score, treatment was effective in 40.5% of shockwave patients and in none of the sham group (p = 0.001). Of patients treated with shockwaves after sham, 56.3% achieved penetration-hard erections (p < 0.005). The authors conclude shockwave treatment is effective even in severe erectile dysfunction with inhibitor nonresponse, while noting longer follow-up is needed.
cards.watchOut: A 0% sham response in a subjective-outcome trial is unusual and flatters the contrast; numbers are small (37 versus 18), follow-up is 1 month, and the same senior group ran both this and the Vardi trial — independent replication is the missing ingredient, not another analysis of the same data.
cards.source: Kitrey ND et al. Penile Low Intensity Shock Wave Treatment is Able to Shift PDE5i Nonresponders to Responders: A Double-Blind, Sham Controlled Study. The Journal of urology. 2016. PMID: 26694904. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dong 2019 (meta-analysis, 7 RCTs, 522 men): pooled IIEF-EF advantage 1.99 points over sham (95% CI 1.35 to 2.63), hardness-score OR 16.02
cards.summary: Dong 2019 (meta-analysis, 7 RCTs, 522 men): pooled IIEF-EF advantage 1.99 points over sham (95% CI 1.35 to 2.63), hardness-score OR 16.02
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of low-intensity extracorporeal shockwave therapy versus sham for erectile dysfunction, January 2010 to June 2018: 7 RCTs, 522 participants, outcomes IIEF-EF and Erection Hardness Score.
cards.result: Men treated with shockwave showed significant improvement in pooled mean IIEF-EF scores from baseline to follow-up compared with sham (mean difference 1.99 points, 95% CI 1.35 to 2.63; p < 0.00001); within-group IIEF-EF change in the treatment group was 3.62 points (95% CI 2.99 to 4.25). The Erection Hardness Score increased significantly in the treatment group across four studies (OR 16.02, 95% CI 7.93 to 32.37; p < 0.00001). Patients with moderate and/or severe erectile dysfunction reported better results in mean IIEF scores (mean difference 3.95, 95% CI 2.44 to 5.46).
cards.watchOut: The pooled between-group IIEF-EF advantage (1.99 points) is smaller than the headline within-group changes quoted from single trials, and below the roughly 4-point change often treated as clinically important for moderate ED — the hardness-score odds ratio of 16 rests on four small studies and is almost certainly inflated. Protocols, devices and energies vary across the pooled trials.
cards.source: Dong L et al. Effect of Low-Intensity Extracorporeal Shock Wave on the Treatment of Erectile Dysfunction: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. American journal of men's health. 2019. cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent short-term gains over sham in small trials, a modest pooled score advantage, and no durability data — possible benefit, not proven restoration
cards.summary: Synthesis: consistent short-term gains over sham in small trials, a modest pooled score advantage, and no durability data — possible benefit, not proven restoration
cards.people: Two sham-controlled trials (67 inhibitor responders; 58 inhibitor nonresponders) plus a 7-RCT, 522-patient meta-analysis, all with follow-up of about 1 month after treatment.
cards.result: IIEF-EF: +6.7 versus +3.0 points (Vardi, p = 0.0322); pooled advantage over sham 1.99 points (95% CI 1.35 to 2.63). Penetration-hard erections regained: 19 treated versus 0 sham (Vardi); 54.1% versus 0% in nonresponders (Kitrey). Haemodynamics: penile blood flow +8.2 versus +0.1 mL/min/dL. Harms: none reported in Vardi. Durability beyond 1 month: not measured in these records. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Commercial provision runs far ahead of this evidence: men are sold multi-session courses at substantial cost on 'restorative' claims that 1-month data cannot support. The honest statement is a probable short-term functional gain of uncertain size and unknown duration. Tier C is set because the randomised base is small, short, and concentrated in one research group.

shelves.title: Adding mirabegron to tibial nerve stimulation cut urgency incontinence episodes further — a 9.4 versus 5.3 episode improvement in one 54-woman trial
shelves.question: In adults with overactive bladder, does posterior tibial nerve stimulation combined with mirabegron beat stimulation alone?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Thiazoles/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · Acetanilides/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Tibial Nerve · Aged · Adult · Treatment Outcome · Urinary Incontinence, Urge/therapy/drug therapy · Combined Modality Therapy · Double-Blind Method
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a single small double-blind randomised trial (54 women with refractory urgency urinary incontinence) compared 12 weeks of posterior tibial nerve stimulation plus mirabegron against stimulation plus placebo. The improvement in urgency incontinence episodes on a 3-day bladder diary was significantly greater with the combination: a mean pre- to post-treatment change difference of 9.4 ± 3.9 episodes with mirabegron versus 5.3 ± 5.5 with placebo (p=0.007), with significant between-arm differences also in urinary frequency and Overactive Bladder Questionnaire symptom-bother and quality-of-life scores. Twelve weeks is short, the sample is small, and no second trial of percutaneous stimulation plus mirabegron was found. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): the combination beat stimulation alone on diary and symptom outcomes in one small trial; replication is needed before this is more than a promising signal.

cards.headline: Stanley 2024: PTNS plus mirabegron improved urgency incontinence episodes by 9.4 versus 5.3 (p=0.007) over 12 weeks
cards.summary: Stanley 2024: PTNS plus mirabegron improved urgency incontinence episodes by 9.4 versus 5.3 (p=0.007) over 12 weeks
cards.people: 54 women aged 18 or older (mean age 56.2 ± 15.6 years, mean BMI 35.0 ± 9.4) with urgency urinary incontinence refractory to second-line treatment or unable to tolerate antimuscarinics, randomised 1:1 to posterior tibial nerve stimulation plus mirabegron or stimulation plus placebo for 12 weeks; participants and providers were blinded to the medication allocation. Outcomes came from 3-day bladder diaries and validated questionnaires.
cards.result: The mean pre- to post-treatment change in urgency urinary incontinence episodes differed significantly between arms: 9.4 ± 3.9 episodes with mirabegron versus 5.3 ± 5.5 with placebo (p=0.007). Significant differences also favoured the combination for urinary frequency and for Overactive Bladder Questionnaire Short Form symptom-bother and symptom health-related quality-of-life scores.
cards.watchOut: Fifty-four participants and 12 weeks: the trial can show a short-term diary effect, not durability, and its episode counts carry wide standard deviations relative to the means. The abstract reports change scores rather than final absolute episode rates, so the residual symptom burden on the combination is not visible in the record.

shelves.title: Dutasteride on active surveillance: progression in 38% versus 48% at 3 years in the one trial — but the endpoint is biopsy change or starting treatment, and sexual and breast effects were more common
shelves.question: In men on active surveillance for low-risk localised prostate cancer, does dutasteride delay pathological or therapeutic progression compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: 5-alpha Reductase Inhibitors/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anxiety/epidemiology · Azasteroids/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Dutasteride · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Proportional Hazards Models · Prostate-Specific Antigen/blood · Prostatic Neoplasms/drug therapy/pathology/psychology · Surveys and Questionnaires
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single randomised trial, dutasteride slowed the clock on a composite endpoint. In REDEEM, 54 of 144 men (38%) on dutasteride 0.5 mg daily and 70 of 145 (48%) on placebo had pathological or therapeutic progression by 3 years (hazard ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.43–0.89; p=0.009). The catch is what progression means here: a worse biopsy or a decision to start treatment — there were no prostate-cancer deaths and no metastases in either group, so nothing in this record shows dutasteride changes the outcomes surveillance is ultimately trying to protect. The price was modest and mostly sexual: sexual adverse events or breast enlargement or tenderness in 35 men (24%) on dutasteride versus 23 (15%) on placebo, with cardiovascular events equal at 5% in both groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one well-run trial shows dutasteride delays biopsy-or-treatment progression on surveillance, at a small sexual and breast side-effect cost; a mortality or metastasis benefit was not shown.

cards.headline: Fleshner 2012 (REDEEM): progression by 3 years in 38% on dutasteride versus 48% on placebo (HR 0.62) — sexual or breast events 24% versus 15%
cards.summary: Fleshner 2012 (REDEEM): progression by 3 years in 38% on dutasteride versus 48% on placebo (HR 0.62) — sexual or breast events 24% versus 15%
cards.people: 302 men aged 48–82 years with low-volume, Gleason score 5–6 prostate cancer who had chosen active surveillance, at 65 North American centres, randomised to dutasteride 0.5 mg once daily or matching placebo for 3 years, with 12-core biopsies at 18 months and 3 years; 289 men had at least one post-baseline biopsy and entered the primary analysis.
cards.result: By 3 years, 54 of 144 men (38%) in the dutasteride group and 70 of 145 (48%) in the control group had prostate cancer progression (pathological or therapeutic; hazard ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.43–0.89; p=0.009). Sexual adverse events or breast enlargement or tenderness occurred in 35 men (24%) on dutasteride versus 23 (15%) on placebo; cardiovascular adverse events in 8 (5%) versus 7 (5%). There were no prostate cancer-related deaths or instances of metastatic disease in either group.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint mixes a biopsy finding with a treatment decision, and dutasteride shrinks the prostate and lowers PSA, which can itself change biopsy sampling and thresholds for starting therapy — so part of the delay may be measurement rather than biology. A single trial, funded by the manufacturer (GlaxoSmithKline), with no mortality or metastasis events to judge.
cards.source: Fleshner NE et al. Dutasteride in localised prostate cancer management: the REDEEM randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2012. PMID: 22277570. shelves.title: One year of enzalutamide on active surveillance: progression risk cut by 46% relative while on treatment — the advantage was gone a year after stopping, and fatigue and breast swelling were common
shelves.question: In men on active surveillance for low- or intermediate-risk prostate cancer, does adding enzalutamide for one year reduce progression compared with surveillance alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Benzamides/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Canada · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nitriles/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Phenylthiohydantoin/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Prostate-Specific Antigen · Prostatic Neoplasms/pathology · Prostatic Neoplasms, Castration-Resistant/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · Watchful Waiting
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — while the drug is being taken. In the open-label ENACT trial, one year of enzalutamide 160 mg daily reduced the risk of pathological or therapeutic progression versus surveillance alone (hazard ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.33–0.89; p=.02 — a 46% relative reduction), the odds of a negative biopsy at 1 year were 3.5 times higher, and PSA progression was delayed by 6 months (hazard ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.53–0.97). But the biopsy and PSA advantages seen at 1 year were no longer significant at 2 years, a year after treatment stopped — this looks like suppression while on therapy, not a changed trajectory. The burden was real: fatigue in 55.4% and gynecomastia in 36.6% of treated men, and three deaths occurred in the enzalutamide arm, none judged treatment-related and none while receiving the drug. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one open-label trial shows enzalutamide delays progression during a year of treatment, with effects that fade after stopping and a substantial fatigue and breast-symptom cost.

cards.headline: Shore 2022 (ENACT): progression HR 0.54 on enzalutamide, negative-biopsy odds 3.5 times higher at 1 year — no significant difference by 2 years; fatigue 55.4%, gynecomastia 36.6%
cards.summary: Shore 2022 (ENACT): progression HR 0.54 on enzalutamide, negative-biopsy odds 3.5 times higher at 1 year — no significant difference by 2 years; fatigue 55.4%, gynecomastia 36.6%
cards.people: 227 men (mean age 66.1 years) with histologically proven low-risk or intermediate-risk localised prostate cancer diagnosed within 6 months of screening and managed with active surveillance, at 66 US and Canadian sites, randomised to enzalutamide 160 mg monotherapy for 1 year plus surveillance (n=114) or surveillance alone (n=113), with follow-up to 2 years.
cards.result: Enzalutamide reduced the risk of prostate cancer progression by 46% relative versus surveillance alone (hazard ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.33–0.89; P=.02). At 1 year the odds of a negative biopsy result were 3.5 times higher with enzalutamide, the percentage of cancer-positive cores was significantly reduced, and the odds of a secondary PSA rise were significantly lower; none of these differences was significant at 2 years. Enzalutamide delayed PSA progression by 6 months (hazard ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.53–0.97; P=.03). The most common adverse events on enzalutamide were fatigue (62 patients, 55.4%) and gynecomastia (41 patients, 36.6%). Three patients in the enzalutamide arm died; none was receiving the study drug at the time and no death was considered treatment-related.
cards.watchOut: Open-label: men and clinicians knew who was on treatment, and 'therapeutic progression' — a decision to start treatment — is one half of the primary endpoint, so knowledge of allocation can move the result. The trial ran 1 year of treatment with 2 years of follow-up; it cannot speak to metastasis or survival, and the fading effect after stopping is the central interpretive fact.
cards.source: Shore ND et al. Enzalutamide Monotherapy vs Active Surveillance in Patients With Low-risk or Intermediate-risk Localized Prostate Cancer: The ENACT Randomized Clinical Trial. shelves.title: Metformin on active surveillance: no delay in progression in a 408-man phase 3 trial (HR 1.09) — and a prespecified signal of more pathological progression in obese men
shelves.question: In men on active surveillance for low-risk prostate cancer, does metformin delay progression compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Metformin/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Prostatic Neoplasms/drug therapy/pathology/mortality · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Middle Aged · Watchful Waiting · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Progression-Free Survival · Disease Progression
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the preclinical and observational promise did not survive a proper trial. In the MAST phase 3 trial, progression occurred in 70 of 205 men on metformin 850 mg twice daily and 74 of 203 on placebo over a median 36 months, with no significant difference in progression-free survival (hazard ratio 1.09, 95% CI 0.79–1.52; P=.59). Negative biopsy rates at 36 months were 41.0% on metformin versus 31.1% on placebo, also not significant (P=.181). The one signal ran the wrong way: in the prespecified subgroup of obese men (BMI ≥30), metformin was associated with more pathological progression (hazard ratio 2.36, 95% CI 1.21–4.59; P=.0092) — a subgroup finding that needs confirmation but removes any case for casual use. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): metformin does not delay progression on active surveillance in the one large blinded trial, and it may hasten pathological progression in obese men.

cards.headline: Fleshner 2025 (MAST): progression in 70 of 205 on metformin versus 74 of 203 on placebo (HR 1.09, p=.59) — obese subgroup HR 2.36 for pathological progression
cards.summary: Fleshner 2025 (MAST): progression in 70 of 205 on metformin versus 74 of 203 on placebo (HR 1.09, p=.59) — obese subgroup HR 2.36 for pathological progression
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Fleshner 2025, MAST)
cards.people: 408 men with low-risk, localised prostate cancer managed with active surveillance, randomised 1:1 to metformin 850 mg twice daily (n=205) or placebo (n=203) and followed for up to 36 months (median follow-up 36 months); the primary endpoint was time to therapeutic and/or pathological progression.
cards.result: 144 participants experienced progression (70 metformin, 74 placebo), with no significant difference in progression-free survival (hazard ratio 1.09, 95% CI 0.79–1.52; P=.59). Negative biopsy rates at 36 months were 41.0% on metformin versus 31.1% on placebo (P=.181). In a prespecified subgroup analysis, metformin was associated with increased pathological progression among obese patients (BMI ≥30; hazard ratio 2.36, 95% CI 1.21–4.59; P=.0092).
cards.watchOut: The obesity finding is a subgroup result — prespecified, which strengthens it, but still one subgroup among the analyses a trial this size generates, and it should be read as a warning to investigate rather than proof of harm. The trial enrolled low-risk disease only; it says nothing about metformin in higher-risk cancer or in diabetes care, where its role is separate.
cards.source: Fleshner NE et al. Metformin Active Surveillance Trial in Low-Risk Prostate Cancer. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2025. PMID: 41166665. randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (fleshner 2025, mast) 408 men with low-risk, localised prostate cancer managed with active surveillance, randomised 1:1 to metformin 850 mg twice daily (n=205) or placebo (n=203) and followed for up to 36 months (median follow-up 36 months); the primary endpoint was time to therapeutic and/or pathological progression. 144 participants experienced progression (70 metformin, 74 placebo), with no significant difference in progression-free survival (hazard ratio 1.09, 95% ci 0.79–1.52; p=.59). negative biopsy rates at 36 months were 41.0% on metformin versus 31.1% on placebo (p=.181). in a prespecified subgroup analysis, metformin was associated with increased pathological progression among obese patients (bmi ≥30; hazard ratio 2.36, 95% ci 1.21–4.59; p=.0092). the obesity finding is a subgroup result — prespecified, which strengthens it, but still one subgroup among the analyses a trial this size generates, and it should be read as a warning to investigate rather than proof of harm. the trial enrolled low-risk disease only; it says nothing about metformin in higher-risk cancer or in diabetes care, where its role is separate. fleshner ne et al. metformin active surveillance trial in low-risk prostate cancer. journal of clinical oncology. 2025. pmid: 41166665. mesh: humans · male · metformin/therapeutic use/adverse effects · prostatic neoplasms/drug therapy/pathology/mortality · aged · double-blind method · middle aged · watchful waiting · hypoglycemic agents/therapeutic use · progression-free survival · disease progression

cards.headline: Synthesis: a clean null on the main question, with one adverse subgroup signal to take seriously
cards.summary: Synthesis: a clean null on the main question, with one adverse subgroup signal to take seriously
cards.people: One multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (MAST, 408 men) of metformin 850 mg twice daily versus placebo for up to 36 months in low-risk prostate cancer on active surveillance.
cards.result: Progression: 70 of 205 versus 74 of 203 (HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.79–1.52; P=.59). Negative biopsy at 36 months: 41.0% versus 31.1% (P=.181). Obese subgroup (BMI ≥30): pathological progression HR 2.36 (95% CI 1.21–4.59) on metformin. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C: the shelf carries a prespecified subgroup harm signal the developer should see personally.
