shelves.title: Alfuzosin for chronic prostatitis / pelvic pain in alpha-blocker-naive men: 49.3% responded — exactly the same 49.3% as on placebo
shelves.question: In men with chronic prostatitis / chronic pelvic pain syndrome who have not had an alpha-blocker before, does alfuzosin improve pain and urinary symptoms compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic alpha-Antagonists/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Adult · Aged · Chronic Disease · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pelvic Pain/drug therapy · Prostatitis/drug therapy · Quinazolines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Failure · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — as clean a null as this literature produces. In the NIH network's multicentre trial, restricted to men diagnosed within the previous 2 years who had never taken an alpha-blocker — the group earlier small trials suggested would benefit most — 49.3% of men on alfuzosin 10 mg daily and 49.3% on placebo achieved the prespecified response of at least a 4-point fall in the NIH Chronic Prostatitis Symptom Index at 12 weeks (rate difference 0.1%, 95% CI −11.2 to 11.0; P=0.99). Global response assessment was likewise identical (34.8% versus 33.6%, P=0.90), and adverse-event rates were similar. The confidence interval excludes the minimum clinically important difference the trial was built around, so this is evidence of no useful effect in this population, not an underpowered shrug. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): alfuzosin does not improve symptoms of chronic prostatitis / chronic pelvic pain syndrome in alpha-blocker-naive men.

cards.headline: Nickel 2008: NIH-CPSI response in 49.3% on alfuzosin and 49.3% on placebo (difference 0.1%, p=0.99); global response 34.8% versus 33.6%
cards.summary: Nickel 2008: NIH-CPSI response in 49.3% on alfuzosin and 49.3% on placebo (difference 0.1%, p=0.99); global response 34.8% versus 33.6%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Nickel 2008, NIH Chronic Prostatitis Collaborative Research Network)
cards.people: 272 men with chronic prostatitis–chronic pelvic pain syndrome diagnosed within the preceding 2 years and no previous alpha-blocker treatment, randomised to alfuzosin 10 mg daily or placebo for 12 weeks across the NIH network's centres; the primary outcome was a reduction of at least 4 points (the minimal clinically significant difference) in the total NIH Chronic Prostatitis Symptom Index (range 0–43).
cards.result: In both study groups, 49.3% of participants had a decrease of at least 4 points in total NIH-CPSI score (rate difference associated with alfuzosin, 0.1%; 95% CI −11.2 to 11.0; P=0.99). Global response assessment showed similar response rates at 12 weeks: 34.8% in the alfuzosin group and 33.6% in the placebo group (P=0.90). Rates of adverse events in the two groups were also similar.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks is the horizon: the trial does not test longer courses, other alpha-blockers, or men with long-standing symptoms or prior alpha-blocker exposure — the population was deliberately the early, treatment-naive group in which benefit had been claimed. Within that group, the null is precise.
cards.source: Nickel JC et al. Alfuzosin and symptoms of chronic prostatitis-chronic pelvic pain syndrome. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2008. PMID: 19092152. Registry ID: NCT00103402. cards.headline: Synthesis: identical response rates in the population most likely to benefit — the alpha-blocker hypothesis for early CP/CPPS fails its best test
cards.summary: Synthesis: identical response rates in the population most likely to benefit — the alpha-blocker hypothesis for early CP/CPPS fails its best test
cards.people: One multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (272 men, NIH Chronic Prostatitis Collaborative Research Network) of alfuzosin 10 mg daily versus placebo for 12 weeks in alpha-blocker-naive men with recently diagnosed chronic prostatitis / chronic pelvic pain syndrome.
cards.result: Primary response (≥4-point NIH-CPSI fall): 49.3% versus 49.3% (difference 0.1%, 95% CI −11.2 to 11.0). Global response: 34.8% versus 33.6%. Adverse events: similar. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): a single large, well-designed trial with a confidence interval that excludes the prespecified clinically important difference.
cards.watchOut: The high placebo response (49.3%) is itself the clinical lesson: half of these men improve meaningfully in 12 weeks with no active drug, which is what uncontrolled clinic experience with alpha-blockers had been reading as drug effect.
cards.source: Synthesis of Nickel JC et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2008 (PMID: 19092152).

shelves.title: Varicocele repair in subfertile men: pregnancy rates may rise (pooled RR 1.55, low-certainty evidence) — but on live birth, the outcome that matters, the two trials point opposite ways
shelves.question: In subfertile men with varicocele, does surgical repair or embolisation improve pregnancy rates compared with no treatment or delayed treatment?
shelves.mesh: Bias · Confidence Intervals · Embolization, Therapeutic/adverse effects · Female · Humans · Infertility, Male/etiology/surgery/therapy · Live Birth · Male · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Postoperative Complications/etiology · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Rate · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Recurrence · Sclerotherapy/adverse effects/methods · Sperm Count · Testicular Hydrocele/etiology · Varicocele/complications/surgery/therapy
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — treatment may improve pregnancy rates, but the evidence is weak where it counts. The Cochrane review (48 studies, 5,384 participants) found that surgical or radiological treatment may improve pregnancy rates compared with delayed or no treatment (risk ratio 1.55, 95% CI 1.06–2.26; 13 RCTs, 1,193 participants; low-certainty evidence), corresponding to a pregnancy chance of 21% with no or delayed treatment and between 22% and 48% after treatment. For live birth, however, the only two trials disagreed in direction, leaving the effect frankly uncertain (risk ratio 2.27, 95% CI 0.19–26.93; 204 participants; very low-certainty evidence). One comparison does reach moderate certainty: microscopic subinguinal surgery probably improves pregnancy slightly versus other surgical techniques (risk ratio 1.18, 95% CI 1.02–1.36) and probably halves varicocele recurrence (risk ratio 0.48, 95% CI 0.29–0.79). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): varicocele treatment may raise pregnancy rates, but a live-birth benefit is unproven and the choice between surgery and radiological treatment is unresolved.

cards.headline: Persad 2021 (Cochrane): pregnancy RR 1.55 (1.06–2.26) for treatment versus no/delayed treatment — live birth RR 2.27 with a confidence interval from 0.19 to 26.93
cards.summary: Persad 2021 (Cochrane): pregnancy RR 1.55 (1.06–2.26) for treatment versus no/delayed treatment — live birth RR 2.27 with a confidence interval from 0.19 to 26.93
cards.people: 48 randomised studies (5,384 participants) of surgical ligation or radiological treatment (embolisation or sclerotherapy) for varicocele in subfertile men whose female partners were of childbearing age with no fertility problems, compared with no treatment, delayed treatment, other surgical techniques, or other radiological treatments; the review searched to 4 April 2020.
cards.result: Treatment versus non-surgical, delayed, or no treatment: live birth was reported by two studies with differing directions of effect, so whether treatment improves live birth is uncertain (risk ratio 2.27, 95% CI 0.19–26.93; 2 RCTs, N=204; very low-certainty evidence). Pregnancy rates may improve with treatment (risk ratio 1.55, 95% CI 1.06–2.26; 13 RCTs, N=1,193; low-certainty evidence) — couples with no or delayed treatment had a 21% chance of pregnancy, versus between 22% and 48% after treatment. Surgical versus radiological treatment was uncertain for pregnancy (risk ratio 1.13, 95% CI 0.75–1.70; low-certainty). Microscopic subinguinal surgery probably improves pregnancy slightly versus other surgical treatments (risk ratio 1.18, 95% CI 1.02–1.36; 12 RCTs, N=1,473; moderate-certainty) and probably reduces recurrence (risk ratio 0.48, 95% CI 0.29–0.79; 14 RCTs, N=1,565; moderate-certainty).
cards.watchOut: Pregnancy is a couple-level, time-dependent outcome and most included trials were small with methodological limitations; the headline pregnancy pooled estimate carries low certainty and substantial heterogeneity (I²=65%), and the live-birth data — two small trials pointing opposite ways — cannot support the confidence with which repair is often recommended.
cards.source: Persad E et al. Surgical or radiological treatment for varicoceles in subfertile men. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2021. PMID: 33890288. cards.headline: Synthesis: a probable small gain in pregnancies, an unknown gain in babies, and one technique (microscopic subinguinal) with the firmest footing
cards.summary: Synthesis: a probable small gain in pregnancies, an unknown gain in babies, and one technique (microscopic subinguinal) with the firmest footing
cards.people: One Cochrane review of 48 randomised studies (5,384 participants) covering surgical and radiological varicocele treatment in subfertile men, with comparisons against no/delayed treatment, between techniques, and between surgery and radiology.
cards.result: Pregnancy: risk ratio 1.55 (95% CI 1.06–2.26) for treatment versus no or delayed treatment (low certainty); absolute pregnancy chance 21% untreated versus 22–48% treated. Live birth: risk ratio 2.27 (95% CI 0.19–26.93), very low certainty, direction inconsistent between the two trials. Microscopic subinguinal versus other surgery: pregnancy risk ratio 1.18 (1.02–1.36), recurrence risk ratio 0.48 (0.29–0.79), both moderate certainty. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Couples deciding on repair should hear the split plainly: the outcome with any support is pregnancy, not live birth, and assisted reproduction is the competing use of the same time and money — a trade-off this evidence base does not test head-to-head.
cards.source: Synthesis of Persad E et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2021 (PMID: 33890288).

shelves.title: Tadalafil 5 mg daily for prostate symptoms: symptom scores improve about 2–3 points beyond placebo — peak urine flow does not move at any dose
shelves.question: In men with lower urinary tract symptoms from benign prostatic hyperplasia, does tadalafil 5 mg once daily improve symptom scores and flow compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Carbolines/administration & dosage · Cross-Over Studies · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Erectile Dysfunction/drug therapy/etiology · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Maximum Tolerated Dose · Middle Aged · Multivariate Analysis · Phosphodiesterase Inhibitors/administration & dosage · Prostatic Hyperplasia/complications/diagnosis · Reference Values · Severity of Illness Index · Tadalafil · Treatment Outcome · Urination Disorders/drug therapy/etiology/physiopathology · Urodynamics
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for symptoms, not for flow. In the dose-finding trial, the International Prostate Symptom Score fell by 4.9 points on tadalafil 5 mg versus 2.3 points on placebo over 12 weeks (p<0.001), and the 2018 meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (3,973 patients) found the same direction across symptom and erectile-function scores, with more discontinuations for adverse events on tadalafil (odds ratio 1.79, 95% CI 1.12–2.85). The consistent negative is the plumbing: in the dose-finding trial no tadalafil dose — 2.5, 5, 10 or 20 mg — produced a statistically significant effect on peak urine flow versus placebo. So tadalafil makes men feel better and can treat erectile dysfunction at the same time, but it is not doing what an alpha-blocker does to the outlet. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): tadalafil 5 mg daily improves prostate symptom scores modestly beyond placebo across many trials, with no demonstrated improvement in urine flow rate.

cards.headline: Roehrborn 2008: IPSS fell 4.9 points on tadalafil 5 mg versus 2.3 on placebo (p<0.001) — peak flow not significantly different at any dose from 2.5 to 20 mg
cards.summary: Roehrborn 2008: IPSS fell 4.9 points on tadalafil 5 mg versus 2.3 on placebo (p<0.001) — peak flow not significantly different at any dose from 2.5 to 20 mg
cards.people: 1,058 men with benign prostatic hyperplasia lower urinary tract symptoms, after a 4-week placebo run-in, randomised to 12 weeks of once-daily placebo or tadalafil 2.5, 5, 10 or 20 mg.
cards.result: International Prostate Symptom Score least-squares mean change was −3.9 on tadalafil 2.5 mg (p=0.015), −4.9 on 5 mg (p<0.001), −5.2 on 10 mg (p<0.001) and −5.2 on 20 mg (p<0.001), versus −2.3 on placebo, with a dose-response relationship and significant improvements already at 4 weeks. Tadalafil 5, 10 and 20 mg also significantly improved the IPSS irritative and obstructive subscores, IPSS quality of life, and the erectile-function domain in sexually active men with erectile dysfunction. No statistically significant effect of treatment compared with placebo was noted for peak flow at any tadalafil dose. Treatment-emergent adverse events were infrequent in all tadalafil groups, and the authors judged 5 mg to offer the best risk–benefit profile.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks, symptom scores as the currency: the trial shows men report fewer symptoms, but the absent flow effect means the mechanism is unlikely to be outlet relaxation, and there is no information here on retention, progression, or surgery avoided — the long-term outcomes alpha-blockers and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors were judged on.
cards.source: Roehrborn CG et al. Tadalafil administered once daily for lower urinary tract symptoms secondary to benign prostatic hyperplasia: a dose finding study. The Journal of Urology. 2008. PMID: 18722631. cards.headline: Wang 2018 (meta-analysis, 13 RCTs, 3,973 patients): symptom and erectile scores favour tadalafil 5 mg — discontinuation for adverse events higher (OR 1.79)
cards.summary: Wang 2018 (meta-analysis, 13 RCTs, 3,973 patients): symptom and erectile scores favour tadalafil 5 mg — discontinuation for adverse events higher (OR 1.79)
cards.people: 13 publications reporting 13 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials, totalling 3,973 patients, of tadalafil 5 mg once daily for lower urinary tract symptoms and erectile dysfunction, generally over 12 weeks.
cards.result: Tadalafil 5 mg once daily was more effective than placebo on total International Prostate Symptom Score (reported pooled difference −2.02, 95% CI −2.52 to −1.53; P<0.00001), Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia Impact Index (−0.58, 95% CI −0.84 to −0.33), and the erectile-function domain of the International Index of Erectile Function (5.18, 95% CI 4.13–6.23). Discontinuations due to adverse events were more frequent on tadalafil (odds ratio 1.79, 95% CI 1.12–2.85; P=0.01), though the authors judged the drug well tolerated overall.
cards.watchOut: The meta-analysis labels its pooled effects as standardised differences, so its symptom-score figure should be read as corroboration of direction rather than a point estimate in IPSS points; the placebo-subtracted point estimate comes from the individual trials (about 2–3 IPSS points). All included trials were short, and none was powered for retention or surgery.
cards.source: Wang Y et al. Tadalafil 5 mg Once Daily Improves Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms and Erectile Dysfunction: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms. 2018. meta-analysis of randomised trials (wang 2018) 13 publications reporting 13 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials, totalling 3,973 patients, of tadalafil 5 mg once daily for lower urinary tract symptoms and erectile dysfunction, generally over 12 weeks. tadalafil 5 mg once daily was more effective than placebo on total international prostate symptom score (reported pooled difference −2.02, 95% ci −2.52 to −1.53; p<0.00001), benign prostatic hyperplasia impact index (−0.58, 95% ci −0.84 to −0.33), and the erectile-function domain of the international index of erectile function (5.18, 95% ci 4.13–6.23). discontinuations due to adverse events were more frequent on tadalafil (odds ratio 1.79, 95% ci 1.12–2.85; p=0.01), though the authors judged the drug well tolerated overall. the meta-analysis labels its pooled effects as standardised differences, so its symptom-score figure should be read as corroboration of direction rather than a point estimate in ipss points; the placebo-subtracted point estimate comes from the individual trials (about 2–3 ipss points). all included trials were short, and none was powered for retention or surgery. wang y et al. tadalafil 5 mg once daily improves lower urinary tract symptoms and erectile dysfunction: a systematic review and meta-analysis. lower urinary tract symptoms. 2018. pmid: 29341503. mesh: erectile dysfunction/drug therapy · humans · lower urinary tract symptoms/drug therapy/etiology · male · phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitors/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · prostatic hyperplasia/complications/drug therapy · randomized controlled trials as topic · severity of illness index · tadalafil/administration & dosage/therapeutic use

cards.headline: Synthesis: a consistent, modest symptom benefit with a dual erectile benefit — and a flow rate that never moves
cards.summary: Synthesis: a consistent, modest symptom benefit with a dual erectile benefit — and a flow rate that never moves
cards.people: The pivotal dose-finding trial (1,058 men) plus a meta-analysis of 13 randomised placebo-controlled trials (3,973 patients) of tadalafil 5 mg once daily for BPH lower urinary tract symptoms, mostly 12-week studies.
cards.result: IPSS change: −4.9 points on tadalafil 5 mg versus −2.3 on placebo in the dose-finding trial; pooled analyses agree in direction. Erectile function improves in parallel. Peak urine flow: no significant effect at any dose (2.5–20 mg). Discontinuation for adverse events: odds ratio 1.79 (95% CI 1.12–2.85) versus placebo in the meta-analysis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), not Tier C: many concordant randomised trials carry the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Men choosing tadalafil for urinary symptoms should know the trade plainly: it is a symptom-and-erection drug, not an outlet drug — a man whose problem is a weak stream or rising residual volume is not getting that problem treated here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Roehrborn CG et al. The Journal of Urology. 2008 (PMID: 18722631); Wang Y et al. Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms. 2018 (PMID: 29341503).

shelves.title: Vibegron for overactive bladder: about half a void and half a leakage episode a day better than placebo at 12 weeks in the one phase 3 trial — blood-pressure signal no worse than placebo
shelves.question: In adults with overactive bladder, does vibegron 75 mg reduce urgency incontinence and daily voids compared with placebo, and how does it compare with tolterodine?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-3 Receptor Agonists/therapeutic use · Adult · Aged · Delayed-Action Preparations · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Internationality · Male · Middle Aged · Pyrimidinones/therapeutic use · Pyrrolidines/therapeutic use · Tolterodine Tartrate/therapeutic use · Urinary Bladder, Overactive/drug therapy · Urological Agents/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — real but modest, from a single trial. In EMPOWUR, 1,518 patients with overactive bladder were randomised to vibegron 75 mg, placebo, or tolterodine extended-release 4 mg for 12 weeks. Daily voids fell by an adjusted mean of 1.8 on vibegron versus 1.3 on placebo (p<0.001) and 1.6 on tolterodine; among incontinent patients, urge incontinence episodes fell by 2.0 versus 1.4 per day (p<0.0001) and 1.8 on tolterodine. The trial was not designed to declare vibegron superior to tolterodine, so the honest comparison is 'in the same range'. Tolerability was good: discontinuation for adverse events in 1.7% on vibegron versus 1.1% on placebo and 3.3% on tolterodine, and hypertension incidence was 1.7% on both vibegron and placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): vibegron improves overactive bladder symptoms modestly beyond placebo at 12 weeks in one large phase 3 trial, with a clean short-term safety profile.

cards.headline: Staskin 2020 (EMPOWUR): voids −1.8/day on vibegron versus −1.3 on placebo (p<0.001); urge incontinence −2.0 versus −1.4 (p<0.0001); tolterodine −1.6 and −1.8
cards.summary: Staskin 2020 (EMPOWUR): voids −1.8/day on vibegron versus −1.3 on placebo (p<0.001); urge incontinence −2.0 versus −1.4 (p<0.0001); tolterodine −1.6 and −1.8
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo- and active-controlled phase 3 trial (Staskin 2020, EMPOWUR)
cards.people: 1,518 adults with overactive bladder and at least 8 voids per day (up to 25% could have dry overactive bladder, with under 1 urge incontinence episode per day), randomised 5:5:4 to vibegron 75 mg once daily, placebo, or tolterodine extended-release 4 mg for 12 weeks, with 7-day voiding diaries; 90.4% completed the trial.
cards.result: At 12 weeks, micturitions decreased by an adjusted mean of 1.8 episodes per day on vibegron versus 1.3 on placebo (p<0.001, co-primary endpoint) and 1.6 on tolterodine. Among incontinent patients, urge incontinence episodes decreased by an adjusted mean of 2.0 per day on vibegron versus 1.4 on placebo (p<0.0001, co-primary endpoint) and 1.8 on tolterodine. Vibegron was also significantly superior to placebo on urgency episodes, volume per micturition, and the proportion of incontinent patients with at least a 75% reduction in urge incontinence episodes (all p<0.01). Discontinuation because of adverse events: 1.7% on vibegron, 1.1% on placebo, 3.3% on tolterodine. Hypertension incidence was 1.7% on vibegron and 1.7% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks is short for a chronic condition, the placebo response in overactive bladder trials is large (voids fell 1.3/day on placebo), and the tolterodine arm was a reference comparator, not a powered head-to-head test — 'similar-looking numbers' is all this trial licenses. Longer-term persistence and comparative effectiveness against the other beta-3 agonist are outside this record.

shelves.title: Formal one-to-one pelvic-floor training after prostate surgery: incontinence at 12 months was 76% versus 77% after prostatectomy and 65% versus 62% after TURP — no benefit, at extra cost
shelves.question: In men with urinary incontinence after prostate surgery, does formal one-to-one pelvic-floor muscle training speed recovery of continence compared with lifestyle advice alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Exercise Therapy · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pelvic Floor/physiopathology · Prostatectomy/adverse effects/rehabilitation · Transurethral Resection of Prostate/adverse effects/rehabilitation · Urinary Incontinence/etiology/therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — tested properly, in two parallel trials, and found wanting. In MAPS, men incontinent 6 weeks after radical prostatectomy or transurethral resection were randomised to four one-to-one therapist sessions over 3 months or to standard care with lifestyle advice. At 12 months, incontinence rates were 76% (148 of 196) with training versus 77% (151 of 195) with standard care after prostatectomy (absolute difference −1.9%, 95% CI −10 to 6), and 65% (126 of 194) versus 62% (125 of 203) after TURP (difference 3.4%, 95% CI −6 to 13). The training cost more (£180 and £209 extra per patient) with no economically important difference in quality-adjusted life years. The sobering background finding: about two-thirds to three-quarters of men were still incontinent at a year in every arm — a large unmet need that supervised training, at least in settings where exercise information is already widely available, does not meet. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): formal one-to-one pelvic-floor training does not improve continence recovery after prostate surgery beyond standard care and lifestyle advice.

cards.headline: Glazener 2011 (MAPS): incontinence at 12 months 76% versus 77% (prostatectomy trial) and 65% versus 62% (TURP trial) — neither difference significant; costs higher, QALYs identical
cards.summary: Glazener 2011 (MAPS): incontinence at 12 months 76% versus 77% (prostatectomy trial) and 65% versus 62% (TURP trial) — neither difference significant; costs higher, QALYs identical
cards.type: Two parallel randomised controlled trials (Glazener 2011, MAPS)
cards.people: Men in the UK who were incontinent 6 weeks after radical prostatectomy (trial 1, n=411) or transurethral resection of the prostate (trial 2, n=442), recruited across 34 centres, randomised to four one-to-one sessions of pelvic-floor muscle training and bladder training with a specialist therapist over 3 months, or to standard care with lifestyle advice only; primary outcomes were self-reported incontinence and cost per quality-adjusted life year at 12 months, with outcome assessors masked.
cards.result: Trial 1 (prostatectomy): urinary incontinence at 12 months in 148 of 196 men (76%) in the intervention group versus 151 of 195 (77%) in the control group (absolute risk difference −1.9%, 95% CI −10 to 6). Trial 2 (TURP): 126 of 194 (65%) versus 125 of 203 (62%) (risk difference 3.4%, 95% CI −6 to 13). Adjusting for minimisation factors or doing treatment-received analyses did not change the results. No adverse effects were reported. The intervention cost more per patient (£180 in trial 1, £209 in trial 2) with no evidence of an economically important QALY difference (0.002, 95% CI −0.027 to 0.023; and −0.00003, 95% CI −0.026 to 0.026).
cards.watchOut: The control was not 'nothing': men in UK practice already receive pelvic-floor exercise information, so this trial tests the added value of formal one-to-one delivery, not exercises versus no exercises. Self-reported continence by postal questionnaire, and men who never do the exercises dilute the intervention — but the treatment-received analyses were also null.
cards.source: Glazener C et al. Urinary incontinence in men after formal one-to-one pelvic-floor muscle training following radical prostatectomy or transurethral resection of the prostate (MAPS): two parallel randomised controlled trials. Lancet. 2011. PMID: 21741700. Registry ID: ISRCTN87696430. shelves.title: Whole-gland or subtotal HIFU versus prostatectomy (HIFI): salvage-therapy-free survival not inferior at 30 months and continence and erections better preserved — in a non-randomised comparison where HIFU patients were nearly a decade older
shelves.question: In men with low- or intermediate-risk localised prostate cancer, does whole-gland or subtotal high-intensity focused ultrasound preserve continence and erections without compromising cancer control compared with radical prostatectomy?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Humans · Male · France · High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound Ablation/adverse effects · Prospective Studies · Prostatectomy/methods/adverse effects · Prostatic Neoplasms/surgery/pathology/mortality · Treatment Outcome · Ultrasound, High-Intensity Focused, Transrectal/adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — on functional outcomes, in a comparison that cannot fully be trusted on cancer outcomes. The French HIFI study prospectively followed 3,328 men (1,967 HIFU, 1,361 prostatectomy) with low- to intermediate-risk prostate cancer. At 30 months, salvage therapy-free survival was not inferior with HIFU (hazard ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.52–0.97; p=0.008 for noninferiority). Function favoured HIFU: deterioration in urinary continence at 12 months in 29% versus 44%, and a smaller fall in erectile-function scores (median IIEF-5 change −7 versus −13); about 10% of HIFU patients had urinary retention, and grade >IIIa complications were similar (54 of 1,967 versus 29 of 1,361, p=0.3). The structural problem is allocation: this was not randomised, and the HIFU group was much older (median 74.7 versus 65.1 years), so the men, their cancers' management thresholds, and their salvage decisions all differed before treatment began. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): HIFU preserves continence and erections better than prostatectomy with noninferior short-term salvage-free survival in this large prospective non-randomised study; randomised confirmation is lacking.

cards.headline: Ploussard 2025 (HIFI): 30-month salvage therapy-free survival HR 0.71 (noninferior); continence deterioration 29% versus 44%; retention in about 10% after HIFU
cards.summary: Ploussard 2025 (HIFI): 30-month salvage therapy-free survival HR 0.71 (noninferior); continence deterioration 29% versus 44%; retention in about 10% after HIFU
cards.people: 3,328 men with low- to intermediate-risk localised prostate cancer treated at 46 centres in France (2015–2019): 1,967 received whole-gland or subtotal high-intensity focused ultrasound and 1,361 radical prostatectomy, by clinical choice rather than randomisation. Median age was 74.7 years in the HIFU group versus 65.1 years in the prostatectomy group (p<0.001); median PSA was similar (7.1 versus 6.9 ng/ml), and intermediate-risk disease was present in 61% versus 64%.
cards.result: The 30-month salvage therapy-free survival was not inferior in the HIFU group (hazard ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.52–0.97; p=0.008). About 10% of patients experienced urinary retention after HIFU. Grade >IIIa complications occurred in 54 of 1,967 HIFU cases and 29 of 1,361 prostatectomy cases (p=0.3). At 12 months, fewer HIFU patients had deterioration in urinary continence (29% versus 44%), and the decrease in median International Index of Erectile Function-5 score was smaller (−7 versus −13). International Prostate Symptom Scores and quality-of-life scores were comparable.
cards.watchOut: Not randomised, with a 9.6-year median age gap between groups: older men are offered, and accept, salvage therapy differently, which can manufacture 'salvage-free survival' advantage without any difference in cancer behaviour. Thirty months is also short for prostate cancer; metastasis-free and cancer-specific survival were secondary endpoints and the follow-up cannot yet judge them.

cards.summary: Synthesis: the functional advantage is plausible and consistent; the cancer-control claim rests on a comparison the design cannot guarantee
cards.people: One large prospective nationwide non-randomised comparative study (HIFI; 3,328 men, 46 French centres) of whole-gland or subtotal HIFU versus radical prostatectomy in low- to intermediate-risk prostate cancer, with 30-month primary follow-up.
cards.result: Salvage therapy-free survival at 30 months: hazard ratio 0.71 (95% CI 0.52–0.97), meeting noninferiority. Continence deterioration at 12 months: 29% (HIFU) versus 44% (prostatectomy). Erectile-function score fall: −7 versus −13. Grade >IIIa complications: 54 of 1,967 versus 29 of 1,361. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: non-randomised evidence carries this shelf, and the developer should weigh the allocation bias personally.
cards.watchOut: A randomised trial of HIFU versus prostatectomy with long follow-up would settle what HIFI cannot; until then the fairest summary is 'function clearly better preserved, cancer control probably comparable at 30 months in selected men, unproven beyond that'.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ploussard G et al. European Urology. 2025 (PMID: 39632125).

shelves.title: Oral fosfomycin for chronic bacterial prostatitis: cure in roughly three quarters of men in small uncontrolled series — including resistant organisms — with no comparative trial to say what would have happened otherwise
shelves.question: In men with chronic bacterial prostatitis, does oral fosfomycin achieve clinical and microbiological cure, including against resistant organisms?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Chronic Disease · Drug Resistance, Multiple, Bacterial · Enterococcus faecalis/drug effects · Escherichia coli/drug effects · Fosfomycin/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Humans · Klebsiella/drug effects · Male · Microbial Sensitivity Tests · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Prostatitis/drug therapy/microbiology
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — promising numbers, no controls. In the largest prospective series, 44 men with chronic bacterial prostatitis — 59% with multidrug-resistant organisms and all strains fosfomycin-susceptible — were treated with fosfomycin 3 g daily for a week then every 48 hours for 6–12 weeks: the cure rate was 82% at the end of treatment and 73% at 6 months, with microbiological eradication in 86% and 77% respectively, and diarrhoea in 18%. A smaller pilot combining fosfomycin with N-acetyl-L-cysteine in 28 difficult-to-treat men (68% ESBL strains) found microbiological eradication in 75% and clinical cure in 71.4%. What is missing is any comparison: chronic bacterial prostatitis relapses and remits, and without a control group these cure rates cannot be separated from natural history, prior-treatment washout, or selection of men whose organisms happened to be susceptible. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): oral fosfomycin cures about three quarters of selected men with chronic bacterial prostatitis in uncontrolled series, and is a reasonable salvage option where fluoroquinolones have failed — comparative evidence does not exist.

cards.headline: Karaiskos 2019: cure 82% at end of treatment and 73% at 6 months in 44 men (59% multidrug-resistant) — diarrhoea in 18%
cards.summary: Karaiskos 2019: cure 82% at end of treatment and 73% at 6 months in 44 men (59% multidrug-resistant) — diarrhoea in 18%
cards.people: 44 men with chronic bacterial prostatitis, treated prospectively with oral fosfomycin 3 g every 24 hours for 1 week followed by 3 g every 48 hours, for 6 weeks (25 men) or 12 weeks (19 men, prolonged because of prostatic calcifications). Escherichia coli caused 66% of cases, Klebsiella spp. 14% and Enterococcus faecalis 14%; most strains were multidrug-resistant (59%), 23% had an ESBL phenotype, 33 of 44 strains were fluoroquinolone-resistant, and all were fosfomycin-susceptible.
cards.result: The cure rate was 82% at the end of treatment and 80% and 73% at 3 and 6 months. Microbiological eradication was achieved in 86% at the end of treatment and 77% at 6 months. Failure was observed in 12 patients. The most common adverse event was diarrhoea (18%).
cards.watchOut: No control group, no blinding, and a selected population: every isolate was fosfomycin-susceptible by design, and men were treated for 6–12 weeks — far longer than most antibiotic courses — so the cure rate bundles drug effect, duration, and selection together. Relapse after 6 months is unmeasured here.
cards.source: Karaiskos I et al. Oral fosfomycin for the treatment of chronic bacterial prostatitis. The Journal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy. 2019. PMID: 30796442. cards.headline: Cai 2020 (pilot): fosfomycin plus N-acetyl-L-cysteine — eradication in 21 of 28 men (75%), clinical cure in 20 (71.4%), including 15 of 19 with ESBL strains
cards.summary: Cai 2020 (pilot): fosfomycin plus N-acetyl-L-cysteine — eradication in 21 of 28 men (75%), clinical cure in 20 (71.4%), including 15 of 19 with ESBL strains
cards.people: 28 men with clinically and microbiologically confirmed chronic bacterial prostatitis and several previous treatment failures or ESBL-producing strains, at a single urological institution, treated with fosfomycin trometamol 3 g daily for 2 days then 3 g every 48 hours for 2 weeks, combined with N-acetyl-L-cysteine 600 mg daily for 2 weeks; isolates were Escherichia coli (23 patients), Enterococcus spp. (3) and Klebsiella oxytoca (2), with ESBL strains in 19 (67.8%).
cards.result: Microbiological eradication was documented in 21 patients (75%) at the second follow-up visit (6 months after treatment) and clinical cure in 20 patients (71.4%). Fifteen of 19 patients (78.9%) with ESBL strains were cured. No significant side effects were reported.
cards.watchOut: A 28-man single-centre pilot of a two-drug combination: nothing here separates fosfomycin's contribution from N-acetyl-L-cysteine's, and a 2-week course producing 6-month cure rates similar to a 6–12-week course in the other series underlines how much of the signal may be patient selection and natural history rather than regimen.
cards.source: Cai T et al. Fosfomycin trometamol and N-acetyl-L-cysteine as combined oral therapy of difficult-to-treat chronic bacterial prostatitis: Results of a pilot study. cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent cure rates around three quarters in the men clinicians most worry about — and not one controlled comparison
cards.summary: Synthesis: consistent cure rates around three quarters in the men clinicians most worry about — and not one controlled comparison
cards.people: Two uncontrolled prospective series totalling 72 men with chronic bacterial prostatitis, heavily weighted to multidrug-resistant and fluoroquinolone-resistant organisms: fosfomycin alone for 6–12 weeks (44 men) and fosfomycin plus N-acetyl-L-cysteine for 2 weeks (28 men).
cards.result: Cure: 82% at end of treatment and 73% at 6 months (fosfomycin alone); clinical cure 71.4% and eradication 75% at 6 months (combination pilot). ESBL-strain cure: 15 of 19 (78.9%) in the pilot. Main harm: diarrhoea in 18% in the larger series. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C: uncontrolled observational evidence only.
cards.watchOut: The clinical niche is real — few oral options penetrate the prostate against resistant organisms — so these series justify use as salvage therapy and justify a randomised trial; they do not establish that fosfomycin outperforms placebo, watchful waiting, or any comparator.
cards.source: Synthesis of Karaiskos I et al. The Journal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy. 2019 (PMID: 30796442); Cai T et al. International Journal of Antimicrobial Agents. 2020 (PMID: 32156620).

shelves.title: Duloxetine for incontinence after prostatectomy: leakage episodes fall by about half while taking it — and continence flips back within weeks of stopping
shelves.question: In men with stress incontinence after radical prostatectomy, does duloxetine speed return of continence compared with placebo or pelvic-floor training alone?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic Uptake Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Chi-Square Distribution · Double-Blind Method · Duloxetine Hydrochloride · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Paris · Pilot Projects · Placebo Effect · Prospective Studies · Prostatectomy/adverse effects · Quality of Life · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Surveys and Questionnaires · Thiophenes/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Urinary Incontinence/etiology/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — only while the drug is on board. In the small placebo-controlled trial, incontinence episode frequency fell by 52.2% on duloxetine 80 mg daily over 3 months while rising 19.0% on placebo (mean difference 71.2%, 95% CI 41.0–101.4; p<0.0001), with parallel improvements in incontinence quality-of-life scores. The larger trial, of duloxetine added to rehabilitation versus rehabilitation alone, found more men dry at 16 weeks on the combination (39 versus 27, p=0.007) — but four weeks after duloxetine was stopped the picture reversed (23 dry versus 38, p=0.008), converging by 24 weeks (31 versus 41, p=0.08). So duloxetine rents continence rather than restoring it: it suppresses leakage pharmacologically while taken, at an adverse-event rate of 15.2% in the larger trial, and the underlying sphincter recovery proceeds at its own pace underneath. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): duloxetine reduces leakage after prostatectomy in two randomised trials, but the benefit does not survive stopping the drug.

cards.headline: Cornu 2011: incontinence episodes −52.2% on duloxetine versus +19.0% on placebo over 3 months (difference 71.2%, p<0.0001) — in 31 men
cards.summary: Cornu 2011: incontinence episodes −52.2% on duloxetine versus +19.0% on placebo over 3 months (difference 71.2%, p<0.0001) — in 31 men
cards.people: 31 men with mild-to-moderate stress urinary incontinence after radical prostatectomy at a single centre, randomised after a 2-week placebo run-in to duloxetine 80 mg daily (n=16) or matching placebo (n=15) for 3 months; the primary outcome was the relative variation in incontinence episode frequency, with quality-of-life questionnaires and a 1-hour pad test as secondary measures.
cards.result: Reduction in incontinence episode frequency was significantly greater with duloxetine than placebo (mean variation −52.2% ± 38.6 [range −100 to +46] versus +19.0% ± 43.5 [range −53 to +104]; mean difference 71.2%; 95% CI 41.0–101.4; p<0.0001). The IIQ-SF total score, UDI-SF total score, the stress-incontinence subscore of the Urinary Symptom Profile, and question 3 of the ICIQ-SF questionnaire all improved significantly in the duloxetine group (p=0.006, p=0.02, p=0.0004, and p=0.003 respectively). Both treatments were well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-one men at one centre, labelled 'preliminary' by its own authors: the effect size is large but the confidence interval is wide (41.0–101.4 percentage points), and a 3-month on-treatment endpoint cannot distinguish faster recovery from pharmacological suppression — the question the second trial answers.
cards.source: Cornu JN et al. Duloxetine for mild to moderate postprostatectomy incontinence: preliminary results of a randomised, placebo-controlled trial. European Urology. 2011. PMID: 21030144. cards.headline: Filocamo 2007: more men dry on duloxetine plus rehabilitation at 16 weeks (39 vs 27) — four weeks after stopping, fewer (23 vs 38)
cards.summary: Filocamo 2007: more men dry on duloxetine plus rehabilitation at 16 weeks (39 vs 27) — four weeks after stopping, fewer (23 vs 38)
cards.people: 112 men with post-prostatectomy stress incontinence (at least 4 incontinence episodes daily) randomised after catheter removal to rehabilitation plus duloxetine (group A) or rehabilitation alone (group B) for 16 weeks, after which both groups stopped duloxetine/placebo and continued rehabilitation; 102 men completed the study, with bladder diaries and the Incontinence Quality of Life questionnaire.
cards.result: Pad use fell significantly more in group A. After 16 weeks, 39 patients in group A versus 27 in group B were dry (p=0.007). At 20 weeks — 4 weeks after planned duloxetine interruption — the direction reversed: 23 men dry in group A versus 38 in group B (p=0.008). By 24 weeks the counts were 31 versus 41 (p=0.08). The decrease in incontinence episode frequency and improvements in I-QoL scores were significantly greater in group A during the first 16 weeks. The adverse-event rate for duloxetine was 15.2%.
cards.watchOut: Not placebo-controlled for the drug comparison in the way the smaller trial was, and the dry counts are reported without full denominators per time point; but the within-trial reversal after stopping is the key observation and it is internally consistent — the drug holds leakage down, it does not retrain the sphincter.
cards.source: Filocamo MT et al. Pharmacologic treatment in postprostatectomy stress urinary incontinence. European Urology. 2007. PMID: 16942833. cards.headline: Synthesis: two trials agree on an on-treatment benefit and, between them, prove it does not outlast the prescription
cards.summary: Synthesis: two trials agree on an on-treatment benefit and, between them, prove it does not outlast the prescription
cards.people: Two randomised trials in post-prostatectomy stress incontinence: a 31-man double-blind placebo-controlled trial of duloxetine 80 mg for 3 months, and a 112-man trial of duloxetine plus rehabilitation versus rehabilitation alone for 16 weeks with post-stopping follow-up to 24 weeks.
cards.result: On treatment: incontinence episodes −52.2% versus +19.0% on placebo (p<0.0001); dry men 39 versus 27 at 16 weeks (p=0.007). After stopping: dry men 23 versus 38 at 20 weeks (p=0.008), converging by 24 weeks (31 versus 41, p=0.08). Duloxetine adverse-event rate 15.2% in the larger trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), not Tier C: two randomised trials carry the shelf, with the harm and the reversibility on its face.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial was powered for, or reported, the outcomes men ultimately care about — pad-free status at a year, or avoidance of sling or sphincter surgery — so duloxetine's place is symptomatic bridging, judged month by month.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cornu JN et al. European Urology. 2011 (PMID: 21030144); Filocamo MT et al. European Urology. 2007 (PMID: 16942833).

shelves.title: Silodosin versus tamsulosin for prostate symptoms: no better on symptoms or flow in the head-to-head trial — but absent or reduced ejaculation in 14% versus 2%
shelves.question: In men with benign prostatic hyperplasia, does silodosin relieve symptoms better than tamsulosin — and how much more ejaculatory dysfunction does it cause?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic alpha-1 Receptor Antagonists/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Europe · Humans · Indoles/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Male · Middle Aged · Nocturia/drug therapy/etiology · Placebo Effect · Prostatic Hyperplasia/complications/drug therapy · Quality of Life · Sulfonamides/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Tamsulosin · Treatment Outcome · Urination/drug effects · Urination Disorders/drug therapy/etiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on efficacy; the difference between these drugs is in the bedroom, not the bathroom. In the European head-to-head trial (955 men randomised), the placebo-subtracted improvement in total symptom score was −2.3 points (95% CI −3.2 to −1.4) for silodosin 8 mg and −2.0 points (95% CI −2.9 to −1.1) for tamsulosin 0.4 mg, with responder rates of 66.8% versus 65.4% versus 50.8% on placebo; the 5-trial meta-analysis likewise found no significant difference between the drugs in total symptom score, storage symptoms, peak flow, or quality of life. The one clear separation was ejaculation: reduced or absent ejaculation during orgasm in 14% of silodosin-treated men versus 2% on tamsulosin (1.3% stopped silodosin because of it), an effect the trial attributes to silodosin's potent alpha-1A selectivity and describes as reversible. Discontinuation for adverse events was otherwise low and similar (2.1% versus 1.0% versus 1.6% on placebo). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): silodosin is not superior to tamsulosin for symptoms or flow, and it costs substantially more ejaculatory dysfunction.

cards.summary: Chapple 2011: IPSS advantage over placebo −2.3 points (silodosin) versus −2.0 (tamsulosin); ejaculation reduced or absent in 14% versus 2%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo- and active-controlled trial (Chapple 2011)
cards.people: 955 men aged at least 50 years with an International Prostate Symptom Score of at least 13 and maximum flow rate above 4 and at most 15 ml/s, at 72 sites in 11 European countries, randomised (2:2:1) after wash-out and placebo run-in to silodosin 8 mg (n=381), tamsulosin 0.4 mg (n=384), or placebo (n=190) once daily for 12 weeks.
cards.result: The change in total IPSS was significantly superior to placebo for both active drugs (p<0.001): difference versus placebo −2.3 (95% CI −3.2 to −1.4) for silodosin and −2.0 (95% CI −2.9 to −1.1) for tamsulosin. IPSS responder rates (at least 25% improvement) were 66.8% on silodosin and 65.4% on tamsulosin versus 50.8% on placebo (p<0.001). Only silodosin significantly reduced nocturia versus placebo (change −0.9 versus −0.8 versus −0.7; p=0.013 for silodosin). Peak flow rose by 3.77 ml/s on silodosin, 3.53 on tamsulosin and 2.93 on placebo, not statistically significant versus placebo for either drug (p=0.089 and p=0.221). The most frequent adverse event with silodosin was reduced or absent ejaculation during orgasm (14%), higher than with tamsulosin (2%); only 1.3% of silodosin-treated patients discontinued because of it, and overall discontinuation for adverse events was 2.1%, 1.0% and 1.6% respectively.
cards.watchOut: The trial was designed to show superiority to placebo and noninferiority to tamsulosin, not superiority to tamsulosin — so 'no better than tamsulosin' is what the design can support, and the nocturia finding is one secondary endpoint among many. Twelve weeks says nothing about long-term retention or surgery outcomes.
cards.source: Chapple CR et al. Silodosin therapy for lower urinary tract symptoms in men with suspected benign prostatic hyperplasia: results of an international, randomized, double-blind, placebo- and active-controlled clinical trial performed in Europe. European Urology. 2011. PMID: 21109344. Registry ID: NCT00359905. cards.headline: Wu 2013 (meta-analysis, 5 RCTs, 2,595 patients): no significant difference from tamsulosin on total IPSS, storage symptoms, flow or quality of life — retrograde ejaculation higher
cards.summary: Wu 2013 (meta-analysis, 5 RCTs, 2,595 patients): no significant difference from tamsulosin on total IPSS, storage symptoms, flow or quality of life — retrograde ejaculation higher
cards.people: Five randomised placebo- and active-controlled trials of silodosin for lower urinary tract symptoms associated with benign prostatic hyperplasia, totalling 2,595 patients, identified from Medline, Embase and the Cochrane Library.
cards.result: Silodosin significantly improved total IPSS, IPSS subscores and peak flow versus placebo. Compared with tamsulosin, silodosin showed greater improvement in voiding symptoms, but no significant differences were observed in total IPSS, IPSS storage symptoms, peak flow, or quality of life. Silodosin carried a higher incidence of retrograde ejaculation than both placebo and tamsulosin, with the same low incidence of dizziness and headache as placebo and tamsulosin.
cards.watchOut: A 2013 meta-analysis of five trials, several from the drug's development programme; its 'possibly superior for voiding symptoms' phrasing rests on a subscore, while every headline outcome — total symptoms, flow, quality of life — was statistically indistinguishable from tamsulosin.
cards.source: Wu YJ et al. A meta-analysis of efficacy and safety of the new α1A-adrenoceptor-selective antagonist silodosin for treating lower urinary tract symptoms associated with BPH. Prostate Cancer and Prostatic Diseases. 2013. PMID: 22986578. cards.headline: Synthesis: pick between these two alpha-blockers on ejaculation, not on expected symptom relief
cards.summary: Synthesis: pick between these two alpha-blockers on ejaculation, not on expected symptom relief
cards.people: The European head-to-head randomised trial (955 men, 12 weeks) plus a meta-analysis of five randomised trials (2,595 patients) comparing silodosin 8 mg with placebo and with tamsulosin 0.4 mg in BPH lower urinary tract symptoms.
cards.result: Symptom benefit over placebo: −2.3 IPSS points (silodosin) versus −2.0 (tamsulosin); responder rates 66.8% versus 65.4%. Between-drug differences in total IPSS, storage symptoms, peak flow and quality of life: not significant in trial or meta-analysis. Reduced or absent ejaculation: 14% on silodosin versus 2% on tamsulosin. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for the superiority question, with the ejaculatory harm on the face of the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Men who are sexually active and value ejaculation bear the cost difference; men untroubled by it get equivalent relief either way. Neither record addresses combination therapy, long-term outcomes, or men with very large prostates.
cards.source: Synthesis of Chapple CR et al. European Urology. 2011 (PMID: 21109344); Wu YJ et al. Prostate Cancer and Prostatic Diseases. 2013 (PMID: 22986578).

shelves.title: Prostatic urethral lift (UroLift) for BPH: symptom scores beat sham at 3 months and held to 5 years (IPSS improvement 36%, retreatment 13.6%) — and beat TURP on recovery and ejaculation preservation in BPH6
shelves.question: In men with lower urinary tract symptoms from benign prostatic hyperplasia, does the prostatic urethral lift procedure improve symptoms and flow compared with sham — and how does it compare with transurethral resection on recovery and sexual function?
shelves.mesh: Double-Blind Method · Ejaculation · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Minimally Invasive Surgical Procedures · Penile Erection · Prospective Studies · Prostatic Hyperplasia/complications · Prostatism/etiology · Prostatism/physiopathology · Prostatism/surgery · Prostheses and Implants · Quality of Life · Reoperation · Severity of Illness Index · Sexuality · Treatment Outcome · Urodynamics
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a sham-controlled win plus a favourable head-to-head on the outcomes TURP puts at risk. In the L.I.F.T. study (206 men randomised 2:1 to lift or sham), IPSS improvement after the lift was 88% greater than that of sham at 3 months; improvements in IPSS, quality of life, BPH impact index and peak flow were durable through 5 years at 36%, 50%, 52% and 44% respectively, with surgical retreatment in 13.6% over 5 years and no de novo, sustained erectile or ejaculatory dysfunction. In BPH6 (80 men, lift versus TURP), the lift was noninferior and superior on the composite BPH6 responder endpoint, with superior preservation of ejaculation and quality of recovery (p<0.01) and significant symptom relief in both arms. The trade: roughly one in seven lift patients needed surgical retreatment within 5 years, and the studied prostates were 30-80 cc — the evidence does not cover large glands. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): prostatic urethral lift gives durable, sham-beating symptom relief for men with 30-80 cc prostates, preserving ejaculation at the price of a 13.6% 5-year retreatment rate.

cards.headline: Roehrborn 2017 (L.I.F.T., 5-year report): IPSS improvement 88% greater than sham at 3 months; durable 5-year improvements of 36% (IPSS), 50% (quality of life) and 44% (flow), retreatment 13.6%, no de novo sexual dysfunction
cards.summary: Roehrborn 2017 (L.I.F.T., 5-year report): IPSS improvement 88% greater than sham at 3 months; durable 5-year improvements of 36% (IPSS), 50% (quality of life) and 44% (flow), retreatment 13.6%, no de novo sexual dysfunction
cards.people: 206 men aged 50 years or older with IPSS above 12, peak flow rate 12 ml/s or less and prostate volume 30-80 cc, at 19 centres in North America and Australia, randomised 2:1 to prostatic urethral lift (permanent UroLift implants placed to hold open the lateral lobes of the prostate) or blinded sham control; after the randomised comparison at 3 months, lift patients were followed to 5 years.
cards.result: IPSS improvement after the lift was 88% greater than that of sham at 3 months. Symptoms and quality of life were significantly improved by 2 weeks, with return to preoperative physical activity within 8.6 days. Improvements in IPSS, quality of life, BPH impact index and peak flow were durable through 5 years at 36%, 50%, 52% and 44% respectively, with no difference between intention-to-treat and per-protocol populations. Surgical retreatment was 13.6% over 5 years. Adverse events were mild to moderate and transient; sexual function was stable over 5 years with no de novo, sustained erectile or ejaculatory dysfunction.
cards.watchOut: After 3 months there is no control group — the 5-year durability figures are within-arm changes in a cohort whose non-responders could exit to retreatment, which flatters durability. The earlier 3-year report of this trial (Roehrborn 2015) is the same study and is not carded separately.
cards.source: Roehrborn CG et al. Five year results of the prospective randomized controlled prostatic urethral L.I.F.T. study. The Canadian journal of urology. 2017. PMID: 28646935. cards.headline: Sønksen 2015 (BPH6): lift superior to TURP on the composite responder endpoint, with superior ejaculation preservation and recovery quality (p<0.01); symptom relief significant in both arms
cards.summary: Sønksen 2015 (BPH6): lift superior to TURP on the composite responder endpoint, with superior ejaculation preservation and recovery quality (p<0.01); symptom relief significant in both arms
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial versus TURP (Sønksen 2015, BPH6)
cards.people: 80 men with BPH lower urinary tract symptoms at 10 European centres, randomised to prostatic urethral lift or transurethral resection of the prostate; the BPH6 responder endpoint combines symptom relief, quality of recovery, erectile and ejaculatory function preservation, continence preservation and safety, assessed to 12 months.
cards.result: The study demonstrated not only noninferiority but also superiority of the lift over TURP on the BPH6 composite endpoint (one-sided lower 95% confidence limit). Preservation of ejaculation and quality of recovery were superior with the lift (p<0.01). Significant symptom relief was achieved in both treatment arms.
cards.watchOut: Only 80 men, unblinded (participants knew their arm), and the headline endpoint is a novel composite that weights recovery and sexual preservation — domains where a tissue-sparing procedure is structurally favoured — rather than raw symptom or flow superiority; the record does not print the arms' IPSS changes in its abstract.
cards.source: Sønksen J et al. Prospective, randomized, multinational study of prostatic urethral lift versus transurethral resection of the prostate: 12-month results from the BPH6 study. European urology. 2015. PMID: 25937539. Registry ID: NCT01533038. cards.headline: Synthesis: sham-beating relief that lasts, bought with retreatment — and a genuine sexual-function advantage over resection
cards.summary: Synthesis: sham-beating relief that lasts, bought with retreatment — and a genuine sexual-function advantage over resection
cards.people: Two randomised trials of prostatic urethral lift in BPH: L.I.F.T. (206 men, versus sham, follow-up to 5 years) and BPH6 (80 men, versus TURP, 12 months).
cards.result: Versus sham: IPSS effect 88% greater at 3 months; 5-year within-arm improvements 36% (IPSS) and 44% (flow); surgical retreatment 13.6% at 5 years. Versus TURP: composite responder endpoint superior, ejaculation preservation and recovery superior (p<0.01), symptom relief in both arms. De novo sustained erectile or ejaculatory dysfunction: none in L.I.F.T. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The two trials answer different questions (does it work at all; how does it compare with resection) and neither enrols prostates above 80 cc or men in retention; long-term comparative data against TURP beyond 12 months are absent from the carded record.
cards.source: Synthesis of Roehrborn CG et al. The Canadian journal of urology. 2017 (PMID: 28646935); Sønksen J et al. European urology. 2015 (PMID: 25937539).

shelves.title: Aquablation versus TURP (WATER): symptom relief noninferior at 6 months, fewer persistent complications (26% versus 42%) and far less anejaculation (10% versus 36%)
shelves.question: In men with moderate-to-severe lower urinary tract symptoms from benign prostatic hyperplasia, is robot-assisted Aquablation (waterjet ablation) noninferior to transurethral resection for symptom relief, and does it differ on complications and ejaculatory dysfunction?
shelves.mesh: Ablation Techniques/adverse effects · Ablation Techniques/methods · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Ejaculation/physiology · Electrocoagulation/adverse effects · Electrocoagulation/methods · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Postoperative Complications/epidemiology · Postoperative Complications/etiology · Postoperative Complications/physiopathology · Prospective Studies · Prostate/surgery · Prostatic Hyperplasia/diagnosis · Prostatic Hyperplasia/surgery · Robotic Surgical Procedures/adverse effects · Robotic Surgical Procedures/methods · Severity of Illness Index · Sexual Dysfunction, Physiological/epidemiology · Sexual Dysfunction, Physiological/etiology · Sexual Dysfunction, Physiological/physiopathology · Transurethral Resection of Prostate/adverse effects · Transurethral Resection of Prostate/methods · Treatment Outcome · Water
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — as a comparative claim: equal symptom relief with a better safety and ejaculation profile, in one trial. WATER randomised 181 men with moderate-to-severe BPH symptoms to Aquablation or TURP in a double-blind design. At 6 months both groups had large IPSS improvements and the prespecified noninferiority hypothesis for symptom relief was met (p<0.0001). The primary safety endpoint (persistent Clavien-Dindo grade 1, or grade 2 or higher complications) occurred in 26% after Aquablation versus 42% after TURP — meeting noninferiority and then superiority (p=0.0149) — and among sexually active men anejaculation occurred in 10% versus 36% (p=0.0003). Operative time was similar (33 versus 36 minutes) though resection itself was far quicker with the waterjet (4 versus 27 minutes; p<0.0001). The record suggests larger prostates (50-80 ml) gained the most, but 6 months is early for a prostate operation whose comparator is judged over years. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): Aquablation matches TURP's early symptom relief with fewer persistent complications and much less anejaculation, on a single trial with 6-month primary outcomes.

cards.headline: Gilling 2018 (WATER): IPSS noninferiority met (p<0.0001); safety endpoint 26% versus 42% favouring Aquablation (p=0.0149); anejaculation 10% versus 36% (p=0.0003)
cards.summary: Gilling 2018 (WATER): IPSS noninferiority met (p<0.0001); safety endpoint 26% versus 42% favouring Aquablation (p=0.0149); anejaculation 10% versus 36% (p=0.0003)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial versus TURP (Gilling 2018, WATER)
cards.people: 181 patients with moderate-to-severe lower urinary tract symptoms related to benign prostatic hyperplasia, in a double-blind multicentre prospective randomised trial of Aquablation (robot-assisted waterjet ablation) versus transurethral resection of the prostate; primary efficacy endpoint was IPSS reduction at 6 months and the primary safety endpoint was persistent Clavien-Dindo grade 1, or grade 2 or higher, operative complications.
cards.result: At month 6, both groups experienced large IPSS improvements and the prespecified noninferiority hypothesis was satisfied (p<0.0001); the record does not print the arms' absolute IPSS changes in its abstract. The primary safety endpoint occurred in 26% (Aquablation) versus 42% (TURP), meeting noninferiority and demonstrating superiority (p=0.0149). Among sexually active men, anejaculation occurred in 10% versus 36% (p=0.0003). Mean total operative time was similar (33 versus 36 minutes; p=0.2752) but resection time was lower with Aquablation (4 versus 27 minutes; p<0.0001). Larger prostates (50 to 80 ml) showed a more pronounced superior safety and efficacy benefit.
cards.watchOut: A single industry-era pivotal trial with 6-month primary endpoints: retreatment, durability and late bleeding — the outcomes on which prostate procedures are ultimately judged — are outside the primary record, and the absolute IPSS changes are not printed in the abstract, so the size of symptom relief cannot be quoted from the verified record.
cards.source: Gilling P et al. WATER: A Double-Blind, Randomized, Controlled Trial of Aquablation® vs Transurethral Resection of the Prostate in Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia. The Journal of urology. 2018. PMID: 29360529. cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial, a clean comparative win on harm outcomes, durability unproven
cards.people: One randomised double-blind trial (WATER, 181 men with BPH) of Aquablation versus transurethral resection, with primary outcomes at 6 months.
cards.result: Symptom relief: noninferior (p<0.0001 for noninferiority). Persistent complications: 26% versus 42% (p=0.0149). Anejaculation in sexually active men: 10% versus 36% (p=0.0003). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) as a comparative claim, Tier C because a single trial carries it.

shelves.title: Rezūm water-vapour therapy for BPH: IPSS fell 11.2 points versus 4.3 on sham at 3 months, flow up 6.2 ml/s, sustained to 12 months with sexual function preserved
shelves.question: In men with lower urinary tract symptoms from benign prostatic hyperplasia, does transurethral convective water-vapour (steam) ablation with the Rezūm system improve symptoms and flow compared with a sham control procedure?
shelves.mesh: Cystoscopy · Double-Blind Method · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Hyperthermia, Induced/methods · Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms/etiology · Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms/physiopathology · Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms/surgery · Male · Middle Aged · Minimally Invasive Surgical Procedures/methods · Prostatic Hyperplasia/complications · Prostatic Hyperplasia/diagnosis · Prostatic Hyperplasia/surgery · Steam · Time Factors · Transurethral Resection of Prostate/methods · Treatment Outcome · Urodynamics/physiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one sham-controlled trial with a large symptom margin. McVary's multicentre trial randomised 197 men (prostate 30-80 cc, IPSS at least 13, flow 15 ml/s or less) 2:1 to Rezūm water-vapour ablation or a rigid-cystoscopy sham with simulated treatment sounds. At 3 months IPSS had fallen by 11.2 ± 7.6 points on active treatment versus 4.3 ± 6.9 on sham (p<0.0001); in treated men the baseline IPSS of 22 fell by 50% or more at 3, 6 and 12 months, and peak flow rose by 6.2 ml/s at 3 months and stayed up through 12 months (p<0.0001). No de novo erectile dysfunction was reported, and adverse events were mild to moderate and resolved quickly. What one trial cannot show: how steam ablation compares with resection or with the lift procedure, and durability beyond a year. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): Rezūm gives rapid, sham-beating symptom and flow improvement sustained to 12 months in men with 30-80 cc prostates, preserving erectile and ejaculatory function in the trial record.

cards.headline: McVary 2016: IPSS reduction 11.2 versus 4.3 points at 3 months (p<0.0001); peak flow +6.2 ml/s sustained to 12 months; no de novo erectile dysfunction
cards.summary: McVary 2016: IPSS reduction 11.2 versus 4.3 points at 3 months (p<0.0001); peak flow +6.2 ml/s sustained to 12 months; no de novo erectile dysfunction
cards.people: 197 men aged 50 years or older with IPSS of 13 or greater, maximum flow rate of 15 ml/s or less and prostate size 30-80 cc, randomised 2:1 at multiple centres to convective water-vapour thermal therapy with the Rezūm System (n=136) or control rigid cystoscopy with simulated active-treatment sounds (n=61); treated subjects were followed for 12 months.
cards.result: IPSS fell by 11.2 ± 7.6 points on thermal therapy versus 4.3 ± 6.9 on control at 3 months (p<0.0001). In treated men, baseline IPSS of 22 decreased by 50% or more at 3, 6 and 12 months (p<0.0001); peak flow rate increased by 6.2 ml/s at 3 months and was sustained throughout 12 months (p<0.0001). Improvement was already significant at 2 weeks (IPSS 18.6; p=0.0006). No de novo erectile dysfunction was reported; adverse events were mild to moderate and resolved quickly.
cards.watchOut: A single trial with a 3-month blinded comparison and 12-month uncontrolled follow-up; the sham's 4.3-point IPSS fall shows the size of the procedural placebo effect the 11.2-point result must be read against. Ejaculatory outcomes are asserted qualitatively in the record ('preserves erectile and ejaculatory function') without printed rates.
cards.source: McVary KT et al. Minimally Invasive Prostate Convective Water Vapor Energy Ablation: A Multicenter, Randomized, Controlled Study for the Treatment of Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms Secondary to Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia. The Journal of urology. 2016. PMID: 26614889. shelves.title: Low-intensity shockwave therapy for erectile dysfunction: 57% could have intercourse without medication after treatment versus 9% on placebo at 5 weeks — but the validated IIEF erectile score did not significantly improve
shelves.question: In men with organic erectile dysfunction, does low-intensity extracorporeal shockwave therapy improve erectile function compared with placebo (sham) treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Double-Blind Method · Erectile Dysfunction/therapy · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome · Ultrasonic Therapy/methods
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — one small placebo-controlled trial whose two outcome measures disagree. Olsen randomised 112 men with organic erectile dysfunction who could not have intercourse with or without medication to five weekly shockwave treatments or placebo; 105 were assessed (51 active, 54 placebo). Five weeks after treatment, 29 men (57%) in the active group could obtain an erection and have intercourse without medication versus 5 (9%) on placebo (p=0.0001), and Erection Hardness Scale scores improved significantly — but the IIEF Erectile Function domain, the field's standard validated score, showed no significant result. By 24 weeks, after the placebo group had crossed to active treatment, only 7 (19%) of the active group and 9 (23%) of the crossed-over group remained able to have intercourse without medication. The trialists themselves call for a larger multicentre trial. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): shockwave therapy may restore medication-free intercourse in some men with organic ED, but the single small trial's null validated-score result and fading effect keep this at MAYBE.

cards.headline: Olsen 2015: medication-free intercourse in 57% versus 9% at 5 weeks (p=0.0001), significant Erection Hardness gains — but no significant IIEF Erectile Function result, and only 19% still medication-free at 24 weeks
cards.summary: Olsen 2015: medication-free intercourse in 57% versus 9% at 5 weeks (p=0.0001), significant Erection Hardness gains — but no significant IIEF Erectile Function result, and only 19% still medication-free at 24 weeks
cards.people: 112 men with erectile dysfunction of organic origin, unable to have intercourse with or without medication, randomised to low-intensity extracorporeal shockwave therapy (n=51 assessed) or placebo (n=54 assessed), five treatments over 5 weeks, with assessments at 5, 12 and 24 weeks using interview, the Erection Hardness Scale and the IIEF-15 questionnaire; after 10 weeks the placebo group received active treatment.
cards.result: After treatment, 29 men (57%) in the active group could obtain an erection and have sexual intercourse without medication, versus 5 men (9%) in the placebo group (p=0.0001). Erection Hardness Scale scores at 5 weeks improved significantly in the active group, but no significant result was found on the IIEF Erectile Function domain. At 24 weeks, 7 men (19%) in the active group and 9 (23%) in the crossed-over placebo group were still able to have intercourse without medication.
cards.watchOut: The positive headline rests on a dichotomous interview outcome while the validated continuous score (IIEF-EF) was null — the pattern of a fragile result. The placebo group crossed over at 10 weeks, so there is no controlled comparison beyond 5 weeks, and the 24-week percentages are within-arm remnants of a much smaller denominator.
cards.source: Olsen AB et al. Can low-intensity extracorporeal shockwave therapy improve erectile dysfunction? A prospective, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Scandinavian journal of urology. 2015. PMID: 25470423. shelves.title: Fesoterodine 8 mg beats tolterodine ER 4 mg on leakage in two head-to-head trials — diary dry rates 64% versus 57%, paid for with roughly double the dry mouth
shelves.question: In adults with overactive bladder, does fesoterodine beat tolterodine for incontinence episodes?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Benzhydryl Compounds/therapeutic use · Cresols/therapeutic use · Delayed-Action Preparations · Epidemiologic Methods · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Muscarinic Antagonists/therapeutic use · Patient Satisfaction · Phenylpropanolamine/therapeutic use · Quality of Life · Tolterodine Tartrate · Treatment Outcome · Urinary Bladder, Overactive/complications/drug therapy · Urinary Incontinence, Urge/drug therapy/etiology · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a small, consistent head-to-head edge, bought with anticholinergic side effects. Two 12-week double-blind trials compared fesoterodine (4 mg for one week, then 8 mg) with tolterodine extended-release 4 mg and placebo. In Herschorn 2010 (1,590 patients), fesoterodine improved urgency incontinence episodes significantly more than tolterodine ER (P = 0.017) and placebo (P < 0.001), with diary dry rates of 64% versus 57% and 45%; Kaplan 2011 (2,417 patients) found the same superiority pattern across diary endpoints and patient-reported outcomes, visible by week 4. The price is dose-typical: dry mouth in 28% on fesoterodine versus 13–16% on tolterodine ER and 5–6% on placebo, and discontinuation for adverse events in 5–6% versus 3–4% and 2%. Both trials compare fesoterodine's top dose against tolterodine's standard dose, which is exactly the comparison the dose asymmetry should make the reader notice. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): fesoterodine 8 mg is modestly more effective than tolterodine ER 4 mg for urgency incontinence in two concordant trials, with about double the dry mouth.

cards.headline: Herschorn 2010: fesoterodine beat tolterodine ER on urgency incontinence (P = 0.017) — diary dry rates 64% versus 57% versus 45% on placebo; dry mouth 28% versus 16% versus 6%
cards.summary: Herschorn 2010: fesoterodine beat tolterodine ER on urgency incontinence (P = 0.017) — diary dry rates 64% versus 57% versus 45% on placebo; dry mouth 28% versus 16% versus 6%
cards.people: 1,590 patients with overactive bladder symptoms for at least 3 months, at least 8 voids and at least 1 urgency urinary incontinence episode per 24 hours on baseline diaries, randomised 2:2:1 to fesoterodine (4 mg for 1 week then 8 mg, 636 patients), tolterodine extended-release 4 mg (641) or placebo (313) for 12 weeks, double-dummy.
cards.result: Fesoterodine significantly improved urgency urinary incontinence episodes at week 12 (primary endpoint) compared with tolterodine ER (P = 0.017) and placebo (P < 0.001), and improved mean voided volume more than tolterodine ER (P = 0.005). Diary dry rates were 64% on fesoterodine versus 57% on tolterodine ER (P = 0.015) and 45% on placebo (P < 0.001) — absolute rates printed alongside. Dry mouth and constipation rates were 28% and 5% on fesoterodine, 16% and 4% on tolterodine ER, and 6% and 3% on placebo; discontinuations for treatment-emergent adverse events were 6%, 4% and 2%.
cards.watchOut: The comparison is fesoterodine's maximum dose (8 mg after forced escalation) against tolterodine's standard 4 mg dose — a real-world prescribing comparison, but not a dose-matched one, and tolterodine patients had no escalation option. Twelve weeks of diary endpoints in a chronic condition; no data on persistence, cognition or falls, the outcomes that dominate anticholinergic decisions in older patients.
cards.source: Herschorn S et al. Comparison of fesoterodine and tolterodine extended release for the treatment of overactive bladder: a head-to-head placebo-controlled trial. BJU International. 2010. PMID: 20132103. cards.headline: Kaplan 2011: fesoterodine 8 mg superior to tolterodine ER 4 mg on incontinence episodes and most diary endpoints in 2,417 patients — dry mouth 28% versus 13%
cards.summary: Kaplan 2011: fesoterodine 8 mg superior to tolterodine ER 4 mg on incontinence episodes and most diary endpoints in 2,417 patients — dry mouth 28% versus 13%
cards.people: 2,417 adults with overactive bladder (more than 1 urgency urinary incontinence episode and at least 8 micturitions per 24 hours at baseline) randomised to fesoterodine (4 mg for 1 week, then 8 mg for 11 weeks), tolterodine extended-release 4 mg, or placebo for 12 weeks, double-blind, double-dummy, with pre-defined treatment comparisons.
cards.result: At week 12, fesoterodine 8 mg showed superiority over tolterodine ER 4 mg and placebo on urgency urinary incontinence episodes (primary endpoint), micturitions, urgency and most other diary endpoints, and on the Patient Perception of Bladder Condition, Urgency Perception Scale and all OAB Questionnaire scales (all P < 0.05); superiority over tolterodine ER was already present at week 4. Dry mouth and constipation rates were 28% and 4% with fesoterodine, 13% and 3% with tolterodine ER, and 5% and 2% with placebo; discontinuation for adverse events was 5%, 3% and 2% respectively.
cards.watchOut: Same design caveat as its sister trial: top-dose fesoterodine against standard-dose tolterodine, 12 weeks, diary and questionnaire endpoints. The two trials agree because they ask the same sponsor-framed question the same way; neither compares fesoterodine with solifenacin or mirabegron, and neither follows patients long enough to speak to the anticholinergic burden that accumulates with years of use.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two concordant trials, one modest efficacy edge, one consistent side-effect price
cards.summary: Synthesis: two concordant trials, one modest efficacy edge, one consistent side-effect price
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind double-dummy head-to-head trials totalling 4,007 patients with overactive bladder and urgency incontinence, each comparing fesoterodine 8 mg (after 1 week at 4 mg) with tolterodine extended-release 4 mg and placebo over 12 weeks (Herschorn 2010; Kaplan 2011).
cards.result: Fesoterodine was superior to tolterodine ER on the primary urgency-incontinence endpoint in both trials (P = 0.017 in Herschorn 2010; all P < 0.05 in Kaplan 2011). Diary dry rates in Herschorn 2010: 64% versus 57% versus 45% (placebo). Dry mouth: 28% versus 16% and 28% versus 13% across the two trials; discontinuation for adverse events 5–6% versus 3–4%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a genuine but small efficacy advantage, inseparable from the higher anticholinergic load that produces it.
cards.watchOut: Both trials were built around the same asymmetric dose comparison, so concordance confirms the comparison rather than a class truth; flexible-dose practice (fesoterodine 4 mg, tolterodine dose adjustment) is not what was tested. Tier C is set under this band's rules despite the two-trial base.
cards.source: Synthesis of Herschorn S et al. BJU International. 2010 (PMID: 20132103); Kaplan SA et al. BJU International. 2011 (PMID: 20860717).
