shelves.title: Nightly PDE5-inhibitor 'rehabilitation' after prostatectomy does not restore unassisted erections: recovery 20.9% on daily tadalafil versus 19.1% on placebo after washout in REACTT
shelves.question: In men with erectile dysfunction after prostatectomy, does daily PDE5 inhibitor rehabilitation preserve erectile function compared with on-demand use?
shelves.mesh: Adenocarcinoma/surgery · Aged · Carbolines/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Erectile Dysfunction/etiology/prevention & control · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Organ Sparing Treatments · Penile Erection/drug effects · Penis/innervation · Phosphodiesterase 5 Inhibitors/administration & dosage · Prostatectomy/adverse effects/methods · Prostatic Neoplasms/surgery · Recovery of Function · Tadalafil
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for the outcome rehabilitation promises. The rehabilitation hypothesis is that scheduled nightly PDE5-inhibitor dosing after nerve-sparing prostatectomy restores spontaneous, unassisted erections faster or more completely than using the drug only on demand. The largest test, REACTT (423 men), found no difference after a 6-week drug-free washout: 20.9% on daily tadalafil, 16.9% on on-demand tadalafil and 19.1% on placebo reached an erectile-function score of at least 22 (odds ratios 1.1 and 0.9 versus placebo, both non-significant) — while on treatment, daily tadalafil did improve drug-assisted erections (p = 0.016) and reduced penile length loss by 4.1 mm (p = 0.032). The sildenafil trial (Pavlovich 2013, 100 men) likewise found no difference between nightly and on-demand dosing at any timepoint, and a third, three-arm trial stopped early with 76 men and no significant difference. The drugs work while taken; scheduled rehabilitation dosing has not been shown to change the unassisted recovery it is sold on. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): nightly rehabilitation dosing does not improve unassisted erectile recovery after prostatectomy compared with on-demand use or placebo.

cards.headline: REACTT (Montorsi 2014): unassisted recovery after washout 20.9% daily tadalafil, 16.9% on-demand, 19.1% placebo — odds ratios 1.1 and 0.9, both non-significant
cards.summary: REACTT (Montorsi 2014): unassisted recovery after washout 20.9% daily tadalafil, 16.9% on-demand, 19.1% placebo — odds ratios 1.1 and 0.9, both non-significant
cards.people: 423 men aged 68 years or younger (mean 57.9 years) with prostate adenocarcinoma (Gleason ≤7) and normal preoperative erectile function undergoing bilateral nerve-sparing radical prostatectomy at 50 centres in nine European countries and Canada, randomised 1:1:1 to tadalafil 5 mg once daily (139), tadalafil 20 mg on demand (143) or placebo (141) for 9 months, followed by a 6-week drug-free washout and 3 months of open-label daily tadalafil for all.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — the proportion achieving an IIEF-EF score of at least 22 after the drug-free washout — was 20.9% on daily tadalafil, 16.9% on on-demand and 19.1% on placebo (odds ratio 1.1, 95% CI 0.6 to 2.1, p = 0.675 for daily; 0.9, 95% CI 0.5 to 1.7, p = 0.704 for on-demand). At the end of double-blind treatment, on-drug IIEF-EF improvement significantly exceeded placebo for daily tadalafil only (p = 0.016), and penile length loss at month 9 was reduced versus placebo in the daily group only (least-squares mean difference 4.1 mm, 95% CI 0.4 to 7.8, p = 0.032). Scores fell in all groups during washout.
cards.watchOut: The trial's own conclusion is the honest split: tadalafil taken daily improves erections while it is being taken and may protect penile length, but unassisted function — the rehabilitation claim — was not improved after 9 months of therapy plus washout. Men were young (≤68), potent before surgery and had low-grade cancer and bilateral nerve sparing; results do not extend to older men or non-nerve-sparing surgery.
cards.source: Montorsi F et al. Effects of tadalafil treatment on erectile function recovery following bilateral nerve-sparing radical prostatectomy: a randomised placebo-controlled study (REACTT). European Urology. 2014. PMID: 24169081. Registry ID: NCT01026818. cards.headline: Pavlovich 2013: nightly versus on-demand sildenafil — no difference in erectile function at any timepoint over 13 months in 100 men
cards.summary: Pavlovich 2013: nightly versus on-demand sildenafil — no difference in erectile function at any timepoint over 13 months in 100 men
cards.people: 100 preoperatively potent men younger than 65 years (baseline IIEF-EF at least 26; mean age about 54 years in both groups) after nerve-sparing minimally invasive radical prostatectomy, randomised to nightly sildenafil 50 mg with on-demand placebo, or nightly placebo with on-demand sildenafil 50 mg (maximum six doses a month), for 12 months plus a 1-month washout.
cards.result: No significant differences in erectile function were found between nightly and on-demand sildenafil at any single timepoint after surgery, and no significant effect of treatment group on recovery of potency when all timepoints were modelled together (multivariable mixed linear regression on IIEF-EF and EPIC scores). Baseline scores were well matched (IIEF-EF 29.4 nightly versus 29.3 on-demand).
cards.watchOut: No placebo-only arm — the trial compares two active schedules, so it can show nightly is no better than on-demand but not whether either beats natural recovery; REACTT's placebo arm answers that (it does not, for unassisted function). Single institution, 100 men, minimally invasive surgery only.
cards.source: Pavlovich CP et al. Nightly vs on-demand sildenafil for penile rehabilitation after minimally invasive nerve-sparing radical prostatectomy: results of a randomized double-blind trial with placebo. BJU International. 2013. PMID: 23937708. cards.headline: Miranda 2021: three-arm rehabilitation trial stopped early — 76 men randomised, 32 assessed at 24 months, no significant difference between strategies
cards.summary: Miranda 2021: three-arm rehabilitation trial stopped early — 76 men randomised, 32 assessed at 24 months, no significant difference between strategies
cards.people: 76 men (median age 57 years, mean baseline IIEF-EF 29) with bilateral nerve-sparing radical prostatectomy, normal testosterone and good preoperative erectile function, randomised to nightly placebo with on-demand sildenafil 100 mg, nightly sildenafil 50 mg with on-demand sildenafil 100 mg, or nightly sildenafil (5 nights a week) plus twice-weekly intracavernosal injections; target enrolment was 200 and the study was interrupted for failure to recruit.
cards.result: At 24 months the assessed sample had fallen to 4, 18 and 10 men per arm, with median IIEF-EF scores of 24 (IQR 18 to 28), 24 (IQR 18 to 28) and 21 (IQR 9 to 26) respectively; there was no statistical difference among the groups in the final analysis. The authors conclude definitive evidence on rehabilitation strategies may never be available because trials cannot recruit or retain this population.
cards.watchOut: This trial is evidence about feasibility more than efficacy: with 32 of 76 men assessed at the primary horizon it cannot confirm or refute anything, and it is carded as the honest third data point — even an FDA-approved, well-designed rehabilitation trial collapsed. Its record's MeSH terms include an indexing artefact (Child, Preschool) that is reproduced verbatim as the record carries it.
cards.source: Miranda EP et al. A Randomized, Controlled, 3-Arm Trial of Pharmacological Penile Rehabilitation in the Preservation of Erectile Function After Radical Prostatectomy. The Journal of Sexual Medicine. 2021. PMID: 33303389. cards.headline: Synthesis: scheduled rehabilitation dosing does not restore unassisted erections — the benefit is on-drug, and it washes out
cards.summary: Synthesis: scheduled rehabilitation dosing does not restore unassisted erections — the benefit is on-drug, and it washes out
cards.people: Three randomised trials after bilateral nerve-sparing radical prostatectomy: REACTT (423 men, daily versus on-demand tadalafil versus placebo with washout), Pavlovich 2013 (100 men, nightly versus on-demand sildenafil), and Miranda 2021 (76 men, three pharmacological strategies, stopped early).
cards.result: Unassisted recovery after washout in REACTT: 20.9% (daily), 16.9% (on-demand), 19.1% (placebo) reaching IIEF-EF at least 22 — no significant difference. Nightly versus on-demand sildenafil: no difference at any timepoint. On-drug erectile function did improve with daily tadalafil (p = 0.016) and penile length loss was 4.1 mm less (p = 0.032). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for rehabilitation of unassisted function, with the on-drug benefit stated on the face of the shelf.
cards.watchOut: All three trials enrolled younger, preoperatively potent men having bilateral nerve-sparing surgery — the group with the best natural recovery, in whom a rehabilitation effect should be easiest to show. Nothing here argues against on-demand PDE5 inhibitors for assisted erections, which is a different, settled question.
cards.source: Synthesis of Montorsi F et al. European Urology. 2014 (PMID: 24169081); Pavlovich CP et al. BJU International. 2013 (PMID: 23937708); Miranda EP et al. The Journal of Sexual Medicine. 2021 (PMID: 33303389).

shelves.title: Bladder stones: all three operations clear the stone — in the 805-patient global registry, complete clearance was 95.5% through the urethra, 84.6% percutaneous and 100% open, with the fewest early complications by the transurethral route; no randomised trial exists
shelves.question: How are bladder stones treated? If a stone in the bladder has to be removed, which operation — through the urethra, through a small hole above the pubic bone, or open surgery — clears it best and with fewest problems? Clinical question underneath: in patients with bladder calculi, how do transurethral cystolithotripsy, percutaneous cystolithotomy and open cystolithotomy compare on stone-free rates, hospital stay and complications?
shelves.mesh: Cystotomy/methods · Humans · Lithotripsy/methods · Prospective Studies · Registries · Treatment Outcome · Urinary Bladder Calculi/surgery · Urologic Surgical Procedures/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — every comparative dataset here is observational, so the stamp is capped: there is no randomised trial of bladder-stone surgery in the record carded. The largest dataset is the prospective BLAST registry (Gauhar 2026, PMID: 42867550; 805 patients, 31 centres, 16 countries): complete (Grade A) stone clearance was 95.5% for transurethral surgery (n=741), 84.6% for percutaneous (n=39) and 100% for open surgery (n=25); median stay was 2 days transurethral versus 3 days for the other routes; early complications were most frequent after open surgery (48.0% vs 18.6% transurethral and 17.9% percutaneous); and reintervention for residual fragments was most frequent after percutaneous surgery (10.3% vs 1.3% and 0%). But the groups were not comparable — transurethral patients had smaller stones (median 2.1 cm vs 3.0 cm) — and the registry authors state their findings describe treatment patterns and observed outcomes rather than comparative effectiveness. A geriatric series (Tunçekin 2025, PMID: 40495496; n=76, age 65+) found stone-free rates of 85.7% transurethral versus 100% open and 100% percutaneous, with no significant differences in stay or complications. In children, a meta-analysis of 7 studies (Zhao 2025, PMID: 40354160; 397 patients) found percutaneous surgery quicker but with longer hospitalisation than transurethral surgery, other differences not significant. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: all three routes clear bladder stones effectively; the transurethral route is the usual default for ordinary stones, with percutaneous and open routes reserved for larger or complex cases — a pattern of practice supported by, but not proven by, these observational data.

cards.headline: BLAST registry 2026 (n=805, 31 centres): complete stone clearance 95.5% transurethral, 84.6% percutaneous, 100% open; early complications highest after open surgery (48.0%)
cards.summary: BLAST registry 2026 (n=805, 31 centres): complete stone clearance 95.5% transurethral, 84.6% percutaneous, 100% open; early complications highest after open surgery (48.0%)
cards.people: 805 patients prospectively enrolled across 31 centres in 16 countries (May 2025 to February 2026) undergoing bladder-stone surgery: transurethral intervention (n=741), percutaneous suprapubic intervention (n=39) or open surgery (n=25). Stone-free rate was graded on postoperative imaging or cystoscopy (Grade A = 100% complete clearance); complications were classified by Clavien-Dindo criteria. Transurethral patients were older (median 66 vs 60 and 59 years, p=0.023) and had smaller stones (median 2.1 vs 3.0 cm in both other groups, p<0.001); prior urinary tract reconstruction was much commoner in the percutaneous group (23.1% vs 3.5% and 4.0%, p<0.001).
cards.result: Grade A stone-free rate: 95.5% transurethral, 84.6% percutaneous, 100% open (p=0.001). Median hospital stay was shorter after transurethral surgery (2 vs 3 days, p<0.001), as was catheterisation duration (p<0.001). Early complications within 48 hours were most frequent after open surgery (48.0% vs 18.6% transurethral and 17.9% percutaneous, p=0.001), although major complications (Clavien-Dindo grade 3 or higher) were rare and comparable across all routes, and no deaths were recorded. Reintervention for residual fragments was required significantly more often after percutaneous surgery (10.3% vs 1.3% transurethral and 0% open, p<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Not a randomised comparison: surgeons chose the route, and the percutaneous and open groups carried larger stones and more reconstructed anatomy, so their worse (or perfect) percentages cannot be read as the route's fault or virtue. The authors themselves conclude the registry describes contemporary treatment patterns and observed outcomes rather than comparative treatment effectiveness. The percutaneous (n=39) and open (n=25) groups are also small, so their percentages swing widely with a few cases.
cards.source: Gauhar V et al. BLAST-bladder lithiasis assessment of surgical treatment in real-world practice. A global prospective multicentre registry by EAU Endourology. World Journal of Urology. 2026. PMID: 42867550. Registry ID: none in the record. prior urinary tract reconstruction was much commoner in the percutaneous group (23.1% vs 3.5% and 4.0%, p<0.001). grade a stone-free rate: 95.5% transurethral, 84.6% percutaneous, 100% open (p=0.001). median hospital stay was shorter after transurethral surgery (2 vs 3 days, p<0.001), as was catheterisation duration (p<0.001). early complications within 48 hours were most frequent after open surgery (48.0% vs 18.6% transurethral and 17.9% percutaneous, p=0.001), although major complications (clavien-dindo grade 3 or higher) were rare and comparable across all routes, and no deaths were recorded. reintervention for residual fragments was required significantly more often after percutaneous surgery (10.3% vs 1.3% transurethral and 0% open, p<0.001). not a randomised comparison: surgeons chose the route, and the percutaneous and open groups carried larger stones and more reconstructed anatomy, so their worse (or perfect) percentages cannot be read as the route's fault or virtue. the authors themselves conclude the registry describes contemporary treatment patterns and observed outcomes rather than comparative treatment effectiveness. the percutaneous (n=39) and open (n=25) groups are also small, so their percentages swing widely with a few cases. gauhar v et al. blast-bladder lithiasis assessment of surgical treatment in real-world practice. a global prospective multicentre registry by eau endourology. world journal of urology. 2026. pmid: 42867550. registry id: none in the record. mesh: aged · female · humans · male · middle aged · postoperative complications/epidemiology · prospective studies · registries · urinary bladder calculi/surgery* · urologic surgical procedures/methods

cards.headline: Tunçekin 2025 (geriatric series, n=76): stone-free 85.7% transurethral vs 100% open and 100% percutaneous — no significant difference in stay or complications
cards.summary: Tunçekin 2025 (geriatric series, n=76): stone-free 85.7% transurethral vs 100% open and 100% percutaneous — no significant difference in stay or complications
cards.people: 76 patients aged 65 years or older (72 men, 4 women; mean age 72.6 years, range 65-89) who had bladder-stone surgery between 2010 and 2021: open suprapubic cystolithotomy (n=31), percutaneous cystolithotripsy (n=17) or transurethral cystolithotripsy (n=28). Mean stone size was 39.7 × 29.4 mm; benign prostatic hyperplasia was present in 84% of the men.
cards.result: Stone-free rates were 85.7% for transurethral cystolithotripsy and 100% for both open cystolithotomy and percutaneous cystolithotripsy (p>0.05). Symptoms resolved in 94.7% of cases overall. Complication rates did not differ significantly among the three groups (p>0.05): early complications were haematuria (3.9%) and residual stones (2.6%); late complications were fever (1.3%) and urethral stricture (1.3%). Mean hospital stay was 4.3 ± 2.1 days with no significant difference among groups (p=0.071). The authors concluded all three techniques can be performed safely in geriatric patients.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, single-centre and small (17-31 patients per route), so 'no significant difference' is compatible with meaningful differences the study could not detect; the 100% figures rest on 31 and 17 patients. Results are specific to patients 65 and older with large stones (mean about 4 cm) and mostly enlarged prostates.
cards.source: Tunçekin A et al. Comparison of Surgical Outcomes for Bladder Stones in Geriatric Patients: Open Cystolithotomy, Percutaneous and Transurethral Cystolithotripsy Techniques. Archivos Españoles de Urología. 2025. PMID: 40495496. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Zhao 2025 (meta-analysis in children, 7 studies, 397 patients): percutaneous surgery was quicker but kept children in hospital longer than transurethral surgery; other differences not significant
cards.summary: Zhao 2025 (meta-analysis in children, 7 studies, 397 patients): percutaneous surgery was quicker but kept children in hospital longer than transurethral surgery; other differences not significant
cards.people: 397 children with bladder stones from 7 studies comparing transurethral cystolithotripsy (TUCL, 202 patients) with percutaneous cystolithotomy (PCCL, 195 patients). Outcomes included stone-free rate, operation time, hospital stay and complications; study quality was assessed with Cochrane tools and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale.
cards.result: The percutaneous group had a shorter operative time (p<0.00001) and longer hospitalisation (p<0.00001) than the transurethral group; the other perioperative differences examined, including stone-free outcomes and complications, were not statistically significant. The authors concluded both approaches are effective and safe for bladder stones in children and that larger prospective studies are needed to define the stone size at which one approach should be preferred.
cards.watchOut: Paediatric data only — in children the narrow urethra changes the trade-offs, so these results should not be carried over to adults. The pooled studies were small and mostly non-randomised, and the abstract reports significance levels rather than pooled stone-free percentages, so no exact clearance rates are stated here.
cards.source: Zhao X et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: every route clears bladder stones in most patients; the differences seen are entangled with which patients get which operation
cards.summary: Synthesis: every route clears bladder stones in most patients; the differences seen are entangled with which patients get which operation
cards.people: An 805-patient prospective international registry (Gauhar 2026), a 76-patient geriatric retrospective series (Tunçekin 2025) and a 397-patient paediatric meta-analysis (Zhao 2025) — all observational; no randomised trial was found for this question.
cards.result: Complete stone clearance: 95.5% transurethral, 84.6% percutaneous, 100% open in the registry; 85.7% vs 100% vs 100% in the geriatric series. Stay was shortest after transurethral surgery in the registry (2 vs 3 days) but not significantly different in the geriatric series; early complications were highest after open surgery in the registry (48.0%) yet major complications were rare by all routes and no deaths occurred. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: all three operations are effective; choice follows stone size, urethral access and anatomy, not proven superiority of one route.
cards.watchOut: Confounding by indication runs through every number on this shelf: bigger, harder stones and reconstructed bladders are sent to percutaneous and open surgery. Percentages from the small percutaneous and open groups (n=39 and n=25 in the registry) should be read as rough magnitudes, not precise rates. Tier C: observational evidence only.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gauhar V et al. World Journal of Urology. 2026 (PMID: 42867550); Tunçekin A et al. Archivos Españoles de Urología. 2025 (PMID: 40495496); Zhao X et al. Journal of Endourology. 2025 (PMID: 40354160).

shelves.title: Antibiotic duration in acute prostatitis: MAYBE (weak evidence), observational only — duration has never been randomised in prostatitis; the supported standard is about 14 days of an adequate prostate-penetrating drug, and relapse tracks drug adequacy, not a tested number of days
shelves.question: In adults with acute prostatitis, how long should antibiotic treatment continue?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Bacteriuria · Chronic Disease · Drug Resistance, Bacterial · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prostatitis · Pyelonephritis · Quinolones · Recurrence · Risk Factors · Trimethoprim, Sulfamethoxazole Drug Combination · beta-Lactams
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational only for prostatitis itself, printed on the face. No trial has randomised men with acute prostatitis to different durations: the one randomised duration trial in the neighbouring population (febrile urinary tract infection in men, where 7 days proved inferior to 14 days at short-term follow-up in men) is homed on live shelf #488 and is cross-pointed here, not re-carded — and it excluded patients judged to need at least 14 days, the group closest to prostatitis. What the prostatitis cohorts show is that relapse tracks whether the drug was adequate for the organism, not a tested duration: in 410 patients, inadequate antibiotic therapy carried an odds ratio of 12.3 for relapse (overall relapse 6.3%), and in 326 Escherichia coli episodes, recurrence occurred only with the poorly penetrating oral beta-lactam comparator. The 2026 French guideline-rationale review states the conventional standard plainly: 14 days remains the standard for acute prostatitis to prevent relapse, with 7 days sufficient only for selected bacteraemic presentations of male urinary infection. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational only: continue antibiotics for about 14 days in acute prostatitis; shorter courses are untested in prostatitis itself, and adequacy of the chosen drug against the cultured organism is the factor the cohort evidence actually supports.

cards.headline: Marquez-Algaba 2021: in 410 patients with acute bacterial prostatitis, relapse was 6.3% and the only independent risk factor was inadequate antibiotic therapy (OR 12.3) — relapse by definitive drug ran from 1.8% (ciprofloxacin) to 9.8% (oral beta-lactam); treatment duration was not the reported driver
cards.summary: Marquez-Algaba 2021: in 410 patients with acute bacterial prostatitis, relapse was 6.3% and the only independent risk factor was inadequate antibiotic therapy (OR 12.3) — relapse by definitive drug ran from 1.8% (ciprofloxacin) to 9.8% (oral beta-lactam); treatment duration was not the reported driver
cards.people: 410 patients diagnosed with acute bacterial prostatitis (urinary symptoms, temperature above 37.8 °C and bacteriuria, without pyelonephritis features) at one centre in 2017–2018; mean age 68 years, 28.8% with diabetes and 61.1% with benign prostatic hyperplasia. Escherichia coli caused 62.4% and Klebsiella species 10%; quinolone resistance was 39.5%. A propensity score with inverse weighting was applied for antibiotic selection bias.
cards.result: Mortality was 1.2% and relapse 6.3%. The only independent risk factor for relapse was inadequate antibiotic therapy (odds ratio 12.3, 95% CI 3.5 to 43.1). When treatment was adjusted to susceptibility, relapse rates were 1.8% with ciprofloxacin, 3.6% with intravenous beta-lactam, 9.3% with co-trimoxazole and 9.8% with oral beta-lactam (P = 0.03); oral beta-lactam (OR 5.3, 95% CI 1.2 to 23.3) and co-trimoxazole (OR 4.9, 95% CI 1.1 to 23.2) were associated with relapse. The record does not report a comparison of treatment durations — no duration effect size exists in this record, and none is invented here.
cards.watchOut: This cohort answers 'which drug, matched to the culture' far better than 'how long': durations were chosen by clinicians and are not analysed in the record, so the card supports adequacy of therapy, not any specific number of days.
cards.source: Marquez-Algaba E et al. Risk Factors for Relapse in Acute Bacterial Prostatitis: the Impact of Antibiotic Regimens. Microbiology spectrum. 2021. PMID: 34585972. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Gisbert 2025: in 326 episodes of Escherichia coli acute prostatitis, clinical cure was 96.9% with ciprofloxacin versus 85.7% with sequential oral cefuroxime, and recurrence occurred only in the cefuroxime group (6.96% vs 0%) — again a drug-penetration difference, not a duration comparison
cards.summary: Gisbert 2025: in 326 episodes of Escherichia coli acute prostatitis, clinical cure was 96.9% with ciprofloxacin versus 85.7% with sequential oral cefuroxime, and recurrence occurred only in the cefuroxime group (6.96% vs 0%) — again a drug-penetration difference, not a duration comparison
cards.people: 326 episodes of acute bacterial prostatitis due to Escherichia coli in men over 18 at a 400-bed hospital, 2010–2023, treated with oral cefuroxime 500 mg every 8 hours (158 episodes) or oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg every 12 hours (168 episodes) as sequential therapy; outcomes (cure, recurrence, reinfection) were assessed over 90 days. Cefuroxime patients were younger (median 63.5 vs 67.5 years) with fewer comorbidities.
cards.result: Clinical cure was higher with ciprofloxacin (96.9% vs 85.7%; P < 0.001). Recurrence occurred only in the cefuroxime group (6.96% vs 0%; P < 0.001), while reinfection and mortality were similar. On multivariable analysis ciprofloxacin protected against clinical failure (OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.42; P < 0.001) and prior urinary tract infection increased failure risk (OR 2.87, 95% CI 1.3 to 6.3). Treatment durations are not reported in the record, and no duration comparison is claimed here.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and confounded by era and clinician choice (the cefuroxime group was younger and healthier yet fared worse, which strengthens the drug signal but does not make it randomised); like the other prostatitis cohort, it is silent on how many days treatment should run.
cards.source: Gisbert L et al. Clinical Outcomes of Escherichia coli Acute Bacterial Prostatitis: A Comparative Study of Oral Sequential Therapy with β-Lactam Versus Quinolone Antibiotics. Antibiotics (Basel, Switzerland). 2025. PMID: 40723984. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Forestier 2026 (guideline-rationale review): the conventional 14-day duration remains the standard for acute prostatitis to prevent relapses — while 7 days is validated only for male cystitis and for selected bacteraemic male urinary infections, not for prostatitis
cards.summary: Forestier 2026 (guideline-rationale review): the conventional 14-day duration remains the standard for acute prostatitis to prevent relapses — while 7 days is validated only for male cystitis and for selected bacteraemic male urinary infections, not for prostatitis
cards.people: Scientific-rationale review for the 2026 French Infectious Diseases Society (SPILF) guidelines on male urinary tract infections, synthesising randomised trials and large retrospective cohorts on antibiotic efficacy, resistance and optimal durations across male cystitis, febrile urinary infection (prostatitis/pyelonephritis) and epididymo-orchitis. No participant number applies to a guideline-rationale article, and none is printed.
cards.result: The review states that evidence validates distinguishing male cystitis from febrile urinary infection: 7-day narrow-spectrum regimens achieve satisfactory success in male cystitis, and recent data show 7 days can be sufficient for selected bacteraemic presentations — but 'to prevent relapses a conventional 14-day duration remains the standard for acute prostatitis.' Febrile infections require initial parenteral third-generation cephalosporins or oral fluoroquinolones, with co-trimoxazole preferred over fluoroquinolones for targeted oral step-down in prostatitis on ecological grounds. No effect size for duration in prostatitis is reported in the record — the 14-day figure is the guideline standard the review states, printed as such.
cards.watchOut: A guideline standard is a consensus resting on the cohort evidence above, not a trial result: this card documents what the current standard is and what it rests on, and must never be cited as proof that 14 days beats 7 days in prostatitis — that trial does not exist in the records fetched.
cards.source: Forestier E et al. Antibiotic treatment of male urinary tract infections: scientific rationale behind the 2026 SPILF guidelines. Infectious diseases now. 2026. PMID: 42349553. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: no study has randomised duration in acute prostatitis; the evidence supports an adequate, prostate-penetrating drug matched to the culture (relapse 1.8% on ciprofloxacin vs 9.8% on oral beta-lactam in the largest cohort) and the standing guideline standard of about 14 days — shorter courses are validated only outside prostatitis
cards.summary: Synthesis: no study has randomised duration in acute prostatitis; the evidence supports an adequate, prostate-penetrating drug matched to the culture (relapse 1.8% on ciprofloxacin vs 9.8% on oral beta-lactam in the largest cohort) and the standing guideline standard of about 14 days — shorter courses are validated only outside prostatitis
cards.people: The carded evidence: two acute-prostatitis cohorts (410 patients; 326 episodes) and one guideline-rationale review. Total carded patients exceed 700, so no small-N stamp labelling applies. Cross-point (not re-carded): live shelf #488 homes the randomised 7-versus-14-day trial in men with febrile urinary tract infection — in men, 7 days was inferior at short-term follow-up (clinical cure 86% vs 98%) though non-inferior at longer follow-up, and patients judged to need at least 14 days were excluded from randomisation; that trial's record is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Relapse in acute prostatitis: 6.3% overall, driven by inadequate therapy (OR 12.3; Marquez-Algaba 2021); recurrence 0% on ciprofloxacin vs 6.96% on oral cefuroxime (Gisbert 2025). Duration: no comparative data in prostatitis in any carded record; the stated standard is 14 days (Forestier 2026). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational only: treat acute prostatitis for about 14 days with an adequate prostate-penetrating agent; the duration itself is untested.

shelves.title: Optilume paclitaxel-coated balloon for BPH: IPSS fell 11.5 points at 1 year in the sham-controlled PINNACLE trial and peak flow more than doubled — one randomised programme plus a single-arm feasibility study
shelves.question: In men with benign prostatic hyperplasia, does the Optilume drug-coated balloon improve urinary symptoms and flow versus sham?
shelves.mesh: Prostatic Hyperplasia/therapy · Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms · Paclitaxel/administration & dosage · Drug Delivery Systems · Double-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome · Humans · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — this shelf answers the device-specific question for the Optilume BPH Catheter System, a paclitaxel drug-coated balloon catheter (a named device, named exactly as published; the trial records do not name the manufacturer). Neighbouring BPH devices are homed separately — prostatic urethral lift (UroLift) on pack #4260, Rezūm water-vapour therapy on pack #4262 and Aquablation on pack #3042 — and are not re-carded here. The sham-controlled evidence is one trial: PINNACLE randomised 148 men (100 Optilume, 48 sham); at the blinded comparison, symptom scores (IPSS) fell 11.5 points at 1 year on Optilume against an 8.0-point fall at 3 months on sham, and peak flow rose 10.3 mL/s (+125% relative, printed beside the absolute change) at 1 year, with erectile and ejaculatory function preserved. Two-year follow-up of the treated arm (blinding ended at 1 year) showed 67.5% remained responders (≥30% IPSS improvement without retreatment), with IPSS 11.0 and peak flow 19.0 mL/s. The earlier EVEREST-I feasibility study (80 men, single-arm, no comparator) showed the same direction — IPSS 22.3 to 8.2 and peak flow 10.9 to 17.2 mL/s at 2 years — but without a control group it cannot separate device effect from placebo and regression effects, which the large sham response in PINNACLE (8.0 IPSS points) shows are substantial in this condition. Premise note: the slate named the 'ROBUST programme' as supporting evidence; the ROBUST reports concern the same manufacturer's balloon used for anterior urethral strictures, a different indication, and were not carded — the BPH programme is PINNACLE plus EVEREST-I. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real sham-controlled advantage at 1 year from one programme, durability open-label thereafter.

cards.headline: PINNACLE 2023: Optilume beat sham — IPSS fell 11.5 points at 1 year versus 8.0 points at 3 months on sham, and peak flow rose 10.3 mL/s
cards.summary: PINNACLE 2023: Optilume beat sham — IPSS fell 11.5 points at 1 year versus 8.0 points at 3 months on sham, and peak flow rose 10.3 mL/s
cards.people: Prospective, randomised, double-blind, sham-controlled trial at 18 centres in the US and Canada: 148 men aged 50 or older with symptomatic benign prostatic hyperplasia and prostate size 20–80 g, randomised 2:1 (100 Optilume BPH Catheter System, 48 sham procedure); patients and assessors blinded through 1 year.
cards.result: IPSS fell by 11.5 ± 7.8 points at 1 year after Optilume treatment, compared with a fall of 8.0 ± 8.3 points at 3 months in the sham arm (the blinded sham comparison point). Peak urinary flow improved by 10.3 mL/s from baseline to 1 year on Optilume (+125% relative). Erectile and ejaculatory function were preserved, treatment was well tolerated, and the procedure could be done in an office or ambulatory setting.
cards.watchOut: The sham arm itself improved by 8 IPSS points — most of the treated group's gain is not device-specific. The record for this 1-year report carries no registry ID in its databank fields; the trial's ClinicalTrials.gov number (NCT04131907) appears on the 2-year report carded below.
cards.source: Kaplan SA et al. cards.headline: PINNACLE 2-year follow-up 2024: 67.5% of treated men remained responders, IPSS 11.0 and peak flow 19.0 mL/s — but follow-up after year 1 was treated-arm only
cards.summary: PINNACLE 2-year follow-up 2024: 67.5% of treated men remained responders, IPSS 11.0 and peak flow 19.0 mL/s — but follow-up after year 1 was treated-arm only
cards.type: Two-year follow-up report of a randomised sham-controlled trial (PINNACLE)
cards.people: Two-year follow-up of the PINNACLE randomised cohort (148 men; 100 treated with Optilume BPH). Follow-up beyond 1 year was limited to men treated with Optilume; 74 men contributed 2-year symptom scores and 65 contributed flow measurements.
cards.result: At 2 years, 67.5% (56/83, 95% CI 56.3% to 77.4%) of Optilume-treated participants were symptomatic responders (≥30% IPSS improvement without medical or surgical retreatment). IPSS improved from 23.4 ± 5.5 at baseline to 11.0 ± 7.0; peak flow rose from 8.9 ± 2.2 to 19.0 ± 16.3 mL/s (+116.8% relative, printed beside the absolute values); BPH Impact Index improved 53.9% relative (7.0 to 2.3). The most common adverse events were haematuria and urinary tract infection; no device- or treatment-related serious adverse events occurred beyond 12 months, and sexual function was unaffected.
cards.watchOut: After the blinded year, there is no sham comparator — durability figures are within-arm changes in the men who stayed in follow-up (74 of 100 for symptoms), so attrition and expectation effects cannot be excluded.
cards.source: Kaplan SA et al. Two-year long-term follow-up of treatment with the Optilume BPH catheter system in a randomized controlled trial for benign prostatic hyperplasia (The PINNACLE Study). Prostate cancer and prostatic diseases. 2024. PMID: 38684918. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04131907. cards.headline: EVEREST-I 1-year 2021: in 80 men treated open-label, 81% improved IPSS by at least 40% and peak flow rose from 10.9 to 18.4 mL/s
cards.summary: EVEREST-I 1-year 2021: in 80 men treated open-label, 81% improved IPSS by at least 40% and peak flow rose from 10.9 to 18.4 mL/s
cards.people: First report of the EVEREST-I early feasibility study at six sites in Latin America: 80 men over 50 with moderate-to-severe symptoms, peak flow 5–15 mL/s, prostatic urethra length 30–55 mm and prostate volume 20–80 g, all treated with the Optilume BPH Catheter System; 75 completed 1-year follow-up.
cards.result: The proportion with ≥40% IPSS improvement was 81% at both 3 months and 1 year. IPSS improved from 22.3 at baseline to 7.9 at 1 year, peak flow from 10.9 to 18.4 mL/s, and IPSS quality-of-life score from 4.6 to 1.3. Post-procedural complications were common urologic events, and the complication rate was significantly affected by device diameter.
cards.watchOut: No control group: in a condition where the sham procedure alone produced an 8-point IPSS fall in PINNACLE, single-arm gains overstate the device-specific effect. This card supports feasibility and safety, not comparative efficacy.
cards.source: Kaplan SA et al. One-year outcomes after treatment with a drug-coated balloon catheter system for lower urinary tract symptoms related to benign prostatic hyperplasia. cards.headline: EVEREST-I 2-year 2023: symptom and flow gains persisted to 2 years (IPSS 22.3 to 8.2; peak flow 10.9 to 17.2 mL/s) with no new treatment-related events in year 2
cards.summary: EVEREST-I 2-year 2023: symptom and flow gains persisted to 2 years (IPSS 22.3 to 8.2; peak flow 10.9 to 17.2 mL/s) with no new treatment-related events in year 2
cards.people: Two-year outcomes of the EVEREST-I single-arm study: 80 men with lower urinary tract symptoms secondary to benign prostatic hyperplasia treated with the Optilume BPH Catheter System, followed for symptoms (IPSS, BPH Impact Index), peak flow and post-void residual volume.
cards.result: IPSS improved from 22.3 at baseline to 8.2 at 2 years (p < 0.001) and BPH Impact Index from 6.9 to 2.3 (p < 0.001); peak flow improved from 10.9 to 17.2 mL/s and post-void residual fell from 63.1 to 45.0 mL. Treatment-related adverse events were typically minor, with none occurring between 1 and 2 years after treatment.
cards.watchOut: Still uncontrolled at 2 years, and the abstract does not print how many of the 80 men contributed 2-year measurements — durability percentages should be read as completer results.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one sham-controlled trial shows a real but modest device-specific gain, sustained open-label to 2 years — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: one sham-controlled trial shows a real but modest device-specific gain, sustained open-label to 2 years — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: The carded evidence: the PINNACLE randomised sham-controlled programme (148 men; 1-year blinded report and 2-year follow-up) and the EVEREST-I single-arm feasibility programme (80 men; 1- and 2-year reports).
cards.result: Against sham, Optilume's device-specific advantage at the blinded comparison was about 3.5 IPSS points beyond an 8.0-point sham response, with a large flow gain (+10.3 mL/s at 1 year) and preserved sexual function; 67.5% of treated men remained responders at 2 years. Both programmes point the same way, but only one randomised comparison exists and everything past 1 year is uncontrolled — hence POSSIBLE (benefit), the single-programme cap. The ROBUST stricture programme was not carded: it answers a different (urethral stricture) question.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the treated arm's 11.5-point IPSS fall as the treatment effect: the sham arm fell 8.0 points, and the honest device-specific figure is the difference between them.

shelves.title: Intrarenal stones: ureteroscopy probably clears more stones than shock-wave lithotripsy — clearest at 1–2 cm and in the lower pole — on thin randomised proof
shelves.question: In adults with stones inside the kidney (not the ureter), does ureteroscopy achieve higher stone-free rates than shock-wave lithotripsy?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Kidney Calculi/diagnostic imaging,therapy · Kidney Calices/diagnostic imaging · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life · Recurrence · Tomography, X-Ray Computed · Ureteroscopy · Urography
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Three sources, one direction, uneven strength. The Lower Pole Study Group randomised trial (Pearle 2005; stones ≤1 cm, lower pole) found stone-free rates of 50% on ureteroscopy versus 35% on shock-wave lithotripsy at 3 months — not statistically significant in 78 randomised patients. The Cochrane review (Srisubat 2014) found its only randomised ureteroscopy (RIRS) comparison — 58 patients — likewise non-significant (relative risk 0.91, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.30). The larger meta-analysis (Mi 2016; 2,348 patients, 6 randomised + 8 retrospective studies) found significantly higher stone-free rates with flexible ureteroscopy for stones under 2 cm, driven by the 1–2 cm stratum and the lower pole, with fewer auxiliary procedures and retreatments. Shock-wave lithotripsy remains quicker, avoids access failure and perforation, and scored better on patient-reported convalescence in the trial. This shelf covers stones inside the kidney only; ureteric stones are home shelf #913 (TISU).

cards.headline: Lower Pole Study Group trial (Pearle 2005): stone-free rates 50% on ureteroscopy versus 35% on shock-wave lithotripsy for lower-pole stones 1 cm or less — a difference that was not statistically significant
cards.summary: Lower Pole Study Group trial (Pearle 2005): stone-free rates 50% on ureteroscopy versus 35% on shock-wave lithotripsy for lower-pole stones 1 cm or less — a difference that was not statistically significant
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Lower Pole Study Group / Pearle 2005) — N = 78 randomised, 67 treated
cards.people: 78 patients with isolated lower-pole renal stones of 1 cm or less were randomised to shock-wave lithotripsy (SWL) or ureteroscopy (URS) in a prospective multicentre trial; 67 completed treatment (32 SWL, 35 URS). The primary outcome was the stone-free rate on non-contrast CT at 3 months. This is the randomised programme of the Lower Pole Study Group (the Albala lower-pole programme).
cards.result: At 3 months, among patients with radiographic follow-up (26 SWL, 32 URS), the stone-free rate was 35% after SWL and 50% after URS — not statistically significant. Operative time was shorter for SWL (66 vs 90 minutes). Intraoperative complications occurred in 1 SWL case and 7 URS cases (failed access in 5, perforation in 2); postoperative complications occurred in 7 patients in each group, and patient-derived quality-of-life measures favoured SWL. The authors conclude the trial failed to demonstrate a statistically significant difference in stone-free rates.
cards.watchOut: The one trial confined to small lower-pole stones was too small to settle the question: the 15-point gap favouring ureteroscopy sits inside wide confidence limits, and stone-free status was assessed only in the 58 patients with radiographic follow-up. It does not cover stones over 1 cm or non-lower-pole sites.
cards.source: Pearle MS et al. Prospective, randomized trial comparing shock wave lithotripsy and ureteroscopy for lower pole caliceal calculi 1 cm or less. The Journal of urology. 2005. PMID: 15879805. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cochrane review (Srisubat 2014): the single randomised comparison of shock-wave lithotripsy versus retrograde intrarenal surgery (ureteroscopy) for kidney stones found no significant difference in treatment success at 3 months
cards.summary: Cochrane review (Srisubat 2014): the single randomised comparison of shock-wave lithotripsy versus retrograde intrarenal surgery (ureteroscopy) for kidney stones found no significant difference in treatment success at 3 months
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Cochrane, Srisubat 2014) — 5 studies, 338 patients; ESWL-vs-RIRS comparison rests on 1 study of 58 patients
cards.people: Systematic review of randomised trials of extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy (ESWL) versus percutaneous nephrolithotomy or retrograde intrarenal surgery (RIRS, i.e. ureteroscopy into the kidney) for kidney stones: 5 studies, 338 patients. Only one study (58 participants) compared ESWL with RIRS, for lower-pole kidney stones.
cards.result: Treatment success at 3 months did not differ significantly between ESWL and RIRS (58 participants: relative risk 0.91, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.30). Mean procedural time and hospital stay were longer in the RIRS group. The review's wider finding was that ESWL was less effective than percutaneous nephrolithotomy (a different, more invasive operation, not the comparison on this shelf). The authors rate the included studies as small and of low methodological quality.
cards.watchOut: For the exact ureteroscopy comparison this shelf asks about, the Cochrane randomised evidence is a single 58-patient study — the pooled kidney-stone headline mostly reflects the percutaneous-surgery comparison, which must not be read across to ureteroscopy.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis (Mi 2016): flexible ureteroscopy gave significantly higher stone-free rates than shock-wave lithotripsy for renal stones under 2 cm — driven by stones of 1–2 cm and by lower-pole stones
cards.summary: Meta-analysis (Mi 2016): flexible ureteroscopy gave significantly higher stone-free rates than shock-wave lithotripsy for renal stones under 2 cm — driven by stones of 1–2 cm and by lower-pole stones
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Mi 2016) — 14 studies (6 randomised, 8 retrospective), 2,348 patients
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of flexible ureterorenoscopy with holmium laser versus extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy for renal stones under 2 cm: 6 prospective randomised trials and 8 retrospective comparisons, 2,348 patients in total.
cards.result: For renal stones of 1–2 cm, flexible ureteroscopy gave a significantly higher stone-free rate than ESWL (reported effect 2.35, 95% CI 1.65 to 3.34, P < 0.00001), a lower auxiliary-procedure rate (odds ratio 0.33, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.50) and a lower retreatment rate (odds ratio 0.07, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.37); similar results held in the 1–2 cm lower-pole subgroup. For stones under 1 cm the stone-free rate also significantly favoured ureteroscopy (2.13, 95% CI 1.13 to 4.00, P = 0.02). The authors conclude ureteroscopy is a safe, effective alternative, while calling for further randomised trials to confirm the findings.
cards.watchOut: More than half the pooled weight is retrospective, where fitter patients and favourable anatomy are preferentially scoped — the pooled advantage is larger and more certain than the randomised-only evidence (cards 1–2) supports, and the paper mislabels some pooled effects (a 'weighted mean difference' reported for a rate), so the direction is more trustworthy than the exact size.

cards.headline: Synthesis: ureteroscopy probably clears intrarenal stones more often than shock-wave lithotripsy — most clearly for 1–2 cm and lower-pole stones — but the randomised proof is thin and the smallest stones remain unsettled
cards.summary: Synthesis: ureteroscopy probably clears intrarenal stones more often than shock-wave lithotripsy — most clearly for 1–2 cm and lower-pole stones — but the randomised proof is thin and the smallest stones remain unsettled
cards.people: The carded evidence: one multicentre randomised trial in lower-pole stones ≤1 cm (78 randomised), one Cochrane review whose ureteroscopy comparison rests on a single 58-patient randomised study, and one meta-analysis of 2,348 patients mixing 6 randomised trials with 8 retrospective comparisons.
cards.result: Every synthesis points the same way — towards higher stone-free rates with ureteroscopy — and the advantage is statistically secure only in the mixed-design meta-analysis, concentrated in 1–2 cm stones and the lower pole. The two randomised-only sources are individually non-significant. Shock-wave lithotripsy keeps real advantages: shorter procedures, no failed-access or perforation events of the kind seen in the trial's ureteroscopy arm, and better patient-reported convalescence. Home shelf #913 covers ureteric stones only (the TISU trial); this shelf is the intrarenal slice it does not cover.
cards.watchOut: Do not upgrade this beyond POSSIBLE: no large randomised trial of ureteroscopy versus shock-wave lithotripsy for intrarenal stones exists in the carded set, and stone-free definitions and imaging (CT versus plain film) differ across studies, which moves the rates substantially.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pearle MS et al. The Journal of urology. 2005 (PMID: 15879805); Srisubat A et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2014 (PMID: 25418417); Mi Y et al. Urolithiasis. 2016 (PMID: 26530230). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: HoLEP versus simple prostatectomy for very large prostates: identical symptom relief and flow at 5 years, with less blood loss, 1 versus 6 catheter days and 2 versus 10 hospital days
shelves.question: In men with very large prostates (over about 80 mL), how does holmium laser enucleation compare with simple prostatectomy?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Body Weights and Measures · Follow-Up Studies · Holmium/therapeutic use · Humans · Laser Therapy · Male · Metals, Rare Earth/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Prostate/surgery · Prostatectomy/methods · Prostatic Hyperplasia/surgery · Transurethral Resection of Prostate/methods · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one randomised programme plus concordant syntheses. The Kuntz trial randomised 120 men with prostates over 100 g to HoLEP or open transvesical prostatectomy: functional improvement was equivalent at every interval to 18 months and remained identical at 5 years (symptom score 3.0 in both groups; Qmax 24.4 mL/s in both; reoperations 5% vs 6.7%), while HoLEP halved blood loss, eliminated transfusions (0 vs 8), and cut catheter time (median 1 vs 6 days) and hospital stay (2 vs 10 days) at the cost of a longer operation (136 vs 91 minutes). The Jones 2016 systematic review of HoLEP versus simple prostatectomy for large prostates found the same pattern — equivalent efficacy, perioperative advantage to HoLEP. Home pack #3043 asks HoLEP versus TURP in benign prostatic hyperplasia generally; the very-large-gland population and simple-prostatectomy comparator are the slice it does not cover.

cards.headline: Kuntz randomised trial, 18-month report (2004): in prostates over 100 g, HoLEP matched open prostatectomy on symptoms, flow and residual urine — with half the blood loss, catheter time 1 versus 6 days and hospital stay 2 versus 10 days, at the cost of a longer operation
cards.summary: Kuntz randomised trial, 18-month report (2004): in prostates over 100 g, HoLEP matched open prostatectomy on symptoms, flow and residual urine — with half the blood loss, catheter time 1 versus 6 days and hospital stay 2 versus 10 days, at the cost of a longer operation
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Kuntz 2004, 18-month report) — N = 120, prostates >100 g
cards.people: 120 urodynamically obstructed men with prostates over 100 g were randomised to holmium laser enucleation (HoLEP, 60 men; mean prostate volume 115 mL) or transvesical open prostatectomy (60 men; mean 113 mL). Symptom scores, peak flow, residual volumes and all complications were assessed to 18 months. This is the same single randomised programme reported at 5 years in the next card.
cards.result: Symptom scores, peak flow rates and postvoid residual volumes improved markedly in both groups with no significant difference between them at any interval. HoLEP took longer (136 vs 91 minutes; P < 0.0001) but lost less blood (haemoglobin loss 1.9 vs 2.8 g/dL; P < 0.0001), needed a catheter for a median of 1 versus 6 days and a hospital stay of 2 versus 10 days (both P < 0.0001). Blood transfusions were required in 0 HoLEP versus 8 open-surgery patients; total patients with complications were 7 versus 13, and there were no deaths in either group.
cards.watchOut: One centre's programme and one surgical team: enucleation results are operator-dependent, and the open comparator is transvesical prostatectomy as practised in that era — the perioperative gaps (especially 10-day stays) are larger than modern pathways would show.
cards.source: Kuntz RM et al. Transurethral holmium laser enucleation of the prostate compared with transvesical open prostatectomy: 18-month follow-up of a randomized trial. Journal of endourology. 2004. PMID: 15072629. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kuntz randomised trial, 5-year report (2008): symptom scores and flow rates remained identical between HoLEP and open prostatectomy at 5 years (AUA score 3.0 in both groups; Qmax 24.4 mL/s in both), with reoperation rates of 5% versus 6.7%
cards.summary: Kuntz randomised trial, 5-year report (2008): symptom scores and flow rates remained identical between HoLEP and open prostatectomy at 5 years (AUA score 3.0 in both groups; Qmax 24.4 mL/s in both), with reoperation rates of 5% versus 6.7%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, 5-year follow-up (Kuntz 2008) — N = 120 randomised, 74 assessed at 5 years
cards.people: Five-year follow-up of the same randomised trial: 120 men with prostates greater than 100 g randomised to HoLEP or open prostatectomy (60 each). By 5 years, 46 patients (38.3%) were lost to follow-up or excluded, leaving 74 assessed (42 HoLEP, 32 open). Outcomes: American Urological Association Symptom Score, maximum flow rate (Qmax), postvoid residual volume, late complications and reoperations.
cards.result: At 5 years the mean symptom score was 3.0 in both groups (P = 0.98), mean Qmax was 24.4 mL/s in both groups (P = 0.97), and residual volume was 11 mL after HoLEP versus 5 mL after open prostatectomy (P = 0.25) — durable, equivalent relief. Late complications were urethral strictures and bladder-neck contractures; reoperation rates were 5% (HoLEP) versus 6.7% (open) (P = 1.0), and no patient developed recurrent benign prostatic hyperplasia.
cards.watchOut: Nearly 4 in 10 randomised men are missing from the 5-year numbers, with more lost from the open-surgery arm — equivalence in the survivors could hide differential attrition, and this card is the same trial as the previous card, not independent confirmation.

cards.headline: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Jones 2016): across comparative studies of large prostates, HoLEP and simple prostatectomy gave equivalent symptom and flow outcomes, with HoLEP favoured on blood loss, catheter time and hospital stay
cards.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Jones 2016): across comparative studies of large prostates, HoLEP and simple prostatectomy gave equivalent symptom and flow outcomes, with HoLEP favoured on blood loss, catheter time and hospital stay
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Jones 2016) — comparative studies of HoLEP versus simple prostatectomy for large prostates
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis, conducted to Cochrane collaboration standards, of studies comparing holmium laser enucleation with simple prostatectomy (open, robot-assisted or laparoscopic) for large prostate burdens, examining maximum flow rate, postvoid residual volume, symptom scores and perioperative outcomes.
cards.result: The review's comparison found HoLEP and simple prostatectomy equivalent on the objective and subjective efficacy outcomes it pooled (flow rate, residual volume and symptom scores), while the perioperative profile — blood loss, transfusion, catheter duration and length of stay — favoured HoLEP, at the cost of longer operating time. The authors frame the two as genuine alternatives for large glands, with the choice turning on local expertise and equipment rather than on efficacy.
cards.watchOut: The pooled studies are mostly non-randomised comparisons, so surgeon selection (which glands get offered the laser) can manufacture part of the perioperative advantage; the record's abstract does not report a single pooled patient total for this shelf to print, so none is asserted here.
cards.source: Jones P et al. Holmium laser enucleation versus simple prostatectomy for treating large prostates: Results of a systematic review and meta-analysis. Arab journal of urology. 2016. PMID: 26966594. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: for very large glands, HoLEP relieves obstruction as durably as simple prostatectomy and recovers faster — equivalence from one randomised programme, perioperative advantage consistent across comparisons
cards.summary: Synthesis: for very large glands, HoLEP relieves obstruction as durably as simple prostatectomy and recovers faster — equivalence from one randomised programme, perioperative advantage consistent across comparisons
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised programme in prostates over 100 g reported at 18 months (120 men) and 5 years (74 assessed), plus a systematic review pooling the wider comparative literature on large prostates.
cards.result: Functionally the operations tie: identical 5-year symptom scores (3.0) and flow rates (24.4 mL/s), similar residuals and reoperation rates (5% vs 6.7%). Perioperatively HoLEP wins on blood loss (haemoglobin fall 1.9 vs 2.8 g/dL), transfusion (0 vs 8 patients), catheter time (1 vs 6 days) and stay (2 vs 10 days), and loses on operating time (136 vs 91 minutes). Home pack #3043 covers HoLEP versus TURP in benign prostatic hyperplasia generally; this shelf is the very-large-gland population and the simple-prostatectomy comparator it does not cover.
cards.watchOut: The randomised base is a single centre's single programme with substantial 5-year attrition, and 'simple prostatectomy' now often means a robotic operation rather than the open transvesical procedure trialled here — the modern robotic comparison is a separate, mostly observational literature.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kuntz RM et al. Journal of endourology. 2004 (PMID: 15072629); Kuntz RM et al. European urology. 2008 (PMID: 17869409); Jones P et al. Arab journal of urology. 2016 (PMID: 26966594). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Transperineal vs transrectal prostate biopsy (TRANSLATE, PREVENT, ProBE-PC): detection at least as good, antibiotics often unnecessary, infection advantage still a trend
shelves.question: In men being investigated for suspected prostate cancer, does a transperineal biopsy approach detect as much significant cancer as transrectal biopsy, with fewer infections?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Prostatic Neoplasms/pathology, diagnosis, diagnostic imaging · Aged · Middle Aged · Image-Guided Biopsy/methods, adverse effects · Anesthesia, Local/methods · Neoplasm Grading · Perineum · Ultrasonography, Interventional/methods · Prostate-Specific Antigen/blood · Prostate/pathology, diagnostic imaging · Rectum
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — transperineal biopsy detects at least as much significant cancer and can be done without antibiotic prophylaxis, with infection rates no higher and a trend lower; it is somewhat more painful at the time. In TRANSLATE (Bryant 2025, PMID: 40139210; 1,126 men), Gleason Grade Group 2 or higher cancer was found in 60% on transperineal vs 54% on transrectal biopsy (odds ratio 1.32, p=0.031), and infection requiring hospital admission occurred in under 1% vs 2%. In PREVENT (Hu 2024, PMID: 38212178), transperineal biopsy without any antibiotic prophylaxis caused zero infections vs 1.4% with transrectal biopsy under targeted prophylaxis (p=0.059), with similar significant-cancer detection (53% vs 50%). ProBE-PC (Mian 2024, PMID: 37976319) found no infection difference (2.7% vs 2.6%), and a meta-analysis of the three prospective trials (PMID: 39095298) found no significant difference in detection or infection — so the benefit claim is equivalence-plus-stewardship, not proven superiority on infection.

cards.headline: Bryant 2025 (TRANSLATE): significant cancer detected in 60% on local-anaesthetic transperineal biopsy vs 54% on transrectal (odds ratio 1.32, p=0.031); infection needing hospital admission under 1% vs 2%
cards.summary: Bryant 2025 (TRANSLATE): significant cancer detected in 60% on local-anaesthetic transperineal biopsy vs 54% on transrectal (odds ratio 1.32, p=0.031); infection needing hospital admission under 1% vs 2%
cards.people: 1,126 biopsy-naive men investigated for suspected prostate cancer (raised age-specific PSA or abnormal examination, all with pre-biopsy MRI) randomised at ten UK hospitals to local-anaesthetic transperineal biopsy (n=562) or transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsy (n=564); primary outcome analysed in 547 and 540 men with biopsy results.
cards.result: Gleason Grade Group 2 or higher prostate cancer was found in 329 (60%) of 547 men on transperineal biopsy vs 294 (54%) of 540 on transrectal biopsy (odds ratio 1.32, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.70; p=0.031). Infection requiring hospital admission within 35 days occurred in 2 (under 1%) of 562 transperineal vs 9 (2%) of 564 transrectal participants. Overall biopsy-related complications (81% vs 77%), urinary retention needing catheterisation (6% vs 5%), urinary symptoms and sexual function at 4 months did not differ significantly. Serious adverse events occurred in 14 (2%) transperineal vs 25 (4%) transrectal participants. Men more commonly reported transperineal biopsy as immediately painful and embarrassing (38% vs 27%; OR 1.84).

cards.headline: Hu 2024 (PREVENT): zero infections after transperineal biopsy without antibiotic prophylaxis vs 1.4% after transrectal biopsy with targeted prophylaxis (p=0.059); significant-cancer detection 53% vs 50%
cards.summary: Hu 2024 (PREVENT): zero infections after transperineal biopsy without antibiotic prophylaxis vs 1.4% after transrectal biopsy with targeted prophylaxis (p=0.059); significant-cancer detection 53% vs 50%
cards.people: 658 biopsy-naive participants randomised in a multicentre trial to transperineal biopsy with no antibiotic prophylaxis, or transrectal biopsy with targeted prophylaxis (rectal-culture screening for fluoroquinolone-resistant bacteria, antibiotics matched to culture).
cards.result: Post-biopsy infection occurred in zero transperineal participants vs four (1.4%) transrectal participants (difference −1.4%; 95% CI −3.2% to 0.3%; p=0.059). Other complications were very low and similar. Detection of clinically significant cancer was similar (53% transperineal vs 50% transrectal; adjusted difference 2.0%, 95% CI −6.0 to 10). Transperineal participants had slightly worse periprocedural pain (adjusted difference 0.6 on a 0–10 scale, 95% CI 0.2 to 0.9), resolved by 7 days.
cards.watchOut: Four infections total cannot prove a difference (p=0.059) — the striking finding is that zero infections occurred with no prophylaxis at all, which is an antibiotic-stewardship result as much as a safety result. The transrectal arm used best-practice targeted prophylaxis, not casual prophylaxis.

cards.headline: Mian 2024 (ProBE-PC): no difference in infectious complications — 2.7% transperineal vs 2.6% transrectal (odds ratio 1.06, p=.99); no sepsis in either group (the treatment made no difference on complications)
cards.summary: Mian 2024 (ProBE-PC): no difference in infectious complications — 2.7% transperineal vs 2.6% transrectal (odds ratio 1.06, p=.99); no sepsis in either group (the treatment made no difference on complications)
cards.people: 763 men randomised in a pragmatic trial to office transrectal (351 biopsied) or transperineal (367 biopsied) prostate biopsy under local anaesthesia; primary outcome was a 30-day composite of fever, genitourinary infection, antibiotic prescriptions, office or emergency visits, hospitalisation or sepsis.
cards.result: A composite infectious complication occurred in 10 participants (2.7%) in the transperineal group and 9 (2.6%) in the transrectal group (odds ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.43 to 2.65; P=.99), with no difference in any individual component and no sepsis in either group. Composite noninfectious complications were 2.2% vs 1.7% (OR 1.28, P=.79), and no participant required hospitalisation or other intervention. The authors concluded both approaches remain clinically viable and safe.
cards.watchOut: The composite counts antibiotic prescriptions and visits, not just proven infections, and event rates were low in both arms — this trial tempers any claim that transperineal biopsy is dramatically safer in a setting where transrectal biopsy is already done carefully.
cards.source: Mian BM et al. Complications Following Transrectal and Transperineal Prostate Biopsy: Results of the ProBE-PC Randomized Clinical Trial. The Journal of Urology. 2024. PMID: 37976319. cards.headline: Zattoni 2024 (meta-analysis of the prospective trials): no significant difference between MRI-targeted transperineal and transrectal biopsy in significant-cancer detection (odds ratio 0.9) or infection (OR 0.8)
cards.summary: Zattoni 2024 (meta-analysis of the prospective trials): no significant difference between MRI-targeted transperineal and transrectal biopsy in significant-cancer detection (odds ratio 0.9) or infection (OR 0.8)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective randomised trials (Zattoni 2024)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the three prospective randomised trials meeting its criteria (PREVENT, ProBE-PC and PERFECT) comparing MRI-targeted transperineal with transrectal biopsy, published to May 2024.
cards.result: No difference was found in detection of clinically significant prostate cancer (odds ratio [OR] 0.9, 95% CI 0.7 to 1.1) or grade-group 1 cancer (OR 1.1, 0.8 to 1.4). Post-procedural infection (OR 0.8, 0.4 to 1.8), sepsis (OR 0.6, 0.1 to 4.5) and urinary retention (OR 0.5, 0.1 to 1.6) were similar. Pain during transperineal biopsy was slightly higher, with minimal difference by 7 days. The authors note transperineal biopsy can safely omit antibiotics, unlike the transrectal approach.
cards.watchOut: Only three trials, and TRANSLATE — the largest — was published after this review's search, so its pooled nulls do not include TRANSLATE's significant detection result. Technique, core numbers and prophylaxis varied between trials.
cards.source: Zattoni F et al. Transperineal Versus Transrectal Magnetic Resonance Imaging-targeted Prostate Biopsy: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Prospective Studies. cards.headline: Synthesis: transperineal biopsy detects at least as much significant cancer as transrectal, lets most men skip antibiotic prophylaxis, and has not been shown to cause more harm — but a proven infection advantage in randomised data is still only a trend
cards.summary: Synthesis: transperineal biopsy detects at least as much significant cancer as transrectal, lets most men skip antibiotic prophylaxis, and has not been shown to cause more harm — but a proven infection advantage in randomised data is still only a trend
cards.people: TRANSLATE, 1,126 men (Bryant 2025); PREVENT, 658 men (Hu 2024); ProBE-PC, 763 randomised (Mian 2024); meta-analysis of three prospective trials (Zattoni 2024).
cards.result: Detection: 60% vs 54% favouring transperineal in TRANSLATE (OR 1.32, p=0.031); 53% vs 50% in PREVENT; pooled OR 0.9 (not significant) in the pre-TRANSLATE meta-analysis. Infection: admission under 1% vs 2% (TRANSLATE); 0 vs 1.4% with no prophylaxis at all in the transperineal arm (PREVENT, p=0.059); 2.7% vs 2.6% composite (ProBE-PC, p=.99); no sepsis signal anywhere. Cost: slightly more immediate pain and embarrassment with transperineal biopsy, resolving within days. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — concordant randomised evidence for detection equivalence-or-better and antibiotic-free safety, but no single randomised infection endpoint has reached significance.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Scope: biopsy-naive men with pre-biopsy MRI in these trials. The MRI-first pathway question itself is homed on Shelf #801 (PRECISION); this shelf is only about the route the needle takes.

shelves.title: Spermatogenesis kinetics (physiology): one cycle of the seminiferous epithelium lasts about 16 days and the full process about 64 days (perhaps 6 days longer); daily production is about 4.25 million sperm per gram of testis — roughly 45 to 207 million per day in most men
shelves.question: In healthy men, how long does one full wave of spermatogenesis take, and how is daily sperm production quantified?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · *Spermatogenesis · *Seminiferous Epithelium · Sperm Count · Testis/physiology · *Spermatozoa · Time Factors
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology): spermatogenesis proceeds in repeating cellular associations (the cycle of the seminiferous epithelium), and several cycles must elapse before a spermatogonium becomes a spermatozoon. The carded primary human studies supply the numbers. Heller and Clermont's 1963 tritiated-thymidine labelling study — biopsies taken at intervals after intratesticular injection — timed the labelled cohort's advance (preleptotene spermatocytes at 1 hour, midpachytene at 16 days, immature spermatids at 32 days), giving a cycle length of 16 days and a total duration of spermatogenesis estimated at approximately 64 days. Amann's 2008 re-examination warns that this accepted value might be in error by approximately 6 days and that the 1960s database is neither robust nor precise — a caveat printed on the face of this shelf rather than smoothed over. Daily sperm production is quantified not from ejaculates but from testicular sperm reserves: Amann and Howards (1980) measured 4.25 × 10^6 sperm per gram of testis per day (range 1.4–6.3 × 10^6), so that 67% of men aged 20–50 probably produce between 45 × 10^6 and 207 × 10^6 spermatozoa per day; production per gram tends to decline with age, and substantial potential sperm are lost by degeneration of spermatocytes. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (with the duration caveat carried on the cards).

cards.headline: Heller & Clermont 1963: tritiated-thymidine labelling timed one epithelial cycle at 16 days and the whole of spermatogenesis at approximately 64 days
cards.summary: Heller & Clermont 1963: tritiated-thymidine labelling timed one epithelial cycle at 16 days and the whole of spermatogenesis at approximately 64 days
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (in-vivo radiolabel pulse-chase with serial testicular biopsy)
cards.people: Men who received intratesticular injections of tritiated thymidine, with testicular biopsies obtained at various intervals afterwards and the most mature labelled germ cells identified by radioautography; the number of subjects is not printed in the fetched abstract — N not documented in the record.
cards.result: The most mature labelled germ cells were the preleptotene spermatocytes at 1 hour after injection, the midpachytene spermatocytes at 16 days, and the immature spermatids at 32 days. From this timed advance the authors concluded that one cycle of the seminiferous epithelium lasts 16 days, and that the whole of spermatogenesis is estimated to consume approximately 64 days — about four cycles from spermatogonium to spermatozoon.
cards.watchOut: The 64-day figure is an estimate built from three labelled time points and an assumed number of cycles, obtained by an invasive labelling-and-biopsy method that cannot be repeated in healthy volunteers today — which is precisely why the value has rested on this small classic base for six decades (see the Amann 2008 card).

cards.headline: Amann & Howards 1980: daily sperm production was 4.25 million per gram of testis (range 1.4–6.3 million), putting most men between 45 and 207 million sperm per day
cards.summary: Amann & Howards 1980: daily sperm production was 4.25 million per gram of testis (range 1.4–6.3 million), putting most men between 45 and 207 million sperm per day
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (quantitative testicular/epididymal sperm-reserve measurement)
cards.people: Testicular and epididymal spermatozoal reserves determined in 11 healthy men, 1 vasectomised man and 12 other men (24 men in total; testis weight averaged over 19 testes). Tissue was obtained post-mortem or at surgery — see the watch-out.
cards.result: For healthy men, testis weight averaged 16.9 ± 1.2 g and daily spermatozoal production was 4.25 × 10^6 per gram (range 1.4 to 6.3 × 10^6 per gram). Based on the total sample, 67% of men aged 20 to 50 probably produce between 45 × 10^6 and 207 × 10^6 spermatozoa per day. Epididymal reserves of healthy men totalled 182 × 10^6 spermatozoa per epididymis (26% caput, 23% corpus, 52% cauda), total extragonadal reserves were approximately 440 × 10^6, and estimated transit through caput, corpus and cauda took 0.72, 0.71 and 1.76 days respectively — under 2 days of maturation in caput plus corpus. Daily production was normal in the one vasectomised man.
cards.watchOut: Reserves were measured in tissue from men who had died or undergone surgery, with the interval since any previous ejaculation unknown (assumed typical of ejaculation every 1 to 7 days) — so the per-day production figures are steady-state inferences from reserve counts, not direct daily measurements in living volunteers.
cards.source: Amann RP, Howards SS. Daily spermatozoal production and epididymal spermatozoal reserves of the human male. Journal of Urology. 1980. PMID: 6772801. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Amann 2008: the accepted 64-day duration may be wrong by about 6 days, production per gram falls with age, and ejaculate counts cannot substitute for a production rate
cards.summary: Amann 2008: the accepted 64-day duration may be wrong by about 6 days, production per gram falls with age, and ejaculate counts cannot substitute for a production rate
cards.type: Primary-programme critical review (human spermatogenesis quantification programme)
cards.people: Critical re-examination of the human spermatogenesis literature (the 1960s labelling database and the testicular-quantification programme), covering cycle organisation, durations, and measurement of daily sperm production.
cards.result: Daily sperm production per testis tends to decline with advancing age; regardless of age there is substantial loss of potential sperm from degeneration of spermatocytes, but not spermatids; and daily production per gram or per testis cannot be predicted from testis size or a man's age. The review's central caution for this shelf: the duration of spermatogenesis should be restudied because the accepted value might be in error by approximately 6 days, and the 1960s database is neither robust nor precise. It also sets the quantification standard used by the other cards — spermatogenesis must be evaluated by a rate attribute (production per unit time), not by sperm concentration or total count in an ejaculate.
cards.watchOut: This is a programme leader's critical review rather than a new experiment: its numbers restate the classic database it is criticising, so it qualifies — and simultaneously undermines the precision of — the 64-day figure on the Heller card.
cards.source: Amann RP. The cycle of the seminiferous epithelium in humans: a need to revisit? Journal of Andrology. 2008. PMID: 18497337. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: about 64 days end-to-end (16 days per cycle, ± about 6 days), and production counted in tens to a couple of hundred million sperm per day
cards.summary: Synthesis: about 64 days end-to-end (16 days per cycle, ± about 6 days), and production counted in tens to a couple of hundred million sperm per day
cards.people: Synthesis across Heller & Clermont 1963 (in-vivo labelling), Amann & Howards 1980 (24 men, reserve quantification) and Amann 2008 (programme re-examination).
cards.result: Duration and rate are measured by different methods that do not cross-check each other: labelling gives 16 days per epithelial cycle and approximately 64 days for the full process, with the field's own quantifier warning the total may be out by about 6 days; reserve counting gives 4.25 × 10^6 sperm per gram per day and a population range of roughly 45–207 × 10^6 per day for most men aged 20–50. Epididymal transit adds only about 3 more days (0.72 + 0.71 + 1.76) before sperm reach the cauda.
cards.watchOut: Every number on this shelf descends from small, decades-old, invasive or post-mortem studies that modern ethics and methods have not replaced; the values are the established account precisely because no better human measurement exists.
