shelves.title: Urinary flow–volume nomograms: Qmax and average flow rise with voided volume and fall with age
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how do maximum urinary flow rate (Qmax) and average flow vary with voided volume, age and sex — the flow–volume nomograms (Liverpool and successors) — and how repeatable is uroflowmetry within a person?
shelves.mesh: Urodynamics · Reference Values · Nomograms · Urination/physiology · Age Factors · Sex Characteristics · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall's and Boron & Boulpaep's accounts of micturition — detrusor contraction against urethral resistance, so flow is a joint product of bladder pressure and outlet calibre and cannot be read off a single number without the volume voided — three primary human datasets agree on the shape of normality. In 308 healthy women a single clinic void gave mean Qmax 23.06 ml/s and average flow 13.08 ml/s at a mean voided volume of about 290 ml, with flow–volume and corrected flow–age nomograms built from the data. In 101 healthy Japanese men recording repeated home voids, the flow–volume relationship was best fit by a saturating (quadratic/exponential) curve and Qmax at volumes over 150 ml was about 24 ml/s in men under 50 but 21.8 ml/s in men aged 50–59. In 58 randomly selected symptom-free men contributing 1,286 home voidings, maximum flow again rose with voided volume on nomograms, while a single measurement carried wide uncertainty — the true median Qmax could sit about 5 ml/s below or 6 ml/s above one reading. The settled teaching: quote flow only against volume and age, and treat one void as a sample, not a trait. Cross-point: invasive pressure–flow values in asymptomatic volunteers are shelved separately (urodynamics in healthy volunteers).

cards.headline: Barapatre 2009: in 308 healthy women, mean Qmax was 23.06 ml/s and average flow 13.08 ml/s at a mean voided volume of 290 ml — the basis of flow–volume and flow–age nomograms
cards.summary: Barapatre 2009: in 308 healthy women, mean Qmax was 23.06 ml/s and average flow 13.08 ml/s at a mean voided volume of 290 ml — the basis of flow–volume and flow–age nomograms
cards.people: 308 healthy women of menstrual age (of 343 enrolled; hospital staff, nursing students, visitors and patients' relatives in India), free of voiding symptoms, recent urinary infection and voiding-affecting disease or medication; one sitting free uroflow per woman on a digital uroflowmeter.
cards.result: Mean (±SD) age 33 ± 8.63 years; voided volume 289.79 ± 166.52 ml; maximum flow rate (Qmax) 23.06 ± 9.40 ml/s; average flow rate 13.08 ± 6.00 ml/s; voiding time 23.50 ± 12.52 s; time to Qmax 8.56 ± 6.55 s; post-void residue 2.92 ± 3.69 ml. Corrected Qmax was 1.41 ± 0.43 and corrected average flow 0.80 ± 0.27. Confidence-limit flow–volume nomograms were developed and validated in 25 asymptomatic and 22 symptomatic women, alongside corrected flow–age nomograms.
cards.watchOut: One void per woman in a clinic, in a single population and menstrual-age range: the nomogram describes that setting, and within-person repeatability cannot be judged from this study.
cards.source: Barapatre Y et al. Uroflowmetry in healthy women: Development and validation of flow-volume and corrected flow-age nomograms. Neurourol Urodyn. 2009. PMID: 19260085. cards.headline: Shinohara 2022: in 101 healthy Japanese men with repeated home voids, Qmax at volumes over 150 ml was about 24 ml/s under age 50 but 21.8 ml/s at ages 50–59
cards.summary: Shinohara 2022: in 101 healthy Japanese men with repeated home voids, Qmax at volumes over 150 ml was about 24 ml/s under age 50 but 21.8 ml/s at ages 50–59
cards.type: Prospective normative study with multiple measurements per person
cards.people: 101 Japanese male volunteers without lower urinary tract symptoms, aged 20–59 years (mean age 38.5 years; mean symptom scores near zero), recording flow and volume with a portable uroflowmeter over 2 successive days — multiple voids per man.
cards.result: A quadratic regression best fit the maximum-flow versus voided-volume relationship (mean coefficient of determination 0.93 ± 0.06). At voided volumes over 150 ml, mean maximum flow was significantly lower at ages 50–59 (21.8 ± 5.05 ml/s, P < 0.01) than at 20–29 (24.14 ± 4.94), 30–39 (24.05 ± 6.99) and 40–49 years (24.64 ± 5.72 ml/s). Two age-band nomograms were produced: Y = 28.99 {1 − exp(−0.01 × X)} for ages 20–49 and Y = 25.67 {1 − exp(−0.01 × X)} for ages 50–59, predicting maximum flow from voided volume.
cards.watchOut: Two days of home recording in one national population of men under 60; the age fall is shown only at the 50s step, and the equations should not be extrapolated to older men or other populations.
cards.source: Shinohara M et al. A new nomogram of urinary flow rate and volume based on multiple measurements per healthy adult Japanese men using a portable uroflowmeter (P-Flowdiary®). cards.headline: Folkestad 2004: 58 symptom-free men, 1,286 home voidings — a single Qmax reading can sit 5–6 ml/s from the person's true median
cards.summary: Folkestad 2004: 58 symptom-free men, 1,286 home voidings — a single Qmax reading can sit 5–6 ml/s from the person's true median
cards.people: 58 randomly selected symptom-free men aged 30–75 years from the National Register, registering 1,286 voidings (median 21 per person) at home with a portable uroflowmeter; timed micturition (time to void the first 100 ml) and maximum flow rate taken from the same voidings.
cards.result: Timed micturition increased with age and depended less on voided volume than maximum flow did; normal ranges were ≤9 s for men aged ≤55 years and ≤15 s for men ≥56 years. Maximum flow is presented in the paper as nomograms against voided volume. Repeatability was limited: for men ≥56 the true median timed micturition could be 6 s lower or 2.5 s higher than a single measurement, and for maximum flow rate the corresponding figures were 5 and 6 ml/s — so one void locates a man's usual flow only loosely.
cards.watchOut: A modest sample (N = 58, printed plainly) carrying many voids per man: the repeatability estimates are the durable content, while the exact nomogram percentiles rest on few men at the age extremes.
cards.source: Folkestad B, Spångberg A. Timed micturition and maximum urinary flow rate in randomly selected symptom-free males. Scand J Urol Nephrol. 2004. PMID: 15204399. cards.headline: Synthesis: flow means nothing without volume, age and repetition attached
cards.summary: Synthesis: flow means nothing without volume, age and repetition attached
cards.people: Three primary human datasets (308 women with single clinic voids; 101 men with 2 days of home voids; 58 men with 1,286 home voidings). Framing follows Guyton & Hall's and Boron & Boulpaep's accounts of the micturition reflex and detrusor–outlet mechanics, as textbook context, not as an evidence card. Cross-point: invasive urodynamic (pressure–flow) values in asymptomatic volunteers are covered by the companion urodynamics shelf, not here.
cards.result: Across sexes and methods, maximum and average flow rise with voided volume along a saturating curve — the reason every serious dataset is published as a flow–volume nomogram rather than a single cut-off — and flow falls with age (clearly by the sixth decade in men). Within a person, void-to-void scatter is large: a single Qmax can miss the individual's median by roughly 5–6 ml/s, so abnormality should be called on repeated voids read against the volume- and age-matched nomogram, not on one clinic tracing.
cards.watchOut: Devices, posture, setting (clinic vs home) and population all shift values; nomograms are method-bound. No anchor in this pack was refused: every carded record had a verifiable abstract this session.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Invasive urodynamics in healthy volunteers: normal pressure–flow values, and how poorly they repeat
shelves.question: In healthy asymptomatic volunteers, what do invasive urodynamic studies show — detrusor pressure at maximum flow, bladder capacity and compliance, and pressure–flow parameters — and how reproducible are they on repeat study?
shelves.mesh: Urodynamics/physiology · Reference Values · Urinary Bladder/physiology · Urethra/physiology · Pressure · Reproducibility of Results · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall's and Boron & Boulpaep's accounts of bladder filling and voiding — a compliant reservoir that fills at low pressure, then a coordinated detrusor contraction against a relaxing outlet — four primary human studies in asymptomatic volunteers agree on two settled points. First, normal voiding pressures are substantial: ambulatory studies in young men found maximum detrusor pressures around 59–70 cmH2O depending on fluid intake, and a mean detrusor pressure at maximum flow of 53 cmH2O at a mean Qmax of 24 ml/s, with a urethral resistance (URA) of 21 cmH2O proposed as the upper border of normal outflow. Second, 'normal' overlaps 'abnormal' and repeats poorly: among asymptomatic men aged 47–80, 13% met criteria for unequivocal obstruction and 63% showed unstable contractions, and in healthy women repeated urodynamics — immediate and at 1–5 months — had high coefficients of repeatability, i.e. poor reproducibility. The teaching is therefore double: these are the reference values, and a single invasive study in an individual must be read against their known scatter. Cross-point: non-invasive flow–volume nomograms are shelved separately.

cards.headline: Schmidt 2002: in 39 asymptomatic young men, maximum detrusor pressure was about 59 cmH2O — and rose to 70 cmH2O when water intake doubled
cards.summary: Schmidt 2002: in 39 asymptomatic young men, maximum detrusor pressure was about 59 cmH2O — and rose to 70 cmH2O when water intake doubled
cards.type: Ambulatory invasive urodynamic study in healthy volunteers
cards.people: 39 asymptomatic male volunteers, mean age 25.8 years (range 21–31), monitored ambulatorily for an average of 20.5 hours with a suprapubic bladder catheter and rectal abdominal-pressure balloon, voiding physiologically produced urine; the water-consumption comparison used subgroups drinking 30 ml/kg/day (n = 17) versus 60 ml/kg/day (n = 12).
cards.result: In both groups detrusor pressure rose before voiding and maximum detrusor pressure consistently occurred before micturition started, with an asymptotic pressure–flow pattern. Doubling water consumption raised urethral opening pressure from 51.2 ± 3.2 to 61.5 ± 5.1 cmH2O (P < 0.05), maximum detrusor pressure from 58.9 ± 4.5 to 70.0 ± 6.2 cmH2O (P < 0.01) and contractility from 15.4 ± 1.4 to 17.7 ± 1.4 W/m², and increased voids per day from 5.8 ± 0.5 to 9.8 ± 0.5 (P < 0.001); maximum flow (24.4 ± 1.4 to 25.2 ± 1.8 ml/s) and bladder capacity (286 ± 20 to 329 ± 15 ml) did not differ significantly. The authors conclude normal voiding pressures vary with urine production and sit differently from the then-current standardisation values.
cards.watchOut: Young men only, studied ambulatorily with natural filling — values are not interchangeable with conventional laboratory cystometry at artificial fill rates, and the water-intake subgroups are small (n = 17 and n = 12, printed plainly).
cards.source: Schmidt F et al. Urodynamic patterns of normal male micturition: influence of water consumption on urine production and detrusor function. J Urol. 2002. PMID: 12352417. cards.headline: Rosario 2008: in asymptomatic men aged 18–40, mean detrusor pressure at Qmax was 53 cmH2O at Qmax 24 ml/s; URA 21 cmH2O marked the upper border of normal outflow
cards.summary: Rosario 2008: in asymptomatic men aged 18–40, mean detrusor pressure at Qmax was 53 cmH2O at Qmax 24 ml/s; URA 21 cmH2O marked the upper border of normal outflow
cards.people: 37 healthy male volunteers aged 18–40 years undergoing ambulatory urodynamic monitoring during physiological bladder filling; 66 fill–void cycles in 25 individuals were evaluable.
cards.result: Mean detrusor pressure at maximum flow (pdetQmax) was 53 ± 3 cmH2O with mean Qmax 24 ± 2 ml/s. A urethral resistance factor (URA) of 21 cmH2O defined the upper border of normality for the outflow condition, with corresponding upper limits of AGN (Abrams–Griffiths number) 40 cmH2O and OCO 1 on the other nomograms; results above these values should be considered abnormal in this age group. The linear ICS and Schäfer nomograms gave minimal differences, supporting a single recommended method for comparability.
cards.watchOut: Only 25 of 37 volunteers contributed evaluable cycles, and the limits are defined in young men before age-related lower-urinary-tract change — applying them to older men requires the physiological explanation the authors demand, not automatic labelling.
cards.source: Rosario DJ et al. Definition of normality of pressure-flow parameters based on observations in asymptomatic men. Neurourol Urodyn. 2008. PMID: 18064668. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Walker 2001: among 24 asymptomatic men aged 47–80, 13% were unequivocally 'obstructed' on pressure–flow criteria and 63% had unstable contractions
cards.summary: Walker 2001: among 24 asymptomatic men aged 47–80, 13% were unequivocally 'obstructed' on pressure–flow criteria and 63% had unstable contractions
cards.type: Invasive pressure–flow study in asymptomatic controls (N = 24, printed plainly)
cards.people: 24 male volunteers aged 47–80 years (mean 62.5) attending a general surgical clinic, who had never sought care for urinary symptoms and did not perceive a urological problem (median symptom score 2.0), undergoing symptom scoring, free uroflowmetry, repeat pressure–flow studies and prostate ultrasound.
cards.result: On pressure–flow studies, 3 men (13%) had unequivocal obstruction, 7 (29%) fell in the equivocal zone and 14 (58%) had no obstruction by standard ICS / Abrams–Griffiths / resistance classifications; 15 men (63%) had unstable detrusor contractions on medium-fill cystometry. The authors conclude that asymptomatic obstruction is real, that obstruction may matter less to symptom development than previously thought, and that operating on obstructed but asymptomatic men is probably unwise.
cards.watchOut: A small control group (N = 24) recruited from a surgical clinic rather than the general population — the percentages carry wide uncertainty, but the direction (abnormal-looking traces in symptom-free men) is the durable finding.

cards.headline: Gupta 2004: in 20 healthy women, repeated urodynamics repeated poorly — high coefficients of repeatability immediately and at 1–5 months
cards.summary: Gupta 2004: in 20 healthy women, repeated urodynamics repeated poorly — high coefficients of repeatability immediately and at 1–5 months
cards.type: Reproducibility study of invasive urodynamics in healthy volunteers
cards.people: 20 asymptomatic women, mean age 41.8 years (30–55), undergoing uroflowmetry, post-void residual measurement, medium-fill cystometry and pressure–flow study with surface EMG; the study was repeated immediately without removing the catheters, and 16 women returned for an identical study 1–5 months later.
cards.result: Immediate repeatability of some filling parameters could not even be calculated because the first test influenced the second (an accommodation in bladder filling volumes). Maximum flow, detrusor pressure at maximum flow and voided volume had high coefficients of repeatability on immediate testing, as did all parameters on short-term retesting — indicating relatively poor repeatability; selecting the 'best' pressure–flow value did not consistently improve repeatability. The authors attribute this to true physiological fluctuation plus the relative insensitivity of the instruments.
cards.watchOut: Healthy women only, and the immediate-repeat design is itself perturbed by catheter dwell and accommodation — but that perturbation is part of the clinical lesson: the test changes the system it measures.
cards.source: Gupta A et al. The reproducibility of urodynamic findings in healthy female volunteers: results of repeated studies in the same setting and after short-term follow-up. Neurourol Urodyn. 2004. PMID: 15227647. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: normal voiding pressures are high, 'abnormal' traces occur in symptom-free people, and one study repeats loosely
cards.summary: Synthesis: normal voiding pressures are high, 'abnormal' traces occur in symptom-free people, and one study repeats loosely
cards.people: Four primary human studies in asymptomatic volunteers (39 and 37 young men on ambulatory monitoring; 24 older asymptomatic men; 20 healthy women in a repeatability design). Framing follows Guyton & Hall's and Boron & Boulpaep's accounts of bladder compliance, the micturition reflex and detrusor–outlet coordination, as textbook context, not as an evidence card. Cross-point: non-invasive uroflow nomograms are covered by the companion flow–volume shelf.
cards.result: The reference picture is consistent: a compliant bladder filling at low pressure, then detrusor pressures at maximum flow around 53 cmH2O in young men with Qmax around 24 ml/s, maximum detrusor pressures of roughly 59–70 cmH2O varying with urine production, and proposed upper limits of normal outflow (URA 21 cmH2O; AGN 40). Against that, 13% of symptom-free older men met obstruction criteria and most showed unstable contractions, and repeat studies in healthy women reproduced poorly — so urodynamic numbers define population reference ranges, not a clean normal/abnormal line in an individual.
cards.watchOut: Ambulatory natural-fill and laboratory medium-fill cystometry are different measurements; age bands differ across studies; several cohorts are small (N = 20–39) and their Ns are printed on their cards. No anchor in this pack was refused: every carded record had a verifiable abstract this session.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Semen characteristics in fertile men: WHO 5th-centile limits (concentration 15–16 million/mL, normal forms 4%) are fertile-population percentiles, not infertility cut-offs — and within-man variability is wide
shelves.question: In men of proven fertility, what is the distribution of semen characteristics (volume, concentration, motility, morphology) — the WHO reference values and their lower 5th-percentile reference limits — and how large is within-man variability between samples?
shelves.mesh: Semen Analysis · Reference Values · Sperm Count · Fathers · World Health Organization
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — for the fertile-population distributions, framed by Guyton & Hall / Ganong on semen production and composition as textbook framing, not as an evidence card. The core teaching point, on the face: these are one-sided lower 5th-percentile reference limits from men whose partners conceived within 12 months — descriptions of a fertile population, NOT diagnostic cut-offs separating fertile from infertile men. The WHO 2010 distribution (over 4,500 men, 14 countries) gives 5th centiles of volume 1.5 mL, concentration 15 million/mL, total number 39 million, progressive motility 32% and normal forms 4.0% (Cooper 2010). The updated collation behind the WHO 6th edition (over 3,500 men, 12 countries, five continents) lands almost identically — concentration 16 million/mL, progressive motility 30% (total 42%), normal forms 4% (Campbell 2021) — which is why the stamp is ESTABLISHED: two global collations a decade apart agree. Within-man variability is large: repeated samples from 25 fathers varied widely within and between men for essentially every parameter except pH (Cooper 1991), so a single sample characterises a man poorly. Morphology percentages are criteria-dependent — the 1991 fathers study's 42% lower limit for normal forms used the scoring of its era and is not comparable with the 4% strict-criteria figure; the cards keep them separate rather than averaging them.

cards.headline: Cooper 2010 (WHO): lower 5th-centile reference limits from fertile men — volume 1.5 mL, concentration 15 million/mL, total number 39 million, progressive motility 32%, normal forms 4.0%
cards.summary: Cooper 2010 (WHO): lower 5th-centile reference limits from fertile men — volume 1.5 mL, concentration 15 million/mL, total number 39 million, progressive motility 32%, normal forms 4.0%
cards.type: Human reference-distribution collation (WHO fertile-men semen values), Hum Reprod Update 2010
cards.people: Semen samples from over 4,500 men in 14 countries on four continents, from retrospective and prospective analyses of fertile men, men of unknown fertility and normozoospermic men; the reference distributions come from men whose partners had a time-to-pregnancy of 12 months or less.
cards.result: One-sided lower reference limits (5th centiles, with 95% confidence intervals) from the fertile (time-to-pregnancy ≤12 months) population: semen volume 1.5 mL (1.4–1.7); total sperm number 39 million per ejaculate (33–46); sperm concentration 15 million per mL (12–16); vitality 58% live (55–63); progressive motility 32% (31–34); total (progressive + non-progressive) motility 40% (38–42); morphologically normal forms 4.0% (3.0–4.0). The reference population's semen quality was superior to the general-population and normozoospermic groups — these limits describe fertile men, and the record presents them as a tool alongside clinical data, not as a fertility diagnosis.
cards.watchOut: 5th centiles of a fertile population — by construction 5% of fertile men fall below each limit; a value below a limit is not a diagnosis of infertility. The record is a collation/review of source datasets, carded as the WHO reference distribution it is.
cards.source: Cooper TG, Noonan E, von Eckardstein S, Auger J, Baker HWG, Behre HM, Haugen TB, Kruger T, Wang C, Mbizvo MT, Vogelsong KM. World Health Organization reference values for human semen characteristics. Human reproduction update. 2010. PMID: 19934213. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Campbell 2021 (updated WHO collation): 5th centiles barely move — concentration 16 million/mL, progressive motility 30% (total 42%), normal forms 4% in over 3,500 fertile men
cards.summary: Campbell 2021 (updated WHO collation): 5th centiles barely move — concentration 16 million/mL, progressive motility 30% (total 42%), normal forms 4% in over 3,500 fertile men
cards.type: Human reference-distribution update (WHO 2020/6th-edition semen data), Andrology 2021
cards.people: Published data from 2010–2020 combined with the datasets used for the WHO 2010 distribution — in total data from more than 3,500 subjects from twelve countries and five continents, assembled to provide the updated distribution of values for use by WHO in 2021 (the 6th-edition manual programme).
cards.result: The 5th-centile values for concentration, motility and morphology are: 16 × 10^6/mL concentration, 30% progressive motility (42% total motility) and 4% normal forms — essentially unchanged from the 2010 limits despite a larger, more geographically representative base. The authors state plainly that these values do not represent distinct limits between fertile and subfertile men, that data are still missing from many countries, and that the total (under 4,000 subjects) remains relatively low.
cards.watchOut: This collation overlaps the 2010 source datasets by design (it extends them) — concordance between the two cards is therefore partly built-in, and the shelf says so rather than presenting two fully independent confirmations.

cards.headline: Cooper 1991: repeated samples from 25 fathers vary widely within the same man — single-sample values characterise a man poorly; era morphology lower limit 42% is not the modern 4%
cards.summary: Cooper 1991: repeated samples from 25 fathers vary widely within the same man — single-sample values characterise a man poorly; era morphology lower limit 42% is not the modern 4%
cards.type: Human repeated-samples variability study (semen parameters in fathers), Hum Reprod 1991
cards.people: Several semen samples from each of 25 men (mean age 31 years) who had fathered children within the previous 29 months without clinical assistance; volume, pH, sperm characteristics and ejaculate content of six epididymal, prostatic and seminal-vesicle compounds were measured per sample. N = 25 printed on the face.
cards.result: There was large variation both within and between individuals' samples for concentrations and amounts per ejaculate of all parameters except pH. Lower limits (combined means minus twice the combined within- and between-father standard deviation, spanning 96% of values) were: volume 1.9 mL; pH 7.4; total sperm count 39 × 10^6; normal morphological forms 42%; motility grades a 4%, b 19%, c 1%, d 19%; curvilinear velocity 27 microns/s. The total-count limit (39 million) matches the later WHO figure, while the 42% morphology limit reflects the scoring criteria of its era — not comparable with the 4% strict-criteria centile on the WHO cards.
cards.watchOut: N = 25, printed on the face. Morphology and motility grading schemes have changed since 1991 — only the variability finding and the total-count concordance carry forward; the percentages do not transfer to modern scoring.
cards.source: Cooper TG, Jockenhövel F, Nieschlag E. Variations in semen parameters from fathers. Human reproduction (Oxford, England). 1991. PMID: 1757526. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: fertile-men semen distributions are stable across two WHO collations (5th centiles ≈15–16 million/mL, 4% normal forms), are population percentiles rather than infertility cut-offs, and sit on wide within-man variability
cards.summary: Synthesis: fertile-men semen distributions are stable across two WHO collations (5th centiles ≈15–16 million/mL, 4% normal forms), are population percentiles rather than infertility cut-offs, and sit on wide within-man variability
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human reports above (Cooper 2010; Campbell 2021; Cooper 1991), framed by the Guyton & Hall / Ganong account of spermatogenesis and semen composition as textbook framing, not as an evidence card.
cards.result: The distribution, triangulated: the WHO fertile-men 5th centiles changed negligibly between the 2010 collation (over 4,500 men) and the updated 2020 collation behind the 6th edition (over 3,500 men) — concentration 15 then 16 million/mL, normal forms 4% in both — a stability that supports the ESTABLISHED stamp, with the overlap of source datasets declared on the Campbell card. Two cautions are part of the physiology, not footnotes: the limits are percentiles of fertile men (5% of fertile men fall below each one; neither collation claims a fertile/subfertile dividing line), and within-man variation between samples is large, so repeat sampling is intrinsic to interpreting any man's values. No refusals on this shelf: the slated updated-edition limb verified as Campbell 2021 with an abstract-present record. No animal data are carded.
cards.watchOut: Geographic coverage remains incomplete in both collations (their own caveat); morphology percentages are scoring-criteria-dependent and are never pooled across eras on this shelf.

shelves.title: The normal voiding diary: ~6-8.5 voids and ~1.7 L per 24 hours, ~0.5-1.6 nocturnal voids rising with age, and voided volumes shrinking from ~313 to ~209 mL in men
shelves.question: In asymptomatic adults reporting no voiding complaints, what does a 24-hour frequency–volume chart show — voids per day, nocturnal voids, mean and maximum voided volume and 24-hour urine production — by age and sex?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Circadian Rhythm · Cross-Sectional Studies · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Reference Values · Urination/physiology · Urine · Aged, 80 and over · Urination · Rheology · Urinary Bladder/physiology
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, ch. 26 (micturition); Boron & Boulpaep (bladder function). In 1,152 adults reporting no voiding complaints, the 24-hour frequency-volume chart shows: voiding frequency rising with age in men from 6.0 (third decade) to 8.5 (past 70) and in women from 6.9 to a peak of 8.2 in the sixth decade then 7.8; nocturia rising from 0.5 to 1.6 in men and 0.7 to 1.4 in women; mean voided volume falling from 313 to 209 mL in men and 274 to 240 mL in women; and mean 24-hour urine production of 1,718 mL (men) and 1,762 mL (women) (van Haarst 2004). The classic women's studies establish the instrument: the 48-hour chart is reliable, with mean voided volume its most reproducible parameter (Larsson & Victor 1988, N = 151), and a 12-parameter normal pattern was defined in 33 healthy women (Kassis & Schick 1993, small-N labelled). This diary slice is the third leg of bladder measurement beside uroflowmetry and urodynamics, and supplies the normal thresholds that nocturia treatment shelves presuppose. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: 24-hour frequency-volume charts in 1,152 complaint-free adults: men void 6.0 times/day in their 20s rising to 8.5 past 70, women peak at 8.2 in their 50s; 24-hour urine ~1.72-1.76 L (van Haarst 2004)
cards.summary: 24-hour frequency-volume charts in 1,152 complaint-free adults: men void 6.0 times/day in their 20s rising to 8.5 past 70, women peak at 8.2 in their 50s; 24-hour urine ~1.72-1.76 L (van Haarst 2004)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (24-h frequency-volume chart reference values by age and sex)
cards.people: 1,152 men and women aged over 20 years who denied any voiding complaints, each completing a 24-hour frequency-volume chart (first morning void to first void next morning) with times, volumes and bedtime hours recorded.
cards.result: In men, mean 24-hour voiding frequency rose linearly from 6.0 in the third decade to 8.5 past age 70, and nocturia from 0.5 to 1.6. In women, frequency rose from 6.9 (third decade) to 8.2 (sixth decade) then declined slightly to 7.8 past 70, while nocturia rose more slowly, 0.7 to 1.4. Mean volume per void fell significantly with age in both sexes — 313 to 209 mL in men, 274 to 240 mL in women. Mean 24-hour urine volume was 1,718 mL in men and 1,762 mL in women, and higher 24-hour production was strongly associated with larger voided volumes; maximum voided volume also fell with age, more prominently in men.
cards.watchOut: Self-declared 'no voiding complaints' is the entry criterion, not urodynamic normality: the male frequency rise with age likely already contains subclinical prostatic change, as the authors state.

primary human physiology study (24-h frequency-volume chart reference values by age and sex) 1,152 men and women aged over 20 years who denied any voiding complaints, each completing a 24-hour frequency-volume chart (first morning void to first void next morning) with times, volumes and bedtime hours recorded. in men, mean 24-hour voiding frequency rose linearly from 6.0 in the third decade to 8.5 past age 70, and nocturia from 0.5 to 1.6. in women, frequency rose from 6.9 (third decade) to 8.2 (sixth decade) then declined slightly to 7.8 past 70, while nocturia rose more slowly, 0.7 to 1.4. mean volume per void fell significantly with age in both sexes — 313 to 209 ml in men, 274 to 240 ml in women. mean 24-hour urine volume was 1,718 ml in men and 1,762 ml in women, and higher 24-hour production was strongly associated with larger voided volumes; maximum voided volume also fell with age, more prominently in men. self-declared 'no voiding complaints' is the entry criterion, not urodynamic normality: the male frequency rise with age likely already contains subclinical prostatic change, as the authors state. van haarst ep et al. bju international. 2004. pmid: 15180618. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · age factors · aged · circadian rhythm · cross-sectional studies · female · humans · male · middle aged · reference values · urination/physiology · urine

cards.headline: 48-hour charts in 151 complaint-free women: the chart is reliable, and mean voided volume is its most reproducible parameter (Larsson & Victor 1988)
cards.summary: 48-hour charts in 151 complaint-free women: the chart is reliable, and mean voided volume is its most reproducible parameter (Larsson & Victor 1988)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (frequency/volume chart patterns and reproducibility in healthy women)
cards.people: 151 women without micturition complaints completing a 48-hour frequency/volume chart; distributions of the chart parameters and their reproducibility presented. Classic small normative study — N printed here on the face.
cards.result: The authors found the frequency/volume chart a valuable and reliable instrument for assessing micturition patterns. Of its parameters, the mean voided volume — which combines frequency and total voided volume — showed the best reproducibility and is proposed as the parameter of primary importance. They caution that normal micturition behaviour is highly dependent on social circumstances, so the conditions under which the chart is kept are part of the measurement. The fetched record presents the parameter distributions without headline numeric values, and this card claims only the reproducibility finding.
cards.watchOut: A 1988 supplement paper with a short abstract carrying no numeric table: it anchors the method's reliability and the mean-voided-volume recommendation, while the numeric reference values on this shelf come from the van Haarst cohort.

cards.headline: Synthesis: complaint-free adults void about 6-8.5 times in 24 hours producing ~1.7 L — frequency climbs with age in men as voided volumes shrink, nocturia rises from ~0.5-0.7 to ~1.4-1.6, and mean voided volume is the chart's most reproducible number
cards.summary: Synthesis: complaint-free adults void about 6-8.5 times in 24 hours producing ~1.7 L — frequency climbs with age in men as voided volumes shrink, nocturia rises from ~0.5-0.7 to ~1.4-1.6, and mean voided volume is the chart's most reproducible number
cards.people: Synthesis of the three primary human studies above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (ch. 26, micturition) and Boron & Boulpaep (bladder function). The numeric reference frame is the 1,152-person complaint-free cohort (van Haarst 2004): 24-hour frequency 6.0 rising to 8.5 in men and 6.9-8.2 then 7.8 in women across the decades; nocturia 0.5→1.6 (men) and 0.7→1.4 (women); mean voided volume falling 313→209 mL (men) and 274→240 mL (women); 24-hour urine production ~1,718-1,762 mL. The two classic women's studies supply the method's credentials: the 48-hour chart is reliable and mean voided volume its most reproducible parameter (Larsson & Victor 1988, N = 151), and a 12-parameter normal pattern for young and middle-aged women was defined early (Kassis & Schick 1993, N = 33, small-N labelled). Diary-based daily-life measurement is the third leg of bladder measurement alongside the uroflowmetry nomograms and invasive urodynamics shelves (Slate 8 rows S8-4-33/S8-4-34), and it supplies the 'normal' against which treatment shelves such as desmopressin for nocturia (live #487) define abnormality — both cross-pointed in prose. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: A single 24-hour chart is a sample of behaviour, not a fixed trait: fluid intake, social circumstance and day choice move every parameter, which is why the classic studies insist on the conditions of recording.
cards.source: Synthesis of van Haarst EP et al. BJU international. 2004 (PMID: 15180618); Larsson G et al. Scandinavian journal of urology and nephrology. shelves.title: Age-specific prostate volume in healthy men: Arab TRUS 8–22 mL at 40–49 to 10–33 mL at 70–79; Iranian 95th-percentile ranges to 18–73 mL; German MRI median 31.29 mL
shelves.question: In healthy men, what is the normal prostate volume by age — the age-specific ranges and upper limits on transrectal ultrasound and on MRI — how steeply does volume rise from the fifth to the eighth decade, and how far do population (ancestry / region) reference ranges sit from one another? (The datasets' paired serum PSA and PSA-density ranges are carded as co-analytes of the same reference studies.)
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Arabs · Humans · Kuwait/ethnology · Male · Middle Aged · Oman/ethnology · Prostate/anatomy & histology · Prostate-Specific Antigen/blood · Prostatic Neoplasms/blood,ethnology,pathology · Reference Values · Aging/blood · Health · Iran
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, on three independent population datasets. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, reproductive sections — brief framing only; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so. Prostate volume rises steeply with age in every dataset, but the ranges sit far apart by population and modality: healthy Arab men (transrectal ultrasound) 8–22 mL at 40–49 years to 10–33 mL at 70–79; healthy Iranian men (ultrasound, 95th-percentile ranges) 14–59 mL at 50–59 to 18–73 mL at 70–79; healthy German men (MRI) median 31.29 mL with a 95th percentile of 51.39 mL. The datasets' paired PSA and PSA-density ranges are carded as co-analytes of the same reference studies. Every dataset excluded men with urinary symptoms or known prostate disease — these are healthy-gland ranges, not screening thresholds, and no card presents an upper limit as a biopsy or referral trigger; that question belongs to live #212 (PSA screening), cross-pointed only.

cards.headline: Healthy Arab men (Kehinde 2005): transrectal-ultrasound prostate volumes 8–22 mL at 40–49 years, 9–30 mL at 60–69 and 10–33 mL at 70–79 — lower than reported Caucasian values
cards.summary: Healthy Arab men (Kehinde 2005): transrectal-ultrasound prostate volumes 8–22 mL at 40–49 years, 9–30 mL at 60–69 and 10–33 mL at 70–79 — lower than reported Caucasian values
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (age-specific reference ranges, transrectal ultrasound)
cards.people: 396 healthy Arab men from Kuwait and Oman aged 15–79 years; men over 40 had digital rectal examination and transrectal ultrasonography for prostate volume, with paired serum PSA measured as a co-analyte.
cards.result: Age-specific prostate volumes were 8–22 mL at 40–49 years, 9–30 mL at 60–69 years and 10–33 mL at 70–79 years, as published (the abstract does not print a 50–59 volume range). Paired age-specific serum PSA ranges were 0–0.9 ng/mL at 40–49, 0–2.7 ng/mL at 60–69 and 0–5.5 ng/mL at 70–79. PSA level and prostate volume both correlated with age (P < 0.001). The authors report Arab men had lower PSA levels and prostate volumes than Caucasians, and values similar to those reported for Japanese and Chinese men.
cards.watchOut: Healthy-gland ranges from one Gulf population, measured by transrectal ultrasound: an upper reference limit here is not a biopsy or referral trigger — that screening question belongs to live shelf #212, cross-pointed, not re-carded.
cards.source: Kehinde EO et al. Age-specific reference levels of serum prostate-specific antigen and prostate volume in healthy Arab men. BJU international. 2005. PMID: 16042719. cards.headline: Healthy Iranian men (Khezri 2009): 95th-percentile prostate volumes 14–59 mL at 50–59 years, 16–66 mL at 60–69 and 18–73 mL at 70–79, with age-specific PSA and PSA-density ranges alongside
cards.summary: Healthy Iranian men (Khezri 2009): 95th-percentile prostate volumes 14–59 mL at 50–59 years, 16–66 mL at 60–69 and 18–73 mL at 70–79, with age-specific PSA and PSA-density ranges alongside
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (age-specific reference ranges, transrectal ultrasound)
cards.people: 913 healthy Iranian men aged 50–79 years with no lower urinary tract symptoms and no evidence of prostate cancer; transrectal ultrasound in 633 and serum PSA in 666, with PSA density derived as a co-analyte.
cards.result: Prostate volumes (95th-percentile ranges) were 14–59 mL at 50–59 years, 16–66 mL at 60–69 years and 18–73 mL at 70–79 years. Paired serum PSA ranges (95th percentile) were 0.00–2.61 ng/mL, 0.00–3.59 ng/mL and 0.00–4.83 ng/mL for the same decades, and PSA-density ranges were 0.00–0.076, 0.00–0.10 and 0.00–0.14 ng/mL/mL. PSA correlated with age (r = 0.280; P < 0.001) and prostate volume (r = 0.327; P < 0.001); volume rose with age (r = 0.197; P < 0.001). The authors conclude PSA, volume and PSA density are age- and race-dependent.
cards.watchOut: These upper limits (to 73 mL at 70–79) sit far above the Arab dataset's (33 mL) at the same ages — a population difference printed as content, not reconciled; modality is transrectal ultrasound, never merged with the MRI dataset below.

cards.headline: Healthy German men, MRI (Lindholz 2026): median prostate volume 31.29 mL (5th–95th percentile 20.74–51.39), PSA 0.81 ng/mL and PSA density 0.025 ng/mL² in 1,037 disease-free men from the Study of Health in Pomerania
cards.summary: Healthy German men, MRI (Lindholz 2026): median prostate volume 31.29 mL (5th–95th percentile 20.74–51.39), PSA 0.81 ng/mL and PSA density 0.025 ng/mL² in 1,037 disease-free men from the Study of Health in Pomerania
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (stratified normative reference values, MRI)
cards.people: Men from the population-based Study of Health in Pomerania (Germany) with 10 years of follow-up; of 1,696 men, 1,037 were analysed (median age 46 years, IQR 38–56) after excluding men with diagnosed prostate cancer, benign prostatic hyperplasia or lower urinary tract symptoms. Prostate volume and PSA density came from pelvic MRI with deep-learning segmentation; values were modelled by age, body-mass index and height.
cards.result: Median prostate volume was 31.29 mL (5th–95th percentile 20.74–51.39), median PSA 0.81 ng/mL (0.32–2.79) and median PSA density 0.025 ng/mL² (0.011–0.071); overall 95th percentiles were 51.39 mL, 2.79 ng/mL and 0.071 ng/mL² respectively. Volume and PSA increased progressively with age, whereas PSA density was more age-stable, peaking at 71 years, plateauing to 75 and then declining, and age-adjusted PSA density never exceeded 0.11 ng/mL². Body-mass index correlated positively with volume but inversely with PSA density; PSA was negatively associated with height. An open-access calculator accompanies the paper.
cards.watchOut: MRI-derived volumes are carded as MRI values, never merged with the transrectal-ultrasound datasets; the reference population deliberately excluded BPH and urinary symptoms, so these are healthy-gland norms, not screening thresholds (the screening question is live #212's).
cards.source: Lindholz M et al. Reference values for PSA, PSA density, and MRI prostate volume in healthy German men. European radiology. 2026. PMID: 42789055. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

shelves.title: Testicular volume on ultrasound by population: ~17 mL in European fertile men (lower limits 12 / 11 mL), 13.64 mL in Vietnamese healthy fathers, ~10.4 mL in Somali men (95% intervals 5.7–18.0 / 5.2–17.0 mL)
shelves.question: In healthy adult men, what are the reference values for testicular volume on ultrasound — mean volume and lower and upper reference limits — how far do population reference intervals sit from one another (European fertile men vs Somali vs Vietnamese reference figures), and how well do ultrasound volumes agree with Prader-orchidometer volumes?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Fertility · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Reference Values · Scrotum/diagnostic imaging · Testis/anatomy & histology · Ultrasonography · Ultrasound, High-Intensity Focused, Transrectal · Young Adult · Asian People · Infertility, Male · Retrospective Studies · Testis · Testosterone · Ultrasonics
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, reproductive sections — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so. Three independent datasets, carded per population because the population gradient IS the content: a prospective European Academy of Andrology multicentre standardisation study of 248 healthy fertile men found mean ultrasound volume ~17 mL with lower reference limits of 12 mL (right) and 11 mL (left); a retrospective Vietnamese andrology-service dataset (24,440 attendees; the reference figure is its healthy-fathers subgroup, mean 13.64 ± 3.44 mL — the subgroup's own N is not documented in the record and the headline 24,440 is never printed as the reference N); and a retrospective Somali reference-interval study (212 sonographically normal men) found means of 10.61 / 10.19 mL with 95% intervals of 5.7–18.0 / 5.2–17.0 mL. No interval here may be printed as universal. The EAA overview paper (PMID 35930758) is the same cohort as the EAA dataset carded here and is counted once — it is not a fourth dataset and is not carded. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING (see proposedStamp).

cards.headline: EAA multicentre standardisation study (Lotti 2021): 248 healthy fertile men — mean testicular volume ~17 mL, lower reference limits 12 mL (right) and 11 mL (left), ultrasound ellipsoid volume correlating best with Prader orchidometer
cards.summary: EAA multicentre standardisation study (Lotti 2021): 248 healthy fertile men — mean testicular volume ~17 mL, lower reference limits 12 mL (right) and 11 mL (left), ultrasound ellipsoid volume correlating best with Prader orchidometer
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (prospective multicentre standardisation study, healthy fertile men)
cards.people: 248 healthy fertile men (mean age 35.3 ± 5.9 years) in the European Academy of Andrology multicentre study, evaluated on the same day with clinical, biochemical, seminal and scrotal colour Doppler ultrasound examinations following standard operating procedures. This is a prospective healthy-fertile-men standardisation study — the strongest dataset kind on this shelf.
cards.result: The mean testicular volume of healthy fertile men was ~17 mL. The lowest reference limit for the right and left testis was 12 and 11 mL respectively — the thresholds defining testicular hypotrophy. Ultrasound-measured and Prader-orchidometer volumes were closely related, and the ultrasound volume assessed with the ellipsoid formula showed the best correlation with orchidometer volume. The highest reference limits for epididymal head, tail and vas deferens were 12, 6 and 4.5 mm. Mean testicular volume was associated positively with sperm concentration and total count and negatively with gonadotropin levels and pulse pressure; colour Doppler ultrasound detected varicocele in 37.2% of these healthy fertile men, without association with seminal or hormonal parameters.
cards.watchOut: A fertile-men reference population: these limits describe men of proven fertility under a standardised protocol, and the ~17 mL mean sits well above the other two populations carded — it must not be exported as the adult male norm.
cards.source: Lotti F et al. The European Academy of Andrology (EAA) ultrasound study on healthy, fertile men: Scrotal ultrasound reference ranges and associations with clinical, seminal, and biochemical characteristics. Andrology. 2021. PMID: 33244893. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Vietnamese andrology-service dataset (Nguyen Hoai 2022): healthy-fathers subgroup mean volume 13.64 ± 3.44 mL (left 13.94, right 13.34) — a clinic-based, reference-like figure drawn from 24,440 attendees
cards.summary: Vietnamese andrology-service dataset (Nguyen Hoai 2022): healthy-fathers subgroup mean volume 13.64 ± 3.44 mL (left 13.94, right 13.34) — a clinic-based, reference-like figure drawn from 24,440 attendees
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (retrospective clinic-based reference derivation, healthy-fathers subgroup)
cards.people: 24,440 men who sought consultation at the Andrology and Sexual Medicine–Hanoi Medical University Hospital, reviewed retrospectively and classified into groups including healthy fathers, hypogonadal men, unexplained infertile men, men with unknown fertility, testicular pathologies and other andrological conditions. The reference figure comes from the healthy-fathers subgroup only; that subgroup's own N is not documented in the record, and the 24,440 headline N is the clinic population, never the reference N.
cards.result: The mean testicular volume of the healthy-fathers subgroup was 13.64 ± 3.44 mL (left testis 13.94 ± 3.72 mL; right testis 13.34 ± 3.61 mL; P < 0.001 for the side difference). Hypogonadal men and unexplained infertile men had significantly smaller testicular sizes than healthy fathers. Testicular size was negatively correlated with LH (Rho = −0.16) and FSH (Rho = −0.33) (both P < 0.001) and positively correlated with testosterone after adjustment for confounders; volume was independent of age and smoking habits.
cards.watchOut: Dataset kind matters: this is a retrospective clinic-attendee review, not a screened healthy-volunteer study — men attending an andrology service differ from the general population, and the healthy-fathers mean is a reference-like figure, printed with that provenance and never with the 24,440 headline N attached.
cards.source: Nguyen Hoai B et al. Ultrasonic testicular size of 24,440 adult Vietnamese men and the correlation with age and hormonal profiles. Andrologia. 2022. PMID: 34961956. cards.headline: Somali reference-interval study (Osman 2026): 212 sonographically normal men — means 10.61 (right) / 10.19 (left) mL, 95% reference intervals 5.7–18.0 / 5.2–17.0 mL, minimal detectable asymmetry difference 4.1 mL
cards.summary: Somali reference-interval study (Osman 2026): 212 sonographically normal men — means 10.61 (right) / 10.19 (left) mL, 95% reference intervals 5.7–18.0 / 5.2–17.0 mL, minimal detectable asymmetry difference 4.1 mL
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (retrospective ultrasound reference-interval derivation)
cards.people: 212 sonographically normal Somali men aged 18–84 at Sahan Diagnostic Center, Mogadishu (June 2022 to December 2025), reviewed retrospectively; volumes calculated with the standard ellipsoid formula; reference intervals derived as 2.5th–97.5th percentiles.
cards.result: Mean testicular volumes were 10.61 ± 3.07 mL (right) and 10.19 ± 3.02 mL (left), with a median of 10.0 mL for both. The 95% reference intervals were 5.7–18.0 mL (right) and 5.2–17.0 mL (left). The right testis was significantly larger than the left (P < 0.001) and no significant correlation with age was observed. The minimal detectable difference for asymmetry was 4.1 mL. Cross-population comparisons in the study were large (Cohen's d = 1.90 versus European, 1.88 versus West African and 0.76–2.01 versus East and Southeast Asian cohorts, as published). The authors present these as the first Somali-specific ultrasound benchmarks, established to prevent misapplication of non-representative global norms.
cards.watchOut: The smallest dataset (N = 212) and retrospective, from men attending a diagnostic centre whose scans were sonographically normal — its intervals are the widest relative to its mean, and its ~10.4 mL average shows how far a European-derived lower limit (11–12 mL) would misclassify men in this population.
cards.source: Osman KA et al. Normal Reference Values for Testicular Volume in Adult Somali Men: A Retrospective Study. Research and reports in urology. 2026. PMID: 42327362. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: testicular volume reference values are population property — means of ~17 mL (European fertile men), ~13.6 mL (Vietnamese healthy fathers) and ~10.4 mL (Somali men) mean no interval on this shelf is universal
cards.summary: Synthesis: testicular volume reference values are population property — means of ~17 mL (European fertile men), ~13.6 mL (Vietnamese healthy fathers) and ~10.4 mL (Somali men) mean no interval on this shelf is universal
cards.people: Synthesis of the three primary datasets carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (reproductive sections; the framing is brief and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature). The prospective EAA standardisation study (248 healthy fertile men) gives mean ~17 mL and lower reference limits of 12 mL (right) / 11 mL (left), with ultrasound ellipsoid-formula volume correlating best with Prader-orchidometer volume. The Vietnamese clinic dataset's healthy-fathers subgroup gives 13.64 ± 3.44 mL, and the Somali interval study (212 men) gives means of 10.61 / 10.19 mL with 95% intervals of 5.7–18.0 / 5.2–17.0 mL and a 4.1 mL minimal detectable asymmetry. The EAA overview paper (PMID 35930758, 2022) reports this same 248-man cohort and is counted once — it is not carded as a separate dataset. Semen characteristics in fertile men are a different measurement from the same territory, built at pack #7086 (cross-point only). PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: three datasets agree that ultrasound volume is measurable and side-asymmetric, but only one is a prospective standardisation study, two are retrospective clinic-based derivations, and the between-population spread is larger than any within-population interval is wide.
cards.watchOut: Never present one population's limits as universal: applying the European 11–12 mL lower limits to the Somali distribution would label a large share of normal men hypotrophic. Each card's population and dataset kind are part of the value.
